conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What kind of conditions are ADHD and autism (ASD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Lifelong neurodevelopmental conditions with features present from early childhood that persist into adulthood.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Why are ADHD and autism often diagnosed late in adults?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: They are frequently underdiagnosed, especially in women/girls, who more often mask or camouflage their difficulties.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: How are ADHD and autism diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Clinically, by specialist assessment using history across settings, developmental history and collateral information — there is no single confirmatory test.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What is meant by high co-occurrence in neurodevelopmental conditions?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: ADHD and autism commonly occur together, and both overlap with anxiety, depression, substance misuse, sleep problems and learning differences.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What common comorbidities should you screen for in ADHD and autism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Anxiety, depression, substance misuse and sleep problems (plus emotional dysregulation in ADHD).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What does a neurodiversity-affirming, strengths-based approach mean?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Care focuses on function, environment and wellbeing rather than “curing” the person
  • it respects abilities, autonomy and language preferences and makes reasonable adjustments.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Define adult ADHD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: A neurodevelopmental condition with a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, present before age 12, across ≥2 settings, causing functional impairment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What are the DSM-5 core requirements for ADHD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity present before age 12, in ≥2 settings, causing functional impairment, not better explained by another condition.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: How does hyperactivity typically change in adults with ADHD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Overt physical hyperactivity often becomes inner restlessness or a feeling of being constantly “on the go”.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: List typical inattention features of adult ADHD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Poor sustained focus
  • disorganisation
  • forgetfulness
  • procrastination
  • losing things
  • and difficulty finishing tasks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: List typical impulsivity features of adult ADHD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Interrupting others
  • impulsive decisions (e.g. spending, driving)
  • impatience and blurting out.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What are the three presentations of ADHD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Predominantly inattentive
  • predominantly hyperactive-impulsive
  • and combined.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Which ADHD presentation is most often missed and in whom?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Predominantly inattentive presentation — fewer disruptive signs; commonly missed, and a common picture in women.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What does assessment of adult ADHD involve?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Specialist clinical interview with history and rating scales, developmental/collateral history, confirmation of ≥2 settings and impairment, and consideration of differentials.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Which differentials/comorbidities must be considered in ADHD assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Mood and anxiety disorders
  • substance misuse
  • sleep disorders
  • and organic causes such as thyroid dysfunction.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What non-pharmacological support does NICE recommend in adult ADHD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Psychoeducation and environmental modifications/reasonable adjustments for EVERYONE. A structured, ADHD-focused psychological intervention (which may include CBT) is not universal — it is for those who decline or cannot tolerate medication, or who have residual symptoms or impairment despite it.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What is first-line pharmacological treatment for adult ADHD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Lisdexamfetamine OR methylphenidate — equally first-line, chosen on patient factors and preference. Switch to the other after a 6-week trial at adequate dose if benefit is insufficient. Dexamfetamine is NOT first-line: it is for someone responding to lisdexamfetamine who cannot tolerate its longer duration of effect.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What is the non-stimulant option in ADULT ADHD — and what is the trap?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Atomoxetine, where stimulants are unsuitable, not tolerated, or have failed separate 6-week trials of both. The trap is guanfacine: it is licensed only for ages 6–17, so it is a child/adolescent option and NOT a NICE-recommended adult one.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What is required before and during stimulant treatment for ADHD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Baseline blood pressure, heart rate and cardiac history/examination. A routine ECG is NOT required if these are normal — only for features such as congenital heart disease, exertional syncope, palpitations or a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40. Then monitor BP, HR and weight, watch appetite and sleep, and review annually.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What should be monitored during ADHD stimulant treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Blood pressure, heart rate and weight
  • also watch for appetite suppression, sleep disturbance, and misuse/diversion risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Why is misuse/diversion relevant in ADHD prescribing?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Stimulants carry a risk of misuse and diversion; atomoxetine (a non-stimulant) may be preferred where this is a concern.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What driving considerations apply in adult ADHD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: ADHD is not automatically notifiable. The duty to tell the DVLA arises only if the condition or its treatment affects safe driving, and it rests with the DRIVER — you advise them of it, and notify the DVLA yourself only if they cannot or will not (GMC). Amfetamines are specified drugs under the drug-driving offence, so a patient should be able to show the stimulant is prescribed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Define autism (ASD).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: A lifelong neurodevelopmental condition with differences in social communication/interaction plus restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, present from early development.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What are the two domains of the autism dyad (DSM-5)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• (1) Persistent differences/deficits in social communication and interaction
  • (2) restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities (RRBs).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Give examples of restricted, repetitive behaviours (RRBs) in autism.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Insistence on sameness/routines
  • intense focused interests
  • repetitive movements or speech (stimming)
  • and sensory hyper- or hypo-sensitivity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What sensory differences occur in autism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Hyper- or hypo-sensitivity to stimuli such as sound, light, touch or taste.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What is masking/camouflaging in autism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Consciously or unconsciously hiding autistic traits to fit in; more common in women, it can make a person appear to cope and delays diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What is diagnostic overshadowing?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Attributing a person's symptoms to a known condition (e.g. a diagnosed mental illness) and thereby missing autism or another underlying diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What language do many autistic people prefer, and why does it matter?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Identity-first language (“autistic person”) is often preferred; asking and respecting individual preference is part of respectful, affirming care.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What does specialist autism assessment involve?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: A multidisciplinary clinical assessment with developmental and collateral history, using structured tools (e.g. ADOS, ADI-R), and consideration of co-occurring conditions.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Which conditions commonly co-occur with autism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Anxiety
  • depression
  • ADHD
  • epilepsy
  • GI problems
  • sleep difficulties
  • and a higher suicide risk
  • intellectual disability may coexist.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Which genetic conditions are associated with autism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Fragile X syndrome and tuberous sclerosis — though most autism is idiopathic.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: Is autism caused by vaccines?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: No. Autism is not caused by the MMR or any vaccine — this myth arose from fraudulent, retracted research and has been thoroughly discredited.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What is the core principle of autism management in adults?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: There is no cure and autism is not an illness to be cured — support focuses on function, environment and wellbeing, and on treating co-occurring conditions on their own merits.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What does autism management in adults include?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back:
• Reasonable adjustments
  • structured/predictable environments
  • communication support
  • psychosocial support
  • and treatment of co-occurring conditions
  • avoid unnecessary medication.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: When might antipsychotics be used in autism, and for how long?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Never for the core features. For behaviour that challenges, address triggers and try a psychosocial intervention first; an antipsychotic is specialist-initiated, reviewed at 3–4 weeks and STOPPED by 6 weeks if there is no clear response. Autistic people are prescribed antipsychotics far more often than the general population, and there is a national programme to stop that over-medication.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.front: What legal protections and duties apply to autistic people in the UK?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Adult ADHD & Aut.back: Autism CAN amount to a disability — a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010 — where it has a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities; a formal diagnosis is not required. Healthcare providers have an anticipatory duty to make reasonable adjustments. The Autism Act 2009 requires a national adult autism strategy, and CQC-registered providers must train staff on learning disability and autism.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is gender identity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: A person's internal sense of their own gender.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is gender incongruence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: A marked and persistent mismatch between a person's experienced gender and their sex assigned at birth.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is gender dysphoria?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: The clinically significant distress or impairment that can arise from gender incongruence.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Is being transgender a mental illness?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: No.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: How does ICD-11 classify gender incongruence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: It moved gender incongruence OUT of the mental disorders chapter, into the chapter 'Conditions related to sexual health' — reducing stigma while retaining a code, which is what preserves access to funded specialist care. Gender-variant behaviour or preferences alone are not a basis for the diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What term does DSM-5 use, and what does it emphasise?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: 'Gender dysphoria' — it names the distress, not the identity itself, as the clinical focus.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What does cisgender mean?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Gender identity matches the sex assigned at birth.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What does transgender mean?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Define trans man and trans woman.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back:
• A trans man was assigned female at birth and has a male identity
  • a trans woman was assigned male at birth and has a female identity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What does non-binary mean?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: A gender identity outside the male/female binary.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Which two concepts must be kept separate from gender identity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back:
• Sexual orientation
  • and a difference/disorder of sex development (DSD/intersex).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Which mental-health and neurodevelopmental conditions are over-represented in transgender people?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back:
• Depression, anxiety, self-harm and suicidal ideation
  • eating-disorder symptoms
  • and autistic traits, markedly so among adolescents referred to gender services.
Stigma, discrimination and minority stress contribute, but co-occurring difficulties are also common in their own right and may precede the gender-related distress — assess and treat them on their own merits.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What must always be assessed given the elevated risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Mood, self-harm and suicide risk — and any comorbid mental illness must be treated.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Where are patients referred for specialist gender care?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back:
• Adults: a specialist gender service, often called a Gender Identity Clinic (GIC) — waits are commonly several years.
  • Under-18s: a regional NHS children and young people's gender service, accessed through a national referral route (GP, paediatrics or CAMHS).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is the GP's role in gender dysphoria?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: To be supportive and non-judgemental, refer, manage comorbidities and general health, use the correct name and pronouns, and take part in shared-care prescribing and monitoring BY AGREEMENT with the specialist service. Work within your competence — but unfamiliarity is not a reason to refuse care: seek specialist advice. Do not enter shared care with unregulated providers, and do not support private or unregulated hormone prescribing for under-18s.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What must be offered before starting any fertility-affecting treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Fertility counselling and the option of gamete (egg/sperm) storage.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Is conversion (reparative) therapy offered for gender dysphoria?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: No — it is unethical, ineffective and harmful, is prohibited by UK professional bodies and not offered in the NHS, and doing it would be a fitness-to-practise matter. Note the legal precision: it is not currently a standalone criminal offence in the UK (legislation has been drafted but not enacted), though specific acts may already be criminal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is the feminising hormone therapy for trans women?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Oestrogen, usually with androgen suppression — an anti-androgen or a GnRH analogue — which is stopped after orchidectomy. Transdermal oestradiol is preferred where VTE risk is higher.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is the masculinising hormone therapy for trans men?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Testosterone. Note it is NOT a contraceptive — amenorrhoea is not anovulation, so contraception is still needed if pregnancy is to be avoided (progestogen-only or intrauterine rather than combined methods).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is a key blood-test complication to monitor with testosterone therapy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Polycythaemia (a rising haematocrit) — monitor the FBC.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is a key thrombotic risk to monitor with oestrogen therapy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Venous thromboembolism (VTE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is the current UK position on puberty blockers (GnRH analogues) for gender incongruence in under-18s?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back:
Not routinely commissioned by the NHS, and prohibited on private prescription for this indication under UK-wide legislation. Three exceptions:
  • people already established on treatment may continue
  • other indications are unaffected (e.g. central precocious puberty, endometriosis)
  • and access is possible through an approved clinical trial — now the only route for a new patient.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Which drug class suppresses puberty, and is it available for gender incongruence in UK under-18s?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: GnRH analogues. Not available as routine treatment for this indication in the UK — access only through an approved clinical trial. Other indications, such as central precocious puberty, are unaffected.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is the ongoing cancer-screening principle for transgender patients?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back:
Screening follows the organs a person has — but invitations follow the sex registered with the GP, so it often has to be arranged manually.
  • A trans man registered as male stays eligible for cervical screening but is not invited automatically
  • a trans woman registered as female may be invited for cervical screening she does not need.
Changing the recorded gender means a new NHS number and a new record, which breaks automatic recall.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Name the main types of gender-affirming surgery.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back:
• Non-surgical: speech and language therapy for voice and communication, part of the specialist MDT.
  • Surgical: chest/'top', genital/'bottom', and facial or voice-modifying procedures — NHS availability varies between these.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: What is meant by social transition?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: Living in one's experienced gender through changes in name, pronouns, presentation and role (as opposed to medical transition with hormones/surgery).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.front: Under which UK law is gender reassignment a protected characteristic?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Gender Dysphoria.back: The Equality Act 2010 — gender reassignment is a protected characteristic. Separately, the Gender Recognition Act 2004 provides the route to legal gender recognition via a gender recognition certificate, which is NOT required to access NHS gender services or to change name, title or recorded gender on NHS records.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What causes the Wernicke–Korsakoff spectrum?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency — classically in chronic alcohol excess, but also in malnutrition, hyperemesis, prolonged vomiting and bariatric surgery.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the relationship between Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Two ends of one disease process — Wernicke's is the acute, reversible phase; Korsakoff's is the chronic, often irreversible amnestic aftermath of untreated/under-treated Wernicke's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the organising principle of the Wernicke–Korsakoff spectrum?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Same deficiency, different stage — Wernicke's is an emergency you can reverse (treat now with parenteral thiamine); Korsakoff's is the permanent memory deficit you were trying to prevent.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the hallmark of Wernicke's encephalopathy vs Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back:
• Wernicke's = the classic triad (confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia)
  • Korsakoff's = profound anterograde ± retrograde amnesia with confabulation and apathy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the single most important 'never miss' rule in an at-risk patient?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Give parenteral thiamine BEFORE any glucose/carbohydrate load — a glucose infusion into a thiamine-deplete patient can precipitate Wernicke's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why must Wernicke's be treated empirically on suspicion?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: The full triad appears in only ~10-16% of cases, so it is a clinical diagnosis treated on any one feature in an at-risk patient.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is Wernicke's encephalopathy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: An acute neurological emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most often in chronic alcohol misuse — reversible if treated promptly, but progressing to irreversible Korsakoff's if untreated.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back:
• Confusion
  • ophthalmoplegia/oculomotor signs (nystagmus, CN VI palsy)
  • ataxia (broad-based gait).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How common is the complete triad in Wernicke's, and what is the implication?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: It is present in only ~10–16% — so do NOT wait for all three; any one feature in an at-risk patient warrants treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the commonest oculomotor sign in Wernicke's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Nystagmus (also lateral rectus/CN VI palsy and conjugate gaze palsy).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What other features (beyond the triad) can occur in Wernicke's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back:
• Hypothermia
  • hypotension
  • reduced consciousness/coma
  • and peripheral neuropathy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why is thiamine essential — the biochemical mechanism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (Krebs cycle); deficiency impairs glucose oxidation → energy failure in high-demand brain regions.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Which brain regions are damaged in Wernicke's, and what is the memory link?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: The mammillary bodies and medial thalamus (± periaqueductal grey); the mammillary bodies are part of the Papez circuit, so their damage explains the amnesia of Korsakoff's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why is glucose dangerous before thiamine?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Giving glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient consumes the remaining thiamine to metabolise it, precipitating or worsening Wernicke's — so give thiamine before/with glucose (but still treat hypoglycaemia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: List the non-alcohol at-risk groups for Wernicke's.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back:
• Malnutrition/starvation and anorexia nervosa
  • hyperemesis gravidarum
  • prolonged vomiting
  • bariatric surgery/malabsorption
  • refeeding syndrome
  • dialysis
  • malignancy
  • and prolonged parenteral nutrition without supplementation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How is Wernicke's diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Clinically — treatment must not wait for tests (a response to thiamine can itself be diagnostic); MRI (mammillary body/thalamic changes) is supportive but negative imaging does not exclude it.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why must magnesium be checked and corrected in Wernicke's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Magnesium is required to activate thiamine and for the thiamine-dependent enzymes, so thiamine may fail to work until hypomagnesaemia is corrected.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the Caine criteria for Wernicke's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Dietary deficiency, oculomotor signs, cerebellar signs, and altered mental state OR mild memory impairment — two or more of these support the diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the acute treatment of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Immediate parenteral high-dose thiamine (Pabrinex, parenteral B-vitamins) — 2-3 pairs (1 pair = 250 mg thiamine) three times daily for 3-5 days, continued while improvement continues, given before or with glucose; then oral thiamine 100 mg three times daily. IV is preferred, IM if there is no IV access.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why is thiamine given parenterally (not orally) acutely?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol misusers, so parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) is needed acutely.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What safety consideration applies to IV Pabrinex?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: There is a small risk of anaphylaxis — give it by infusion in 50-100 mL over 30 minutes, with resuscitation facilities available.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Who should receive prophylactic thiamine?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: All patients undergoing alcohol withdrawal or otherwise at risk (malnutrition, refeeding risk). Parenteral (1 pair of Pabrinex once daily for 3-5 days) in higher-risk patients — acute withdrawal in hospital, decompensated liver disease, or malnourished or at risk of malnutrition — and oral (thiamine 100 mg two to three times daily) in lower-risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: A chronic amnestic disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, characterised by profound memory impairment with confabulation — most often the irreversible sequel of untreated Wernicke's encephalopathy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the 'core concept' of Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: It is the chronic, largely irreversible 'memory' end of the thiamine-deficiency spectrum — a selective, dense amnesia in an otherwise relatively intact patient — and it is PREVENTABLE by treating Wernicke's promptly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What are the characteristic features of Korsakoff's syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back:
• Anterograde amnesia (dominant)
  • retrograde amnesia
  • and confabulation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the dominant, most disabling feature of Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Anterograde amnesia — an inability to form/acquire NEW memories.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the pattern of retrograde amnesia in Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Loss of memories from before onset, often with a temporal gradient (recent memories lost more than remote ones).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is confabulation, and is it deliberate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: The unconscious filling of memory gaps with fabricated/distorted information — the patient genuinely believes it; it is NOT deliberate lying.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Why is Korsakoff's described as a 'selective' amnesia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Memory is devastated, but consciousness, attention, immediate memory and other cognitive domains (and procedural memory) are relatively preserved.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How is Korsakoff's distinguished from delirium?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Korsakoff's has a CLEAR sensorium (clear consciousness, preserved attention), whereas delirium has clouded consciousness, inattention and fluctuation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How is Korsakoff's distinguished from dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Korsakoff's is a SELECTIVE amnesia with other cognition preserved, whereas dementia is a global, progressive cognitive decline.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Which brain structures are damaged in Korsakoff's, and what is the memory link?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: The mammillary bodies and medial/dorsomedial thalamus — the mammillary bodies are a key node of the Papez circuit (hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate), essential for memory consolidation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the biochemical mechanism underlying Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; deficiency causes energy failure in high-demand structures (mammillary bodies, medial thalamus).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What are the causes of Korsakoff's beyond alcohol?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back:
Any cause of thiamine deficiency —
  • malnutrition/starvation
  • anorexia nervosa
  • hyperemesis gravidarum
  • bariatric surgery
  • prolonged vomiting
  • malabsorption
  • and refeeding.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: How is Korsakoff's diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: Clinically — a chronic selective amnestic syndrome with confabulation in a patient at risk of thiamine deficiency (usually after a Wernicke's episode); MRI may show mammillary body atrophy and cognitive testing shows impaired delayed recall with preserved immediate memory/attention.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the overarching management principle for Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: It is largely irreversible → the priority is PREVENTION (treat Wernicke's promptly), plus thiamine replacement, abstinence and supportive care.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: What is the management of established Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back:
• Thiamine replacement (still given — modest improvement/halts progression)
  • alcohol abstinence and nutritional support
  • plus supportive/rehabilitative care
  • cognitive support
  • and often long-term supervision (many can't live independently).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.front: Should full recovery be expected in Korsakoff's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsako.back: No — unlike Wernicke's (reversible), Korsakoff's deficits usually persist; it is largely irreversible.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: A sudden, temporary episode of profound memory loss — predominantly anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) — with other cognitive functions preserved, resolving completely within 24 hours.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What is the 'core concept' defining TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Its transience and selectivity — a dramatic but isolated amnesia in an otherwise alert, oriented-to-self, fully-functioning person, that resolves fully; the clinical priority is to distinguish it from dangerous mimics.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: Who typically gets TGA, and what is its prognosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Middle-aged/older adults (50–70); usually a one-off event with an excellent prognosis and low recurrence.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What is the high-yield triad defining TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back:
• Isolated amnesia
  • NO focal neurological signs
  • full recovery within 24 hours.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What is the classic clinical picture of TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Sudden anterograde amnesia — the person cannot form new memories, leading to repetitive questioning ('Where am I? What are we doing?') despite being answered.

Personal identity (knows who they are), alertness/consciousness, attention, language, and complex/learned tasks (can still drive or cook) — the amnesia is selective. The patient must not drive until the episode has fully resolved.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What is a DEFINING feature of TGA regarding neurology?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: No focal neurological deficit — no weakness, sensory loss, aphasia or visual field defect.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How long does TGA last, and what is the person left with?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: It resolves completely within 24 hours (usually 4–8h), leaving a permanent gap for the episode itself.

A trigger shortly before onset —
  • sudden immersion in cold/hot water
  • physical exertion
  • emotional stress
  • Valsalva-type activities (straining, sexual intercourse)
  • or sudden temperature change.
TGA has NO focal neurology; the presence of focal deficits (weakness, aphasia) points to stroke/TIA, which needs urgent assessment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How is TGA distinguished from transient epileptic amnesia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Transient epileptic amnesia causes brief, recurrent episodes (often on waking) with epileptic features → EEG; TGA is usually a single, longer (up to 24h) episode.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: How is TGA distinguished from dissociative amnesia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back: Dissociative amnesia often involves loss of personal identity ('who am I?'), whereas in TGA the person KNOWS who they are.

• Clinically (characteristic syndrome + preserved other functions + resolution)
  • neurological exam must show no focal signs
  • check glucose (exclude hypoglycaemia), U&E, FBC
  • imaging/EEG only for atypical/focal/recurrent features.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.front: What are the Hodges and Warlow diagnostic criteria for TGA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global.back:
• A witnessed attack
  • anterograde amnesia
  • no clouding of consciousness or loss of personal identity
  • no focal neurological/epileptic features
  • resolution within 24 hours
  • and no recent head injury/active epilepsy.
Exclude the mimics, then reassure — it is self-limiting with an excellent prognosis and needs no specific treatment; manage vascular risk factors generally.
TGA = transient with full recovery; Korsakoff's = chronic, irreversible amnesia with confabulation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is a substance use disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: A pattern of substance use leading to dependence, harm or impaired control, despite negative consequences.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the 'core concept' framework for substance use disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Identify the substance, then separate the three clinical problems that need different management: (1) intoxication/overdose, (2) withdrawal, and (3) long-term dependence/relapse prevention — the substance × problem grid.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the two high-yield contrasts between alcohol/benzodiazepine and opioid problems?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• Alcohol + benzodiazepine WITHDRAWAL is dangerous (seizures, delirium) → needs medically-assisted withdrawal
  • opioid withdrawal is miserable but rarely life-threatening, whereas opioid OVERDOSE is the killer (respiratory depression).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How does alcohol intoxication present, and how is severe alcohol overdose dangerous?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Disinhibition, ataxia and slurred speech; in severe cases coma and respiratory depression — plus hypoglycaemia and aspiration of vomit, which is why glucose is checked and the airway protected.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How does opioid overdose present, and what is the antidote?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Reduced consciousness, reduced respiratory rate and pinpoint pupils → reversed with naloxone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the features of dependence (ICD framework)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
Features of the ICD-10 dependence syndrome — three or more present together at some point in the past year:
  • a strong desire or compulsion to use (craving)
  • impaired control
  • tolerance
  • a withdrawal state on stopping
  • salience (the substance takes priority)
  • and persistent use despite harm.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the memory anchor for the features of dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• Craving
  • control loss
  • tolerance
  • withdrawal
  • salience
  • persistence despite harm.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the mechanism of alcohol withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Chronic alcohol enhances GABA and inhibits NMDA/glutamate, so the CNS adapts by downregulating GABA and upregulating NMDA; on stopping, this adaptation is unopposed → CNS hyperexcitability with sympathetic overactivity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why are benzodiazepines the treatment for alcohol withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Because withdrawal is driven by reduced GABA (inhibitory) activity, and benzodiazepines boost GABA, restoring inhibition.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What happens 6–12 hours after the last drink?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• Tremor
  • sweating
  • tachycardia
  • anxiety
  • and nausea.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is alcoholic hallucinosis, and when does it occur?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: At ~12-24 hours — classically AUDITORY hallucinations but they may be visual; the discriminator is CLEAR CONSCIOUSNESS. Clouded consciousness with disorientation and autonomic instability means delirium tremens.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: When is the peak seizure risk in alcohol withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: At ~36 hours ('rum fits').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: When does delirium tremens occur, and what are its features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: At 48-72 hours — coarse tremor, confusion/delirium, agitation, VISUAL hallucinations, delusions, fever, tachycardia and autonomic instability; a medical emergency, with mortality of the order of 15% untreated and still a few per cent even with treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the first-line drug for assisted alcohol withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: A long-acting benzodiazepine — chlordiazepoxide (first-line) or diazepam — in a reducing regimen over ~5–7 days.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which benzodiazepine is preferred for alcohol withdrawal in significant liver impairment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Lorazepam (less accumulation, no active metabolites).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How is delirium tremens managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Oral lorazepam first-line; if symptoms persist or oral medication is declined, parenteral lorazepam or haloperidol (NICE). Withdrawal seizures are treated with a fast-acting benzodiazepine — phenytoin is not used.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why must thiamine always be given in alcohol withdrawal, by what route, and when relative to glucose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: To prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus — the full triad is present in only a minority, so any one feature in a drinker should trigger treatment; untreated it progresses to Korsakoff's syndrome with anterograde amnesia and confabulation). Give parenteral thiamine, as Pabrinex IM or IV, where Wernicke's is suspected or the person is high risk; oral thiamine for prophylaxis in lower-risk harmful drinkers. It must be given BEFORE glucose, because a glucose load in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the three relapse-prevention drugs for alcohol dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Acamprosate and naltrexone are first-line alongside psychosocial support; disulfiram is second-line where those are unsuitable or the patient prefers it and understands the risks (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the mechanism and key note for acamprosate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Modulates glutamate/GABA to reduce craving. It is renally excreted, so it is preferred in mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment — but avoid it in severe hepatic impairment and in significant renal impairment. Started after abstinence is achieved.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the mechanism and key caution for naltrexone in alcohol dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: An opioid antagonist that reduces the reward of drinking; avoid in opioid users (precipitates withdrawal) and use with caution in liver disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the mechanism of disulfiram, and its cautions?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde builds up → an unpleasant reaction (flushing, vomiting, headache) if alcohol is taken. A second-line deterrent needing a motivated patient: the person must be alcohol-free for at least 24 hours before starting, and the reaction can occur up to 2 weeks after the last dose (watch for alcohol in food, mouthwash and medicines). Avoid in cardiac disease, psychosis, severe hypertension and previous stroke.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the classic triad of opioid overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• Reduced consciousness
  • reduced respiratory rate
  • pinpoint pupils (miosis).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the fatal effect in opioid overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Respiratory depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the management of opioid overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Naloxone, an opioid antagonist, titrated to respiratory function — 400 micrograms IV initially, repeated every 2-3 minutes until breathing is adequate (IM if no IV access). In a dependent patient start low to avoid precipitating acute withdrawal (BNF). The aim is adequate ventilation, not full arousal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why may repeated doses or an infusion of naloxone be needed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Naloxone has a SHORT half-life, so the patient may re-sedate as it wears off (opioids outlast it). Observe for at least 6 hours after the last dose and never discharge straight after a good response; consider an infusion for long-acting opioids such as methadone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What harm-reduction measure exists for opioid overdose in at-risk patients?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Take-home naloxone (intramuscular or intranasal), supplied with training for the person and their contacts — call 999, because it wears off before the opioid does.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the features of opioid withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
Flu-like —
  • agitation
  • sweating
  • rhinorrhoea
  • lacrimation
  • yawning
  • DILATED pupils (mydriasis)
  • abdominal cramps
  • diarrhoea
  • piloerection
  • and myalgia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is the key pupil contrast between opioid overdose and withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Overdose = pinpoint pupils (miosis); withdrawal = dilated pupils (mydriasis).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Is opioid withdrawal dangerous?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: It is very unpleasant (flu-like) but rarely life-threatening — unlike opioid overdose, which is the killer.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is lofexidine, and its role in opioid withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: An α2-agonist used to treat opioid withdrawal symptoms. Methadone or buprenorphine are first-line for opioid detoxification; lofexidine is an option for mild or uncertain dependence, a short detoxification, or if the person declines an opioid substitute (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What symptomatic treatments are used for opioid withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• Lofexidine (α2-agonist) for withdrawal symptoms
  • loperamide (diarrhoea)
  • antiemetics (nausea)
  • and benzodiazepines (agitation).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What drugs are used for opioid detox/maintenance (substitution)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Methadone (a full agonist; prolongs QTc, and has a long half-life so it accumulates — most dangerous during induction, so start low, titrate slowly and supervise consumption) OR buprenorphine (a partial agonist).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why must buprenorphine be started once the patient is in withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: As a partial agonist it can precipitate withdrawal if given too soon after a full agonist, so it is started only once objective withdrawal is established — typically at least 6-12 hours after a short-acting opioid such as heroin, and longer (at least 24-72 hours) after methadone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What is used for relapse prevention after opioid detox?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Naltrexone, an opioid antagonist that blocks the effect of opioids. The patient must be opioid-free for about 7-10 days first or it precipitates acute withdrawal, and must be warned that tolerance is lost after detox, so relapse at the previous dose can be fatal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What harm-reduction measures apply to opioid dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• Needle exchange
  • blood-borne virus testing (HIV, hepatitis B and C)
  • and hepatitis B vaccination (plus hepatitis A where indicated).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Give examples of stimulant drugs of misuse.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Cocaine and amphetamines.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How does stimulant intoxication present?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• Agitation
  • raised HR/BP
  • mydriasis (dilated pupils)
  • hyperthermia
  • a risk of MI/stroke/arrhythmia
  • and stimulant psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Is there a substitution therapy for stimulant dependence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: No — there is no substitution therapy; management is supportive plus psychological, with benzodiazepines for agitation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How is stimulant intoxication/agitation managed acutely?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Supportively, with benzodiazepines for agitation and the cardiovascular effects — plus active cooling for hyperthermia, which is the main driver of death. Avoid beta-blockers in cocaine toxicity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What are the key problems with cannabis use?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Dependence and an increased risk of anxiety and psychosis; management is psychological.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Why is benzodiazepine dependence significant, and how does its withdrawal compare to alcohol?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Dependence is common, and withdrawal is like alcohol — it can cause seizures and be dangerous.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: How is benzodiazepine dependence managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Gradual dose reduction — switch to a long-acting agent (e.g. diazepam), then taper slowly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which two substances share a dangerous, seizure-prone withdrawal?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Alcohol and benzodiazepines.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What should the history cover in a substance use assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• The substance(s), quantity/frequency, route and duration
  • features of dependence
  • previous withdrawal (seizures/DTs)
  • overdose history
  • injecting and blood-borne virus risk
  • and the forensic/social context.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which screening tools are used for alcohol?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• AUDIT is the UK-recommended screening tool, with AUDIT-C and FAST as brief versions (CAGE is a legacy 4-item screen still widely quoted)
  • SADQ measures severity of dependence
  • CIWA-Ar measures withdrawal severity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What does AUDIT assess, and what are its thresholds?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: It screens for problematic alcohol use over 10 items: 8 or more suggests hazardous or increasing-risk drinking, 16 or more harmful drinking, and 20 or more possible dependence, prompting assessment for assisted withdrawal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What does the CIWA-Ar score measure, and how is it used?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: The severity of alcohol withdrawal — broadly under 8 mild, 8-15 moderate, and 15 or more severe with a high risk of seizures and delirium tremens. It guides symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing, which is used in inpatient or residential settings with trained staff, not in the community.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which bloods are checked in a substance use assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back:
• FBC
  • U&E
  • LFTs + GGT
  • clotting
  • glucose
  • and a blood-borne virus screen (HIV, hepatitis B/C).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: Which blood results suggest chronic alcohol use?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: A raised MCV and a raised GGT.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What should always be screened for alongside a substance use disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Comorbid mental illness and risk — including self-harm/suicide risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.front: What examination findings are looked for in a substance use assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Di.back: Signs of chronic use and liver disease (and evidence of injecting/blood-borne virus risk).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What are somatisation / medically unexplained symptom disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: A group of disorders where physical symptoms — whether or not they are explained by organic disease — cause distress or impairment, or where the psychological response to them is disproportionate, sitting at the interface of mind and body. UK practice increasingly prefers 'persistent physical symptoms' to 'medically unexplained symptoms'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What two questions organise the whole somatisation group?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: (1) Is the patient CONSCIOUSLY producing/feigning the symptoms? and (2) if feigning, is there EXTERNAL gain? These two questions separate every diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: If symptoms are NOT consciously produced, which group of disorders is it?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: The non-feigned somatic disorders — somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder and functional neurological disorder — the patient is genuinely experiencing them and is NOT faking. Note that FND is diagnosed by positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency, not by judging whether symptoms are consciously produced.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: If symptoms are consciously produced and the gain is the sick role, what is the diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Factitious disorder (Munchausen's syndrome) — deliberate feigning for internal/psychological gain (to be a patient).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: If symptoms are consciously produced for external/tangible gain, what is it?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Malingering — deliberate feigning for external reward (money, drugs, time off, avoiding prosecution); NOT a psychiatric diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is the key axis distinguishing factitious disorder from malingering?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Both involve deliberate feigning — they differ only in MOTIVE: factitious = the sick role (internal); malingering = external reward.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What are these disorders now called?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: The 'somatic symptom and related disorders'; the classification the NHS is adopting groups most of them as a single category, bodily distress disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is somatic symptom disorder (old name: somatisation disorder)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: One or more distressing physical symptoms PLUS disproportionate thoughts, feelings or behaviour about them, usually persisting more than 6 months. The symptoms may or may not be explained by a medical condition — it can be diagnosed alongside genuine organic disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is illness anxiety disorder (also called hypochondriasis)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: An excessive preoccupation with HAVING a serious illness (e.g. cancer), despite minimal or no actual symptoms — with 'doctor shopping'. Hypochondriasis remains a current term and is now grouped with the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is the high-yield distinction between somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Somatic symptom disorder = distress about REAL symptoms (many, multi-system); illness anxiety disorder = FEAR of having a disease with few/no symptoms ('doctor shopping').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is functional neurological disorder (FND; old name: conversion disorder)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Neurological symptoms (motor/sensory loss, weakness, dissociative seizures, blindness) that are internally inconsistent with organic disease, often after a stressor, and NOT consciously produced. In UK practice it is a neurological diagnosis, usually made and explained by neurology.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is Hoover's sign, and what does it demonstrate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: A rule-IN sign for functional leg weakness — when the patient lifts the unaffected leg against resistance, you feel involuntary downward pressure (hip extension) in the 'paralysed' leg that was absent on direct testing, showing the motor pathway is intact and the weakness is functional. It rules in functional weakness but does not exclude coexisting neurological disease; the two often occur together.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is factitious disorder (Munchausen's syndrome)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Deliberately faking or inducing symptoms (e.g. injecting insulin, contaminating samples) for the sick role itself — no external reward.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen's by proxy)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Fabricating or inducing illness in another person, usually a child — known in UK safeguarding practice as fabricated or induced illness (FII). A safeguarding EMERGENCY: discuss with the safeguarding lead and refer urgently to children's social care.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: Why should over-investigation be avoided in somatoform disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Repeated tests reinforce illness behaviour and cause iatrogenic harm; the diagnosis should be a POSITIVE one, not endless exclusion — but new, changed or red-flag symptoms must still be assessed on their merits, as a functional diagnosis does not protect against later organic disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: Is 'no organic cause found' the same as 'faking'?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: No — the somatoform disorders are genuinely experienced; the diagnosis is positive, not merely one of exclusion, and the patient is NOT faking.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is the overarching management principle for the somatoform group?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back:
• A single, trusted clinician
  • limited investigation
  • validation of distress
  • and treatment of comorbidity
— NOT repeated referral/testing.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is the psychological mainstay of treatment for the somatoform disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: CBT — for somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder; in FND, CBT is used particularly for dissociative seizures, while specialist physiotherapy leads for functional motor symptoms.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: How is FND specifically managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back:
• A clear positive explanation
  • physiotherapy (for functional motor symptoms)
  • and MDT input

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: What is often the highest-yield intervention in somatoform disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Treating comorbid depression/anxiety (e.g. SSRI + psychological therapy) — very common and treatable.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: How is malingering 'managed'?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: It is not treated as an illness — manage the situation (don't provide the sought secondary gain), but consider genuine comorbidity. Malingering should only be considered where there is clear evidence of deliberate feigning; suspicion alone is not enough to label a patient.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.front: How is factitious disorder managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / M.back: Difficult to manage — avoid aggressive confrontation and take a non-judgemental approach, minimise iatrogenic harm from investigations, and involve psychiatry. Where the person is inducing dangerous illness, immediate physical safety and safeguarding come first.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: A transient, temporary inability to move or speak at the transition between sleep and wakefulness — on waking (hypnopompic) or, less often, on falling asleep (hypnagogic).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What is the mechanism of sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: It is the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep persisting briefly into wakefulness — the mind wakes before the body's REM atonia has switched off, making it benign and self-limiting.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What is the key distinction to make when assessing sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Isolated/benign sleep paralysis (occurs alone, often with sleep deprivation → reassurance) vs sleep paralysis as part of narcolepsy (with excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy and hypnagogic hallucinations → needs sleep studies).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: When should narcolepsy be suspected in a patient with sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: If it occurs WITH excessive daytime sleepiness + cataplexy + hypnagogic hallucinations, think narcolepsy — sleep paralysis is one of its four cardinal features.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: Why does REM atonia normally exist, and what goes wrong in sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: During REM sleep the skeletal muscles are normally paralysed (atonia) to prevent us acting out dreams; in sleep paralysis this atonia persists briefly into wakefulness, so the person is consciously aware but unable to move.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: How long does sleep paralysis last, and how does it resolve?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Seconds to a couple of minutes; it resolves spontaneously (or when the person is touched or spoken to).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: How is sleep paralysis the 'mirror image' of REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: In RBD the REM atonia is LOST (dreams are acted out); in sleep paralysis the atonia PERSISTS into wakefulness — both are disorders of REM-atonia timing.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What are the core clinical features of sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Transient paralysis of skeletal muscles on waking/falling asleep — conscious but unable to move or speak, with breathing and eye movements preserved and awareness intact.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What hallucinations characteristically occur in sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Vivid, frightening hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations — classically a sense of a threatening presence, pressure on the chest, or a figure (the 'Old Hag' phenomenon).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: Why does intact awareness help distinguish sleep paralysis from other events?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: The person is awake and aware throughout, distinguishing it from a seizure or a faint (syncope).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What are the common triggers/associations of sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back:
• Sleep deprivation and irregular sleep schedules (commonest — shift work, jet lag)
  • sleeping supine
  • stress/anxiety
  • and narcolepsy

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: How is sleep paralysis diagnosed and assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Clinically — a characteristic history of transient paralysis at sleep-wake transitions with intact awareness; the key task is to screen for narcolepsy and refer for sleep studies/MSLT if features are present.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What conditions should be distinguished from sleep paralysis?
What is the overarching management principle for sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back:
• Reassurance and sleep hygiene for isolated cases
  • treat any underlying narcolepsy
  • medication only for frequent/distressing episodes

• Adequate, regular sleep
  • avoiding sleep deprivation
  • avoiding sleeping supine
  • reducing stress
  • and limiting stimulants/alcohol before bed

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.front: What medication can be used for frequent/troublesome sleep paralysis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis.back: Clonazepam, or a REM-suppressing antidepressant (e.g. an SSRI or TCA), to reduce frequency — both off-label, as no drug is licensed for sleep paralysis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are sleep disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A group of conditions that disrupt the quantity, quality or timing of sleep, or produce abnormal events during sleep — with major impact on mood, cognition and physical health.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How are sleep disorders categorised?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
They sort into a few categories —
  • can't sleep (insomnia)
  • can't stay awake (hypersomnias/narcolepsy)
  • abnormal events (parasomnias)
  • disordered breathing (OSA)
  • abnormal movements (RLS)
  • and mistimed sleep (circadian)
— placing the complaint in the right category is the key diagnostic step.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Match the category to its core complaint: insomnia, hypersomnia, parasomnia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Insomnia = can't fall/stay asleep
  • hypersomnia = excessive daytime sleepiness despite adequate opportunity (e.g. narcolepsy)
  • parasomnia = abnormal events during sleep (e.g. sleepwalking, night terrors)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Match the category to its core complaint: sleep-related breathing, movement, circadian.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Sleep-related breathing = snoring + apnoeas + daytime sleepiness (OSA)
  • movement = urge to move/abnormal movements (RLS)
  • circadian = sleep at the wrong time (delayed sleep phase, shift-work, jet lag)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the two main stages of sleep, and their features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Non-REM (N1–N3, including deep slow-wave sleep) and REM sleep (dreaming, with physiological muscle atonia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: From which sleep stage do NON-REM parasomnias arise, and what are their features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Deep slow-wave sleep — occurring early in the night, with NO dream recall, and common in children (e.g. sleepwalking, night terrors).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: From which sleep stage do REM parasomnias arise, and what are their features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: REM sleep — occurring later in the night and dream-related (e.g. nightmares, sleep paralysis, REM sleep behaviour disorder).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How does insomnia relate to psychiatric illness?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: It is frequently comorbid — insomnia both causes and results from mental illness (depression, anxiety, PTSD).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Difficulty falling or staying asleep, with daytime impairment, despite adequate opportunity to sleep.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is chronic insomnia defined?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Symptoms ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months (acute/short-term insomnia is <3 months, often stress-related).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Which insomnia pattern specifically suggests depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Early-morning waking suggests depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: List the main causes/associations of insomnia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Psychiatric (depression, anxiety)
  • physical (pain, nocturia, respiratory)
  • substances (caffeine, alcohol, stimulants)
  • poor sleep hygiene
  • and other sleep disorders (OSA, RLS)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is insomnia assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• History plus a sleep diary
  • bed-partner collateral
  • screening for depression/anxiety and for OSA/RLS
  • and a medication/substance review

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia (NICE/CKS)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: CBT for insomnia (CBT-i) — the key modern point is that CBT-i, NOT drugs, is first-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the first steps in managing insomnia before considering drugs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: General sleep-hygiene advice and addressing the cause — treat depression/pain, cut caffeine/alcohol, establish a regular routine. But sleep hygiene alone is not effective treatment for chronic insomnia; CBT-i is the first-line treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: When and how should a hypnotic be used in insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Only short-term if severe/acute — a z-drug (zopiclone, zolpidem) or short-acting benzodiazepine, at the lowest dose for the shortest time (≤2 weeks), because of dependence, tolerance and falls.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the role of melatonin in insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Modified-release melatonin is an option in adults aged 55 and over — licensed for a maximum of 13 weeks (3 weeks initially, continued a further 10 weeks only if there is a response).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is daridorexant, and its role in insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A dual orexin receptor antagonist, an option for long-term insomnia (symptoms at least 3 nights a week for at least 3 months) where daytime functioning is considerably affected, only if CBT-i has been tried and not worked, or is unavailable or unsuitable; review within 3 months and stop if there is no adequate response (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the overarching prescribing principle in insomnia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Avoid long-term hypnotics — drugs are only a temporary adjunct; CBT-i is first-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A chronic disorder of excessive daytime sleepiness with sudden sleep attacks, caused by loss of orexin (hypocretin) signalling — the defining lesion of narcolepsy type 1 — the wakefulness neuropeptide.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the underlying mechanism of narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Loss of orexin (hypocretin) → intrusion of REM phenomena into wakefulness (cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations are all REM/dream elements breaking through).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the classic tetrad of narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Excessive daytime sleepiness (with sleep attacks)
  • cataplexy
  • sleep paralysis
  • and hypnagogic hallucinations

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the core feature of narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Excessive daytime sleepiness with irresistible sleep attacks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is cataplexy, and why is it significant?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion (e.g. laughter) — highly specific to narcolepsy type 1.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is sleep paralysis in narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A transient paralysis on waking or falling asleep (a REM phenomenon intruding into wakefulness).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are hypnagogic hallucinations?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Vivid hallucinations occurring at sleep onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is narcolepsy diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Sleep studies plus the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT); a low CSF orexin (hypocretin) level supports the diagnosis where it is measured, though this is a specialist test rarely needed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is the excessive daytime sleepiness of narcolepsy managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Sleep hygiene and scheduled naps, plus a wakefulness-promoting agent such as modafinil for the sleepiness — not in pregnancy, and it reduces the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives, so effective non-hormonal contraception is needed during treatment and for 2 months afterwards (MHRA). The patient must not drive and must notify the DVLA until symptoms are satisfactorily controlled.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is cataplexy managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: SSRIs/SNRIs or sodium oxybate.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are parasomnias?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Abnormal events occurring during sleep — e.g. sleep paralysis, night terrors, sleepwalking, nightmares and REM sleep behaviour disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is sleep paralysis, and its sleep stage?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A REM-related transient paralysis of skeletal muscles on waking (or falling asleep), ± hallucinations — the normal REM atonia persisting into wakefulness; common and benign.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is sleep paralysis managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Reassurance and sleep hygiene (adequate regular sleep, avoid sleep deprivation and the supine position); medication only if frequent and distressing — a REM-suppressing antidepressant or clonazepam, both off-label.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are night terrors, and their sleep stage?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A non-REM (deep sleep) parasomnia — sudden arousal with terror, screaming and an autonomic surge; the child is not fully awake and has no memory; occurs early in the night, in childhood.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is sleepwalking, and its sleep stage?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A non-REM (deep sleep) parasomnia — complex behaviours while asleep, with no memory; commonest in childhood but can persist into or begin in adulthood. Secure the sleep environment and do not forcibly wake the person; guide them gently back to bed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are nightmares, and their sleep stage?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A REM parasomnia — frightening dreams WITH recall, occurring later in the night.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: A REM parasomnia — loss of the normal REM atonia, causing the person to act out dreams (punching, kicking). Management is bedroom safety measures (remove sharp or hard objects, pad or lower the bed, consider the partner sleeping separately), reviewing antidepressants which can unmask it, and melatonin or clonazepam.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the clinical significance of REM sleep behaviour disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: It is strongly associated with future alpha-synucleinopathies (Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy) and often precedes them by years.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How are night terrors distinguished from nightmares?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Night terrors = non-REM, early night, NO recall, child not woken
  • nightmares = REM, later night, RECALLED

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep → apnoeas/hypopnoeas → repeated arousals → fragmented sleep.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the key clinical features of OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Loud snoring
  • witnessed apnoeas (reported by a bed-partner)
  • excessive daytime sleepiness
  • morning headache and poor concentration

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the risk factors for OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Obesity
  • a large neck circumference
  • male sex and alcohol

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is OSA assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: The Epworth Sleepiness Scale to quantify daytime sleepiness (not used alone to decide referral, as not everyone with OSA is sleepy) plus the STOP-Bang questionnaire, and home respiratory polygraphy to confirm the diagnosis — polysomnography only if polygraphy is inconclusive. Severity is graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the lifestyle measures in OSA management?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Weight loss and avoiding alcohol/sedatives.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the first-line treatment for moderate–severe OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) — also offered in mild OSA where symptoms affect daytime activities. A customised mandibular advancement splint is the alternative at any severity if CPAP is declined or not tolerated.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the DVLA implications of OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Excessive sleepiness, not the OSA diagnosis itself, is the trigger. The patient must stop driving immediately while sleepiness affects, or is likely to affect, driving.
