It is the driver's legal duty to notify the DVLA if confirmed OSA is moderate or severe with excessive sleepiness, or if mild OSA with excessive sleepiness is not controlled within 3 months. Driving may resume once the sleep clinic confirms satisfactory control with treatment adherence. OSA without excessive sleepiness: no restriction and no need to notify.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the consequences of untreated OSA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Hypertension
  • cardiovascular disease and road-traffic accidents

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is restless legs syndrome (RLS)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: An irresistible urge to move the legs, worse at rest and in the evening, relieved by movement, and disrupting sleep.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the characteristic pattern of RLS symptoms?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Worse at rest/in the evening and relieved by movement — the urge to move the legs improves when the person walks or moves.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are the associations of RLS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Iron deficiency (check ferritin — reversible, and a trial of iron is warranted even at a low-normal level)
  • pregnancy
  • renal failure and neuropathy
Also review drugs that worsen RLS: antidepressants, antipsychotics, metoclopramide and sedating antihistamines.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What is the key reversible cause to check for in RLS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Iron deficiency — check ferritin, as treating it can resolve the symptoms.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How is RLS managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Treat iron deficiency and review culprit drugs, apply sleep hygiene, and — if symptoms remain troublesome — a gabapentinoid (gabapentin or pregabalin, both off-label) first-line. Dopamine agonists are no longer recommended first-line because of augmentation and impulse-control disorders.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: What are circadian rhythm sleep disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back: Disorders where sleep occurs at the wrong TIME, but the sleep itself is normal — e.g. delayed sleep phase (common in adolescents), shift-work disorder and jet lag.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: Give examples of circadian rhythm sleep disorders.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Delayed sleep phase disorder (common in adolescents)
  • shift-work disorder
  • and jet lag

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.front: How are circadian rhythm disorders managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders.back:
• Sleep scheduling
  • timed light exposure
  • and melatonin (off-label for this indication)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the difference between self-harm and suicide risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Self-harm is a BEHAVIOUR (intentional self-injury or self-poisoning, irrespective of motive or degree of suicidal intent); suicide risk is a clinical ASSESSMENT of a person's current risks, protective factors and needs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: How do self-harm and suicide overlap?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Self-harm is the single strongest risk factor for later suicide, but most self-harm is NOT a suicide attempt — and many who die by suicide have never self-harmed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the organising principle linking self-harm and suicide assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Every self-harm presentation triggers a psychosocial assessment including a risk formulation, and every assessment asks about self-harm — assess the behaviour and the risk together.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Does asking directly about suicide increase risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: No — asking directly and sensitively about suicide does NOT increase risk or 'plant the idea'; it is safe, essential, and often brings relief. Always ask.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is self-harm defined as?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Intentional self-poisoning or self-injury, irrespective of the apparent motive — a behaviour, not a diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: By how much does self-harm increase the risk of suicide in the following year?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Around 30–50× increased risk — self-harm is the single strongest risk factor for future suicide.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Which conditions are strongly associated with self-harm?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
• Depression
  • borderline PD (EUPD)
  • PTSD
  • eating disorders
  • and substance misuse

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the single most important change in current UK guidance on self-harm?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: A move AWAY from risk stratification — risk-prediction tools and scales must not be used, and 'low/medium/high' stratification must not be used, either to predict risk or to decide who gets treatment or is discharged (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Why does NICE advise against risk-stratification tools?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Risk is dynamic and these tools don't reliably predict individual outcomes; stratifying can wrongly deny care to people labelled 'low-risk'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What replaces risk stratification under NICE?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: A collaborative, compassionate psychosocial assessment producing a risk FORMULATION — a narrative understanding of the person's risks, protective factors and needs, not a category or score.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: If asked 'how do you risk-stratify a self-harm patient?', what is the current correct answer?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: You DON'T stratify into low/medium/high — you undertake a needs-based psychosocial assessment and risk formulation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the status of SAD PERSONS-type mnemonics now?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Worth knowing they exist historically, but they are exactly the risk-scoring tools NICE now says must not be used to predict risk or to decide who is treated or discharged.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Who carries out the psychosocial assessment, and when?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: A mental health professional, at the earliest opportunity — do NOT delay it until medical treatment is completed, and do NOT use intoxication (alcohol) to delay it.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the purpose of the psychosocial assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: To build a collaborative therapeutic relationship, develop a shared understanding of WHY the person self-harmed, identify their needs, and produce a risk formulation — not a stratified score.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What does the psychosocial assessment explore?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
• The events/context of the act and mental state
  • current difficulties and strengths
  • social circumstances, support and coping resources
  • mental illness and substance use
  • and modifiable factors that could increase safety

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the strongest single predictor of future suicide?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Previous self-harm / a previous suicide attempt.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: List demographic and social factors associated with suicide.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
• Male sex (higher suicide rates)
  • middle age (the highest UK rates are in men in their late 40s to early 50s)
  • and also young adults
  • unemployment
  • social isolation
  • being unmarried/divorced/widowed
  • bereavement
  • debt and imprisonment

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Why is hopelessness particularly high-yield in suicide assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: It is one of the most significant psychological markers — often MORE predictive than depression severity itself.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What act-related features suggest higher suicidal intent?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
• High lethality/planning
  • precautions against discovery
  • and a 'final act' such as leaving a note or putting affairs in order

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: List protective factors against suicide.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
• Strong social support
  • dependent children
  • religious/cultural beliefs against suicide
  • help-seeking
  • engagement with services
  • hopefulness/future orientation
  • and reasons for living

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Along what continuum is suicidal ideation explored?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Thoughts (passive 'better off not here' → active thoughts of ending life) → plan → intent → preparation, alongside protective factors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What does NICE emphasise about HOW ideation is assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: The approach matters more than the checklist — a compassionate, collaborative conversation to understand WHY the person feels this way, rather than mechanically ticking risk items.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the immediate management of a self-harm/overdose presentation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
• Treat the physical consequences of the act (e.g. paracetamol → N-acetylcysteine; opioids → naloxone; TOXBASE guides specifics)
  • ensure immediate safety
  • do the psychosocial assessment early
  • and engage with compassion and without judgement

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the overarching principle of ongoing management (NICE)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Needs-led care — co-produced safety planning, means restriction, and treating the underlying condition — NOT risk-tool-driven disposal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is a safety plan, and what does it include?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
A plan co-produced with the person covering
  • warning signs/triggers
  • coping strategies
  • sources of support
  • means restriction
  • and emergency contacts

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: Why is means restriction important?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Reducing access to means is one of the most effective, evidence-based suicide-prevention measures.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the recommended timing of initial aftercare?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment if there are ongoing concerns.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is often the highest-yield intervention in self-harm/suicide management?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Treating the underlying condition (depression, EUPD, PTSD, bipolar, psychosis, substance use).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What psychological interventions are used for self-harm?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
• Adults — a CBT-based intervention tailored to self-harm
  • children/young people — consider DBT adapted for adolescents (DBT-A), especially with recurrent self-harm + emotional dysregulation

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is 'safer prescribing' for people at risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back:
• Prescribe medications least dangerous in overdose
  • in limited quantities
  • and review access to medicines (prescribed, OTC, herbal) that could be taken in overdose

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What caution applies to antidepressants in under-25s?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Some antidepressants may transiently INCREASE suicidal thoughts in under-25s → arrange closer early review.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: On what basis is admission decided?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: On clinical need and safety — NOT on a risk score. The Mental Health Act is used only if its criteria are met and needed mental health care is refused; refusal of medical treatment for the overdose itself is a capacity question decided under the Mental Capacity Act.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: How should borderline PD (EUPD) with recurrent self-harm be managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Respond consistently and compassionately, avoid punitive responses, and manage per the PD approach (DBT; don't medicate the disorder itself).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.front: What is the correct attitude to repeated self-harm presentations?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suic.back: Treat each episode on its own merits with the same compassion — never assume 'attention-seeking'; the therapeutic relationship itself affects outcomes and future engagement.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: A loss of contact with reality, defined by POSITIVE symptoms — delusions (fixed false beliefs), hallucinations (perceptions without a stimulus) and thought disorder (disorganised speech/thinking). Psychosis is a symptom/syndrome, not a diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is schizophrenia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: A chronic psychotic disorder with positive + negative symptoms + functional decline, with at least 1 month of active symptoms in UK practice (the American criteria add a 6-month total) — one cause of psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the organising principle in approaching psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Psychosis is a syndrome with many causes — the diagnostic job is (1) exclude organic and drug causes, then (2) characterise the primary psychiatric disorder using the positive/negative framework and duration.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Describe the epidemiology of schizophrenia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: ~1% lifetime risk; peak onset late teens–20s in men and 20s–30s in women; strong genetic component (highest risk with an affected identical twin).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Why does schizophrenia matter for mortality?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Patients die ~15–20 years early, mostly from cardiovascular disease, with suicide the leading cause of the early deaths and concentrated in the first years after diagnosis — so both CVD risk and suicide risk need active management.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the first and most important split when assessing psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Primary (psychiatric) vs secondary (organic/drug-induced) — always exclude organic and drug causes before diagnosing a primary psychotic disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Give primary psychiatric causes of psychosis.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Schizophrenia
  • schizoaffective disorder
  • bipolar/mania
  • psychotic depression
  • and acute and transient psychotic disorder

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Give secondary (organic/drug) causes of psychosis.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Drugs (stimulants, cannabis, steroids, dopaminergics, withdrawal states) and organic causes (delirium, dementia, temporal lobe epilepsy, encephalitis incl. anti-NMDA, SLE, brain tumour, B12 deficiency).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What clues suggest a SECONDARY (organic/drug) cause of psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Acute onset
  • older age
  • clouded/fluctuating consciousness
  • VISUAL hallucinations
  • focal neurology
  • and abnormal observations/bloods

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the high-yield rule about visual hallucinations and consciousness?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Visual hallucinations + clouded consciousness → think organic/delirium, NOT schizophrenia; schizophrenic hallucinations are characteristically auditory with a clear sensorium.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the positive symptoms of schizophrenia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
Added experiences —
  • delusions (esp. persecutory, delusions of control)
  • hallucinations (esp. auditory — 3rd-person, running commentary, thought echo)
  • thought disorder
  • and passivity phenomena

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the negative symptoms of schizophrenia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
Lost function —
  • blunted/incongruous affect
  • anhedonia
  • alogia (poverty of speech)
  • and avolition (poor motivation) with social withdrawal

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the '4 A's' of negative symptoms?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Affect (blunted)
  • Anhedonia
  • Alogia
  • and Avolition

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: How do positive and negative symptoms differ in treatment response and impact?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Positive symptoms respond well to antipsychotics; negative symptoms are harder to treat and drive long-term disability.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What features point to schizophrenia over a brief or drug-induced psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Negative symptoms plus a preceding prodrome of social withdrawal.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are Schneider's first-rank symptoms (and are they diagnostic)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Auditory hallucinations (3rd-person voices, thought echo, running commentary)
  • thought alienation (insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting)
  • passivity phenomena
  • and delusional perception
— a classic exam framework, NOT diagnostic alone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is delusional perception?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: A normal perception given sudden bizarre delusional meaning (e.g. 'the traffic light turned green, therefore I am the King') — a first-rank symptom.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is thought alienation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Thought insertion, thought withdrawal and thought broadcasting — a first-rank symptom.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Name three other classic schizophrenia features beyond first-rank symptoms.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Catatonia (immobility/bizarre posturing)
  • neologisms (made-up words)
  • and impaired insight

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Define circumstantiality vs tangentiality.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Circumstantiality = excessive detail but eventually answers the question; tangentiality = wanders off and never returns to the point.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the high-yield discriminator between knight's move thinking and flight of ideas?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Knight's move thinking = illogical leaps with NO discernible link (schizophrenia); flight of ideas = rapid leaps WITH discernible links (a manic feature).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Define clang associations and word salad.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Clang associations = words linked by rhyme/sound; word salad = an incoherent string of real words.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Define perseveration and echolalia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Perseveration = repeating ideas/words despite a change of topic; echolalia = repeating others' speech.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Match delusion type to classic disorder: persecutory, grandiose, nihilistic.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Persecutory (being conspired against) = the classic persecutory presentation of schizophrenia
  • grandiose (special powers/identity) = mania
  • nihilistic (dead/world ended) = psychotic depression (Cotard's)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are delusions of control (passivity) and somatic delusions?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Delusions of control/passivity = thoughts or actions controlled by an external force; somatic delusions = a false belief in a physical/medical problem despite no evidence.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What investigations exclude an organic/drug cause of psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium, B12/folate)
  • a urine drug screen
  • CT/MRI head if new-onset/focal/atypical
  • an autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA) screen if rapid onset with neuro features
  • and HIV/syphilis serology if indicated

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What baseline tests are needed BEFORE starting antipsychotics, and why?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Weight/BMI/waist
  • pulse and blood pressure
  • glucose/HbA1c
  • lipids
  • prolactin
  • U&E and LFT
— because antipsychotics cause metabolic, QTc and prolactin effects. An ECG is needed where the drug's product information specifies it, where there are cardiovascular risk factors or disease, or where the person is an inpatient.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: How is schizophrenia diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Clinically — in UK practice at least 1 month of active psychotic symptoms, with at least two symptoms and at least one from the core group (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking, or experiences of passivity/influence). The American criteria additionally require 6 months of total disturbance. There is no diagnostic test.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the first-line management of a first-episode psychosis (NICE)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Refer urgently to an Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) service — the access standard is to start treatment within 2 weeks of referral — and do not start antipsychotic medication yourself for a first presentation except on the advice of a consultant psychiatrist. Treatment is an oral antipsychotic chosen jointly with the person and guided by side-effect profile, PLUS CBT (offer to all, at least 16 sessions) and family intervention.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the key antipsychotic prescribing principles?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Trial one antipsychotic at an adequate dose for 4-6 weeks before switching
  • if inadequate, switch to a second, different antipsychotic
  • use a long-acting IM depot for poor adherence (maintenance, not acute treatment)
  • and monitor weight weekly for 6 weeks then at 3 months, 1 year and annually, with glucose/HbA1c and lipids at 3 months, 1 year and annually, plus pulse and BP at each review

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What defines treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and what is the treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: An inadequate response to ≥2 adequate antipsychotic trials (at least one a non-clozapine second-generation antipsychotic) → clozapine, the most effective antipsychotic for TRS (reserved because of agranulocytosis risk).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is the mechanism of antipsychotics, and how does it cause side effects?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Mainly dopamine D2 antagonism — mesolimbic block reduces positive symptoms, but off-target D2 blockade causes side effects (nigrostriatal → EPSEs; tuberoinfundibular → raised prolactin).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Compare typical vs atypical antipsychotics.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Typical (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) — strong D2 antagonism, causing EPSEs + hyperprolactinaemia; atypical (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, clozapine) — D2 + 5-HT2 antagonism, causing metabolic side effects, with aripiprazole a D2 partial agonist rather than a pure antagonist. Risperidone is a marked exception and raises prolactin strongly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Name the four EPSEs with their treatments.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Acute dystonia (torticollis/oculogyric crisis) → procyclidine 5-10 mg IM or IV, then a short oral course
  • akathisia (severe inner restlessness — do not mistake it for agitation and increase the dose; it is linked to suicidality) → reduce dose or switch, propranolol may help
  • parkinsonism → reduce dose/anticholinergic
  • tardive dyskinesia (months to years, choreoathetoid) → review the antipsychotic and stop any anticholinergic, tetrabenazine for moderate-to-severe cases (often irreversible)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: Give the key drug-specific antipsychotic points.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Aripiprazole = a D2 partial agonist with the least prolactin rise and low metabolic risk, but a high rate of akathisia
  • haloperidol = QTc prolongation
  • olanzapine/clozapine = most metabolic/weight gain.
All antipsychotics carry a VTE risk and can cause NMS; most raise prolactin, but aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine are prolactin-sparing; in elderly people with dementia antipsychotics increase the risk of stroke and death (MHRA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What are the key adverse effects and rules for clozapine?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Agranulocytosis/neutropenia — the patient must be registered with a monitoring service and clozapine dispensed only against a satisfactory neutrophil count: FBC weekly for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to one year, then four-weekly
  • Myocarditis — highest risk in the first few weeks, so baseline ECG plus active surveillance during titration for unexplained tachycardia, fever, chest pain or breathlessness
  • Reduced seizure threshold
  • Constipation — ask about bowel habit at every contact and treat actively, as untreated it can progress to fatal ileus (MHRA)
  • Hypersalivation
  • Missed >48h → re-titrate from a low dose; smoking cessation raises clozapine levels

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: A life-threatening reaction to dopamine blockade — fever, 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, autonomic instability and confusion, with markedly raised CK (rhabdomyolysis → AKI) and raised WCC.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: How is NMS managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: Stop the antipsychotic, give supportive care with IV fluids and active cooling, and use dantrolene ± bromocriptine in severe cases.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: How is NMS distinguished from serotonin syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back: NMS = rigidity + hyporeflexia, onset over days; serotonin syndrome = hyperreflexia/clonus + agitation, rapid onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: List poor prognostic factors in schizophrenia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Insidious (gradual) onset
  • no clear precipitant
  • prominent negative symptoms
  • a prodrome of social withdrawal
  • low IQ
  • strong family history
  • male sex
  • early onset
  • and poor premorbid functioning

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.front: List good prognostic factors in schizophrenia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia /.back:
• Acute onset
  • an obvious precipitant
  • prominent positive (not negative) symptoms
  • and good premorbid functioning

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: A disorder developing after exposure to a traumatic event (actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence — experienced, witnessed or learned of), characterised by re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal and negative mood/cognition.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is the 'core concept' defining PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: The persistence of a trauma response beyond 1 month — the body stays 'stuck' in threat mode long after the danger has passed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is the decisive timing rule distinguishing PTSD from an acute stress reaction?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Within 1 month of the trauma = acute stress reaction; symptoms persisting at least 1 month = PTSD. Treatment does not wait for the 1-month mark — trauma-focused CBT is offered inside the first month if symptoms are clinically important.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: How does adjustment disorder differ from PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Adjustment disorder is a maladaptive response to an identifiable stressor (divorce, job loss, illness) — preoccupation with it plus failure to adapt — arising within ~1 month and usually resolving within ~6 months of the stressor ending. It is separated from PTSD by the ABSENCE of re-experiencing, avoidance and a persistent sense of current threat, not by how severe the stressor was.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What are the symptom clusters of PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back:
UK practice (ICD) requires three:
  • re-experiencing the trauma in the here and now
  • deliberate avoidance of reminders
  • and a persistent sense of current threat (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle)
The American criteria add a fourth, negative mood/cognition and emotional numbing — in ICD those features instead point towards complex PTSD. Memory hook: reliving, avoiding, on-edge (and numb, in the American set).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What features make up the RE-EXPERIENCING cluster?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back:
• Flashbacks
  • nightmares
  • and intrusive distressing images/memories of the event

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What features make up the AVOIDANCE cluster?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Avoiding people, places, situations or reminders of the trauma.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What features make up the HYPERAROUSAL cluster?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back:
• Hypervigilance
  • an exaggerated startle response
  • irritability
  • sleep disturbance
  • and poor concentration

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What features make up the negative mood/cognition (emotional numbing) cluster?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: A cluster in the American criteria — detachment, an inability to feel emotions, negative beliefs, and guilt/shame. In ICD these features point towards complex PTSD rather than PTSD alone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What duration and impact are required to diagnose PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Symptoms from the clusters present for ≥1 month and causing significant distress or impairment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What are the key risk factors for PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back:
• Interpersonal/deliberate trauma (assault, combat, sexual violence) more than accidental
  • repeated/prolonged trauma
  • previous mental illness
  • prior trauma
  • lack of social support
  • and female sex

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What conditions is PTSD strongly associated with?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Depression, substance misuse and suicide risk — always screen for these.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is complex PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Full PTSD plus disturbances in self-organisation — affect dysregulation, negative self-concept and relationship difficulties. Prolonged or repeated trauma (childhood abuse, captivity) is typical but not required.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: How is PTSD assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Clinically — a careful trauma history (ask directly, as patients often avoid disclosing) + symptom clusters + ≥1 month duration; screen for comorbid depression/substance misuse/suicide risk and exclude other diagnoses. There is no diagnostic test.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is the overarching management principle for PTSD (NICE)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Trauma-focused psychological therapy is first-line — NOT drugs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: How are subthreshold PTSD symptoms within 1 month of the trauma managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Active monitoring, with follow-up contact arranged within 1 month. Psychologically-focused debriefing is not offered — it does not prevent PTSD and may worsen outcomes (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: How are clinically important symptoms in the first month managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Offer individual trauma-focused CBT for an acute stress reaction or clinically important PTSD symptoms within the first month — don't wait for the 1-month mark.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What are the first-line psychological therapies for established PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Individual trauma-focused CBT (typically 8-12 sessions, more if clinically needed), offered to any adult presenting more than 1 month after trauma — the named interventions are cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy for PTSD, narrative exposure therapy and prolonged exposure therapy. EMDR is not equivalent: it is offered only after a non-combat-related trauma and only from 3 months, and considered between 1 and 3 months if the person prefers it (NICE). Both come before drug treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is the important caveat about EMDR?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: EMDR is NOT recommended for combat-related trauma.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: When is drug treatment used in PTSD, and what is first-line?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Second-line/adjunct — considered if the person has a preference for drug treatment or declines therapy. A drug is not a substitute for trauma-focused therapy that is indicated but unavailable. First-line is venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline (NICE). Paroxetine is UK-licensed for PTSD; sertraline's UK licence covers women only; venlafaxine and fluoxetine are off-label (BNF). Review regularly, warn about early worsening of anxiety and increased suicidal thinking in under-25s, and check blood pressure on venlafaxine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: When is an antipsychotic added in PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: Consider an antipsychotic such as risperidone in addition to psychological therapy, only where disabling symptoms (e.g. severe hyperarousal or psychotic symptoms) have not responded to other drug or psychological treatment — started and reviewed regularly by a specialist, and off-label for PTSD (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: What is the place of prazosin in PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: It is sometimes used off-label for trauma-related nightmares, but it is not recommended for PTSD in UK guidance (NICE) and is unlicensed for it here. It risks first-dose hypotension and syncope — start low at night and titrate slowly, on specialist advice. Treating the PTSD itself with trauma-focused therapy comes first.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.front: Why should benzodiazepines NOT be used for PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic S.back: They are not a treatment for PTSD, and UK guidance explicitly says not to offer drug treatments including benzodiazepines to prevent it (NICE); they also risk dependence and sedation that impedes trauma-focused therapy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the five major psychotropic drug classes?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Antipsychotics
  • antidepressants
  • mood stabilisers
  • anxiolytics/hypnotics
  • and stimulants

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the 'core concept' unifying psychopharmacology?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Most psychotropics act on monoamine or GABA neurotransmission, and their side effects are largely predictable from their receptor actions — so a class → mechanism → key side effects → monitoring grid lets you reason out most of the pharmacology.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the main mechanism and prototype use of antipsychotics?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Dopamine D2 antagonism (± 5-HT2) — used for schizophrenia, mania and psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the main mechanism and prototype use of antidepressants?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Increasing monoamines (serotonin ± noradrenaline) — used for depression, anxiety, OCD and PTSD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the main mechanism and prototype use of mood stabilisers?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Varied mechanisms (lithium, anticonvulsants) — used for bipolar prophylaxis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the main mechanism and prototype use of anxiolytics/hypnotics?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Increasing GABA (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs) — used for short-term anxiety, insomnia, withdrawal and sedation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the main mechanism and prototype use of stimulants?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Increasing dopamine/noradrenaline — used for ADHD and narcolepsy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the five cross-class psychiatric drug emergencies to recognise?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
  • serotonin syndrome
  • lithium toxicity
  • clozapine agranulocytosis
  • and the tyramine (MAOI) crisis

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the main mechanism of antipsychotics?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Mainly dopamine D2 antagonism — mesolimbic block reduces positive symptoms, while off-target D2 block elsewhere causes side effects.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Give examples of typical (1st-generation) antipsychotics and their main side effects.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Haloperidol and chlorpromazine — strong D2 antagonism; main side effects are extrapyramidal (EPSEs) and hyperprolactinaemia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Give examples of atypical (2nd-generation) antipsychotics and their main side effects.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole and clozapine — D2 + 5-HT2 antagonism, except aripiprazole which is a D2 partial agonist. Main side effects are metabolic (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is acute dystonia, and how is it treated?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: An extrapyramidal side effect — torticollis or oculogyric crisis occurring early; treated with procyclidine given IM or IV, since oral is too slow for an acute crisis, then a short oral course to prevent recurrence.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is akathisia, and how is it managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: An extrapyramidal side effect of severe inner restlessness — do not mistake it for agitation and increase the dose; it causes marked distress and is linked to suicidality. Managed by reducing the dose or switching; propranolol may be added, but avoid it in asthma.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is drug-induced parkinsonism, and how is it managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: An extrapyramidal side effect — bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor. Reduce the dose or switch to a lower-EPSE antipsychotic first; an anticholinergic only if that fails, since they impair cognition and worsen tardive dyskinesia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is tardive dyskinesia, and how is it treated?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: A late extrapyramidal side effect appearing after months to years — choreoathetoid movements (chewing, jaw, blinking). Review the antipsychotic first: reduce, stop or switch it and stop any anticholinergic; tetrabenazine for moderate-to-severe cases. Often irreversible.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which antipsychotic causes the least prolactin elevation and the least metabolic burden?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Aripiprazole ('aripiPPrazole is aPPropriate'), a D2 partial agonist — but akathisia is common with it, so it is not the antipsychotic with the fewest side effects overall.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which antipsychotic is most associated with QTc prolongation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Haloperidol.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which antipsychotics cause the most metabolic side effects?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Olanzapine and clozapine (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What class-wide risks do all antipsychotics carry?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Venous thromboembolism, and in older people with dementia an increased risk of stroke and death (MHRA). Prolactin rise is common but NOT universal — aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine spare it, while risperidone and amisulpride raise it markedly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: When is clozapine used, and why is it reserved?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: For schizophrenia unresponsive to at least two antipsychotics, each tried at an adequate dose for 6-8 weeks, one of which was a non-clozapine second-generation agent. It is the most effective but carries serious risks (agranulocytosis, myocarditis), so it is reserved and closely monitored.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the key serious adverse effects of clozapine?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Agranulocytosis/neutropenia — FBC weekly for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to one year, then 4-weekly
  • Myocarditis — usually in the first 2 months, so a baseline ECG does not exclude it: suspect it with tachycardia, fever, chest pain or breathlessness and check troponin and CRP
  • Reduced seizure threshold
  • Constipation from gut hypomotility (can be fatal — ask about bowels at every review and give prophylactic laxatives)
  • Hypersalivation

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What must happen if a patient misses clozapine for more than 48 hours?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: It must be re-titrated from a low dose (missing >48h means restarting titration).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: How does smoking affect clozapine levels?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Smoking induces its metabolism, lowering levels; smoking cessation increases clozapine levels (risk of toxicity).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: A psychiatric emergency from antipsychotics — fever, 'lead-pipe' rigidity, autonomic instability, confusion and markedly raised CK; managed by stopping the antipsychotic, supportive care, and dantrolene ± bromocriptine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which antidepressant class is first-line, and its mechanism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) — they increase serotonin by blocking its reuptake.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which SSRI is preferred in adults, and which in children/young people?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Sertraline is a common first choice in adults and is preferred where there is cardiac disease; fluoxetine in children and young people, started after specialist review and only alongside concurrent psychological therapy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the key side effects of SSRIs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: GI upset, hyponatraemia and sexual dysfunction, plus GI bleeding — review whether the NSAID is needed, and co-prescribe a PPI if it must continue.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which SSRI is most associated with QT prolongation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Citalopram and escitalopram. Maximum citalopram 40 mg daily (20 mg if over 65 or in hepatic impairment) and escitalopram 20 mg (10 mg if over 65); both are contraindicated with known QT prolongation, congenital long QT, or other QT-prolonging drugs (MHRA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is SSRI discontinuation syndrome, and how is it avoided?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Flu-like symptoms, dizziness and electric-shock sensations if stopped abruptly. All antidepressants are stopped by gradual dose reduction; fluoxetine's long half-life makes symptoms milder and often delayed, but it is still reduced rather than stopped abruptly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What caution applies to SSRIs with warfarin/aspirin/NSAIDs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Increased bleeding risk. With warfarin or heparin, avoid an SSRI and consider mirtazapine instead; with aspirin or an NSAID, review whether it is needed and add a PPI if it must continue.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Give examples of SNRIs and their mechanism.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Venlafaxine and duloxetine — they increase both serotonin AND noradrenaline.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the key side effect and overdose caution of SNRIs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Hypertension (check the BP); venlafaxine is toxic in overdose and has a notable withdrawal syndrome.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the mechanism of mirtazapine, and its memory hook?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: A tetracyclic α2 antagonist that increases noradrenaline/serotonin release; the hook is 'zzz + mmm' — sedation + increased appetite.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: In which patients is mirtazapine especially useful?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Those with insomnia, poor appetite, or the elderly (using its sedative and appetite-stimulating effects).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Give examples of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) and their mechanism.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Amitriptyline, imipramine and clomipramine — they increase 5-HT and noradrenaline, and block histamine, muscarinic and adrenergic receptors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Why are TCAs not first-line, and what are they used for?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: They have more side effects and are dangerous in overdose; they are used for neuropathic pain and (clomipramine) for OCD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the anticholinergic side effects of TCAs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: 'Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't shit' — blurred vision, urinary retention, dry mouth and constipation; also QT prolongation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the dangers of TCA overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: A wide QRS, arrhythmias and seizures. Managed with IV sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmia or acidosis, and benzodiazepines for seizures; class Ia and III antiarrhythmics are avoided.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Give examples of MAOIs, their use and their key danger.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Phenelzine and tranylcypromine — used for atypical depression. The key danger is a tyramine ('cheese') reaction causing a hypertensive crisis. They must also not be combined with an SSRI, SNRI, TCA, triptan, tramadol, pethidine or sympathomimetics, and a 2-week washout is needed when switching (5 weeks after fluoxetine).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: When should antidepressant treatment be reviewed after starting?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: At 2 weeks — or at 1 week if the patient is under 25 or judged to be at increased suicide risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: For how long should an antidepressant be continued after remission?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: At least 6 months after remission — and at least 12 months in OCD/anxiety disorders.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is serotonin syndrome, and how is it treated?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Excess serotonin (e.g. SSRI + MAOI/triptan/tramadol) causing clonus + hyperreflexia + autonomic instability + agitation. Stop all serotonergic drugs and give supportive care with IV fluids, cooling and benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine if severe.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: How is serotonin syndrome distinguished from NMS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Serotonin syndrome = clonus + HYPERreflexia (rapid onset); NMS = 'lead-pipe' rigidity + HYPOreflexia (slower onset).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the first-line mood stabiliser for bipolar prophylaxis, and its mechanism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Lithium — it interferes with cAMP and inositol triphosphate signalling. It has a narrow therapeutic index: target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L (0.8-1.0 after relapse or persisting symptoms), with toxicity above about 1.5 mmol/L.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the side effects of lithium (LITHIUM mnemonic)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Lethargy
  • Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus)
  • Tremor (fine)
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Insides (GI upset)
  • Urine ↑ (polyuria)
  • Metallic taste

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Besides the LITHIUM mnemonic, what other adverse effects does lithium cause?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Weight gain
  • nephrotoxicity
  • hyperparathyroidism → hypercalcaemia
  • benign leucocytosis
  • and T-wave changes on ECG

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What precipitates lithium toxicity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Dehydration
  • NSAIDs
  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs
  • and thiazide diuretics
(all reduce lithium excretion).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the features of lithium toxicity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Often GI symptoms first, then neurological — coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, seizures and arrhythmias.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: How is lithium toxicity managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Stop lithium, give IV fluids, and consider haemodialysis in severe cases.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: How is a fine tremor distinguished from a coarse tremor in a patient on lithium?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: A fine tremor is an expected side effect at therapeutic levels; a COARSE tremor suggests lithium TOXICITY.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: When are lithium levels checked, and how often?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Levels are taken 12 hours post-dose; weekly after starting and after each dose change until stable, then 3-monthly for the first year and 3-6-monthly thereafter, staying 3-monthly in higher-risk people.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What additional monitoring is required for lithium besides drug levels?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Thyroid function, renal function and calcium, checked 6-monthly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the key concern with sodium valproate as a mood stabiliser?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: It is highly teratogenic and carries a risk to the offspring of treated men. Do NOT start it in anyone under 55, male or female, unless two specialists independently document there is no alternative. Men under 55 already on valproate may be continued by a single prescriber, but they and their partners need effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after stopping. In women of childbearing potential it must not be used unless the Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions are met, and in bipolar disorder it is contraindicated in pregnancy (MHRA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is lamotrigine used for as a mood stabiliser, and its key risk?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: An option in bipolar DEPRESSION, where fluoxetine with olanzapine or quetiapine alone come first. The key risk is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, so titrate slowly and stop immediately if any rash appears in the first 8 weeks. Valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine levels, so start lower and titrate more slowly when the two are combined.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which antipsychotics are also used as mood stabilisers?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Quetiapine and olanzapine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the mechanism of benzodiazepines?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: They enhance GABA-A receptor activity, increasing chloride influx and hence neuronal inhibition.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Give examples of benzodiazepines and their key usage principle.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide — for SHORT-TERM use only because of dependence and tolerance: a maximum of 2-4 weeks including the taper, for severe, disabling or distressing anxiety (BNF).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the clinical uses of benzodiazepines?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Acute crisis/agitation
  • alcohol withdrawal
  • seizures (status epilepticus)
  • and sedation

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which benzodiazepine is used for alcohol withdrawal, and which is preferred in liver failure?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Chlordiazepoxide for alcohol withdrawal; lorazepam is preferred in liver failure (it has no active metabolites).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the key side effects of benzodiazepines?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Sedation, falls (especially in the elderly), and respiratory depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the reversal agent for benzodiazepines?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Flumazenil (rarely used — it can precipitate seizures).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What happens on abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal, and how is it avoided?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Withdrawal can cause seizures; it is avoided by tapering the dose gradually.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are Z-drugs, their mechanism and use?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Zopiclone and zolpidem — GABA-A agonists used for short-term insomnia; they carry a similar dependence risk to benzodiazepines.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the role of pregabalin in anxiety, and how does gabapentin differ?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Pregabalin is a calcium channel modulator used in GAD when an SSRI or SNRI is not tolerated or effective. Gabapentin is for neuropathic pain, not GAD. Both are Class C, Schedule 3 controlled drugs, with a risk of severe respiratory depression, especially with opioids (MHRA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is buspirone, and its role?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: A 5-HT1A partial agonist — a non-sedating anxiolytic, but not first-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the role of melatonin as a hypnotic?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: A melatonin receptor agonist licensed for the short-term treatment of insomnia — up to 13 weeks — in people aged 55 and over.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is daridorexant, and when is it used?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: An orexin receptor antagonist for long-term insomnia when CBT for insomnia (CBT-i) has failed (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the high-yield principle about benzodiazepine prescribing?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Benzodiazepines are for short-term/crisis use only — NOT for chronic anxiety (GAD), PTSD, or long-term insomnia, because of dependence and worse outcomes.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the first-line stimulant for ADHD, and its mechanism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Methylphenidate — it increases dopamine and noradrenaline neurotransmission.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the key side effects of methylphenidate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Reduced appetite and growth suppression
  • insomnia
  • and increased heart rate and blood pressure

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What monitoring is required for a child on methylphenidate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Monitor growth (height and weight) and cardiovascular parameters (heart rate and blood pressure).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Give the amphetamine-based stimulant options for ADHD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Lisdexamfetamine and dexamfetamine (amphetamine-based). In adults, lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate is first-line; in children they are an option when methylphenidate is not tolerated or effective.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the non-stimulant option for ADHD, and its mechanism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Atomoxetine — a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor. Warn about hepatic injury (stop and investigate if jaundice, dark urine or unexplained abdominal pain) and monitor for suicidal ideation, especially in children and young people early in treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Which drug is used for the daytime sleepiness of narcolepsy?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Modafinil.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: Why must growth be monitored in children taking stimulants for ADHD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Stimulants can suppress appetite and growth, so height and weight should be tracked over time.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What cardiovascular caution applies before and during stimulant treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure, so cardiovascular status should be assessed at baseline and monitored during treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What are the five cross-class psychotropic emergencies?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back:
• Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
  • serotonin syndrome
  • lithium toxicity
  • clozapine agranulocytosis
  • and the tyramine ('cheese') reaction

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What causes neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and its features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Dopamine blockade by antipsychotics; features are fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, markedly raised CK and HYPOreflexia, with a slower onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: How is neuroleptic malignant syndrome managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Stop the antipsychotic; supportive care with IV fluids, cooling and benzodiazepines, watching for rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury; dantrolene with or without bromocriptine in severe cases.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What causes serotonin syndrome, and its features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Excess serotonin (drug combinations, e.g. SSRI + MAOI/triptan/tramadol); features are clonus, HYPERreflexia, autonomic instability and agitation, with a rapid onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: How is serotonin syndrome managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Stop all serotonergic drugs; supportive care with IV fluids, cooling and benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine if severe.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is the high-yield distinction between NMS and serotonin syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: NMS = rigidity + HYPOreflexia, slower onset (antipsychotic); serotonin syndrome = clonus + HYPERreflexia, rapid onset (serotonergic drug).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What precipitates lithium toxicity, and its features?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: Raised lithium levels from dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs or thiazides; features are coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion and seizures.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What is clozapine agranulocytosis, and how is it managed/prevented?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: A dangerous fall in neutrophils risking severe infection. Prevented by mandatory FBC monitoring — weekly for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly to one year, then 4-weekly while treatment continues and for 4 weeks after stopping — with clozapine dispensed only against a satisfactory count; managed by stopping clozapine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.front: What causes the tyramine ('cheese') reaction, and its consequence?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Dru.back: An MAOI taken with tyramine-rich foods (e.g. mature cheese); it causes a hypertensive crisis. Prevented by avoiding tyramine-containing foods; if it occurs, stop the MAOI and reduce the blood pressure in a controlled way with IV phentolamine.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is a personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: An enduring, pervasive pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from cultural expectations, is stable over time, and causes distress or functional impairment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What distinguishes a personality disorder from an illness like depression or psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: A personality disorder is a long-standing TRAIT pattern — present since adolescence/early adulthood and across situations — rather than a discrete episode (a state disorder).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: When do personality disorders emerge?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: They emerge by late adolescence or early adulthood — and can be diagnosed in under-18s (except antisocial PD), with referral to CAMHS where the full range of treatments should be available.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Into how many clusters do the personality disorders group, and by what?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Three clusters, grouped by their dominant character. This is the older categorical (American) model — the current international classification instead grades personality disorder as mild, moderate or severe with trait domains.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Name the three personality disorder clusters and their themes.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back:
• Cluster A = odd/eccentric ('Weird')
  • Cluster B = dramatic/emotional/erratic ('Wild')
  • Cluster C = anxious/fearful ('Worried')

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Which disorders make up Cluster A?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Paranoid, Schizoid and Schizotypal personality disorders (the 'odd/eccentric', schizophrenia-spectrum flavour).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Which disorders make up Cluster B?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Antisocial, Borderline (EUPD), Histrionic and Narcissistic personality disorders (the 'dramatic/emotional/erratic' group).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Which disorders make up Cluster C?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Avoidant, Dependent and Obsessive-Compulsive personality disorders (the 'anxious/fearful' group).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the memory hook for the three clusters?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: 'Weird, Wild, Worried' — A = odd, B = dramatic, C = anxious.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the overall theme of Cluster A personality disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Odd / eccentric — a 'schizophrenia-spectrum' flavour, characterised by difficulty forming and sustaining relationships.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises paranoid personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: A pervasive distrust and suspiciousness — questioning others' loyalty, reluctance to confide, bearing grudges, and reading hidden threatening meanings into events.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the discriminator for paranoid personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Suspicion WITHOUT psychosis or magical thinking — persistent mistrust that never reaches delusional/psychotic level.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises schizoid personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Detachment and emotional coldness — preferring solitude, having few friends, indifference to praise or criticism, and little interest in sex or relationships.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the memory hook for schizoid personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: 'SchizOID = devOID of emotion/interest' — like the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, but WITHOUT psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises schizotypal personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back:
• Odd beliefs/magical thinking
  • ideas of reference (with insight)
  • unusual perceptual experiences
  • odd speech/affect
  • suspiciousness
  • and few close friends

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Why is schizotypal PD the 'almost-psychotic' one, and how is it distinguished from psychosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: It is the closest to schizophrenia, but its ideas of reference retain INSIGHT — unlike true delusions, where insight is lost.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Summarise the three Cluster A discriminators.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back:
• Schizoid = withdrawn + emotionally cold (no desire for contact)
  • schizotypal = odd + magical thinking + eccentric (the 'almost-psychotic' one)
  • paranoid = suspicious

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the overall theme of Cluster B personality disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Dramatic / emotional / erratic — impulsivity, intense emotion and interpersonal chaos.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Which four disorders make up Cluster B?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Antisocial, Borderline (EUPD), Histrionic and Narcissistic personality disorders.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises antisocial personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: A pervasive disregard for others' rights and social norms — repeated law-breaking, deceit, impulsivity, no remorse, irritability/aggression and irresponsibility.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the discriminator (and key criteria) for antisocial personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Lack of remorse + rule-breaking; commoner in men. Under the American criteria the person must be aged 18 or over with evidence of conduct disorder before age 15; the international classification sets no such age threshold.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises borderline (emotionally unstable) personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Instability of mood, self-image and relationships — fear of abandonment, chronic emptiness, self-harm, impulsivity, and relationships alternating between idealisation and devaluation ('splitting'), with transient paranoia/dissociation under stress. This is the borderline subtype of emotionally unstable personality disorder; the impulsive subtype has the emotional instability and impulsivity without the identity disturbance and self-destructive pattern.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is 'splitting' in borderline personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Relationships alternating between idealisation and devaluation — seeing others as all-good or all-bad.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the discriminating picture of borderline personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: The combination of self-harm + fear of abandonment + unstable, intense relationships (plus chronic emptiness).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises histrionic personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Attention-seeking and excessive emotionality — dramatic, seductive/sexually inappropriate behaviour, considering relationships more intimate than they are, and being easily influenced.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the discriminator for histrionic personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: A need to be the centre of attention — theatrical and attention-seeking, but WITHOUT the self-destructive instability of borderline PD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises narcissistic personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Grandiosity + a need for admiration + a lack of empathy — a sense of entitlement, exploiting others, arrogance, and preoccupation with fantasies of success.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the discriminator for narcissistic personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Grandiosity + entitlement + no empathy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Summarise the four Cluster B discriminators.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back:
• Antisocial = no remorse/breaks rules
  • borderline = unstable + self-harm + fear of abandonment
  • histrionic = attention-seeking/theatrical
  • narcissistic = grandiose + entitled

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: How is borderline distinguished from histrionic personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Borderline has self-harm, chronic emptiness and self-destructive instability; histrionic is more purely attention-seeking/theatrical, without that self-destructive instability.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the overall theme of Cluster C personality disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Anxious / fearful — fear-driven patterns of behaviour.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Which three disorders make up Cluster C?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Avoidant, Dependent and Obsessive-Compulsive (OCPD) personality disorders.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises avoidant personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: A fear of criticism/rejection — avoids interpersonal and occupational contact, feels inept/inferior, and won't engage unless certain of being liked.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the discriminator for avoidant personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: The person WANTS relationships, but fear of rejection holds them back (in contrast to schizoid PD, where there is no desire for contact).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises dependent personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: An excessive need to be cared for — submissive and clinging, unable to make decisions alone, urgently seeking a new relationship when one ends, and lacking self-confidence/initiative.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the discriminator for dependent personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: The person cannot function without others' support — they need others to take responsibility for them.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What characterises obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Perfectionism + rigidity + control — preoccupation with rules, order and detail, inability to delegate, being a workaholic at the expense of leisure, and rigidity on morals/ethics.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the discriminator for OCPD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: A rigid perfectionist who values order and control — and crucially, OCPD is NOT the same as OCD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the critical distinction between OCPD and OCD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: OCPD = an EGO-SYNTONIC personality trait (rigid perfectionism/orderliness the person sees as correct, with no true obsessions/compulsions); OCD = an EGO-DYSTONIC obsessive-compulsive disorder with intrusive obsessions and compulsions the person finds distressing and wants rid of.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Summarise the three Cluster C discriminators.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back:
• Avoidant = wants contact but fears rejection
  • dependent = needs others to take responsibility
  • OCPD = rigid perfectionist

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: How is a personality disorder diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Clinically — an enduring, pervasive pattern present since adolescence/early adulthood, across multiple situations, causing distress or impairment; a longitudinal history plus collateral is essential. The diagnosis can be made in under-18s (except antisocial PD); refer under-18s to CAMHS, where the full range of treatments should be available.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What must be excluded before diagnosing a personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: A state disorder that better explains the picture (depression, psychosis, bipolar, substance use) and organic causes — but personality disorder commonly coexists with these rather than excluding them, and the diagnosis must never be used to explain away new symptoms or to withhold care.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What must always be screened for in someone with a personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Comorbid depression, anxiety and substance misuse, and self-harm/suicide risk — especially in borderline PD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: How does the current international classification grade personality disorder, and why is the cluster model still used?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: It grades personality disorder as mild, moderate or severe (with a sub-threshold 'personality difficulty'), specified by five trait domains — negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition and anankastia — with only a borderline pattern retained as a specifier. The older cluster/type framework is retained in teaching and examinations.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the overarching management principle for personality disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Psychological therapy is the mainstay; drugs are NOT used to treat the personality disorder itself. Borderline PD in particular has a good prognosis with treatment, with substantial symptomatic remission over time.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the best-evidenced psychological therapy, and for which PD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) — best-evidenced, especially for borderline PD; NICE suggests considering a comprehensive DBT programme for women with borderline PD where reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: Name other structured psychological therapies used in personality disorder.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back:
• Mentalisation-based therapy (MBT)
  • cognitive/schema-focused therapy
  • and therapeutic communities

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the key NICE point about drug treatment in borderline PD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Do NOT use drugs specifically to treat borderline PD or its individual symptoms; antipsychotics should not be used for medium/long-term treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: When are drugs appropriate in personality disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Only for comorbid conditions (e.g. depression, anxiety) — not for the personality disorder itself. A short-term sedative may be considered cautiously in a crisis, for no longer than about 1 week, choosing an agent that is relatively safe in overdose and agreeing target symptoms, monitoring and duration with the patient. Review anyone already on drugs without a diagnosed comorbid illness, aiming to reduce and stop unnecessary treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: For how long may a sedative be used in a personality disorder crisis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: No longer than about 1 week — a short-term measure in a crisis only, with the target symptoms, monitoring and duration agreed in advance, and an agent chosen for relative safety in overdose.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: What is the preferred setting for treating personality disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: In the community where possible — avoid long, unstructured hospital admissions, which can worsen borderline PD. Admit only for a crisis involving significant risk to self or others that cannot be managed elsewhere, or where detention is needed, and agree the length and purpose of the admission in advance.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.front: How is antisocial personality disorder managed?
