conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Personality Diso.back: Assess and manage risk; consider group-based cognitive and behavioural interventions, adjusting intensity to the assessed level of risk; treat comorbid substance misuse. Drugs should not be routinely used for the disorder or for associated aggression, anger and impulsivity (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What are the two distinct legal frameworks in mental health law (England & Wales)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA) — decision-making for those who may lack capacity, any decision, any setting
  • and the Mental Health Act 1983/2007 (MHA) — compulsory assessment and treatment of a mental disorder (detention).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What question does the Mental Capacity Act ask?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: 'Can this person make THIS decision, at THIS time?' — capacity is presumed, decision- and time-specific; if absent, act in their best interests, least restrictively.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What question does the Mental Health Act ask?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: 'Does this person need compulsory admission/treatment for a mental disorder in the interests of their health, their safety, or the protection of others?'

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: At the interface, which Act governs treatment of a mental disorder in a detained patient?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: The MHA — treatment for a mental disorder in a detained patient falls under the MHA; do not use the MCA to give compulsory psychiatric treatment where the MHA is the appropriate route.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Can a patient be subject to both the MCA and the MHA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: Yes — a patient can be subject to both; the MCA/DoLS covers deprivation of liberty in those who lack capacity but are not detainable under the MHA (e.g. dementia in hospital).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is 'capacity'?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: The ability to make a SPECIFIC decision at a SPECIFIC time — it is decision-specific and time-specific, and can fluctuate; you never assess capacity in the abstract.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: List the five statutory principles of the Mental Capacity Act.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• (1) Presumption of capacity
  • (2) support to decide (all practicable help first)
  • (3) unwise decisions do not prove incapacity
  • (4) best interests
  • (5) least restrictive option.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What are the two highest-yield MCA principles?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• You presume capacity (the burden is to prove its absence)
  • and an unwise decision is NOT incapacity (a competent Jehovah's Witness can refuse a transfusion).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Can a person with capacity refuse life-saving treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: Yes — a capacitous adult can make an 'unwise' decision and refuse even life-saving treatment; the MCA only steps in when capacity is lacking.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is Stage 1 (the diagnostic test) of the capacity assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: Is there an impairment of, or disturbance in, the functioning of the mind or brain? (e.g. dementia, delirium, intoxication, brain injury, psychosis, learning disability) — permanent or temporary.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is Stage 2 (the functional test) of the capacity assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: Because of that impairment, is the person unable to do ANY ONE of: Understand, Retain, Weigh/use the information, or Communicate their decision? Failing any one = lacks capacity for that decision.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is the memory hook for the four abilities in the functional capacity test?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: 'URWC' — Understand, Retain, Weigh/use, Communicate; failing any single one means no capacity for that decision.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Both stages of the capacity test must be met — what does this mean?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: There must be an impairment (Stage 1) AND an inability to decide (Stage 2) that is CAUSED by the impairment — a diagnosis alone is not enough.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Is capacity based on the outcome of the decision?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: No — capacity is about the PROCESS of deciding, not whether the decision seems sensible; an unwise decision does not indicate incapacity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What framework governs consent in under-16s?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• Gillick competence — a child under 16 can consent if they have sufficient understanding
  • Fraser guidelines apply specifically to contraceptive advice.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: How does consent/refusal work for 16–17 year olds?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: They are presumed able to consent to treatment, but a REFUSAL may be overridden by a court (unlike adults). Do not rely on parental consent alone to override a competent young person's refusal — take legal advice.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: When a person lacks capacity, on what basis are decisions made?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: In their best interests (Principle 4) — considering their past/present wishes, values and beliefs, the views of family/carers/those with legal authority, whether capacity might return, and the least restrictive option.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Who is the decision-maker for a person lacking capacity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: Whoever proposes the act (often the treating clinician for medical decisions) — NOT the family, unless they hold legal authority (e.g. an LPA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: When must an IMCA be instructed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: An Independent Mental Capacity Advocate must be instructed for serious decisions (serious medical treatment, change of accommodation) when the person has no family or friends to consult.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is a Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA), and what are the two types?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: A capacitous person appoints an attorney to decide later; the two types are health & welfare and property & financial affairs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is an advance decision to refuse treatment (ADRT), and is it binding?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: A capacitous person's decision to refuse specified future treatment ('living will'); it is legally binding if valid and applicable (and if it refuses life-sustaining treatment it must be in writing, signed, witnessed, and expressly state that it applies even if life is at risk).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Can an advance decision demand a specific treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: No — an ADRT can only REFUSE treatment (and is binding even for life-sustaining treatment if valid/applicable); it cannot demand a specific treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is a court-appointed deputy, and what is the Court of Protection?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• A deputy is appointed by the Court of Protection to decide when no LPA exists
  • the Court of Protection resolves disputed or serious capacity decisions.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What are the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: The authorisation framework making it lawful to deprive of liberty (continuous supervision and control + not free to leave) a person who lacks capacity in a hospital or care home. Liberty Protection Safeguards were legislated for as a replacement but have not been implemented, so DoLS remains the operative framework. DoLS applies from age 18; for a 16-17 year old a Court of Protection order is needed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Does best-interests care automatically permit detaining someone?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: No — depriving someone of their liberty needs separate legal authorisation (DoLS); best-interests care alone does not permit it.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What are the criteria for detention under the MHA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• (1) A mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention
  • (2) it is necessary in the interests of the person's own health or safety, or for the protection of others
  • (3) appropriate treatment is available (treatment includes nursing and care, not just drugs) — this third criterion applies to the treatment sections such as s3, not to s2.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Can the MHA treat a patient WITH capacity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: Yes — the MHA can detain and treat a mental disorder even in a person WITH capacity, if the detention criteria are met (a key contrast with the MCA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is the scope rule for MHA treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: The MHA only permits treatment of the mental disorder — NOT unrelated physical illness — unless the physical problem is a cause or consequence of the mental disorder (e.g. refeeding in anorexia, treating an overdose taken as part of the disorder).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Who is the AMHP, and what is their role?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: The Approved Mental Health Professional (usually a social worker) — makes the APPLICATION for detention.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is a Section 12(2) approved doctor?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• A doctor with special MHA training (usually a psychiatrist)
  • one of the two doctors for a Section 2 or 3 must be Section 12-approved.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Who is the Responsible Clinician (RC)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: The clinician in overall charge of the detained patient's care.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is the application principle for detention (who recommends vs applies)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: Detention needs medical recommendation(s) from doctors PLUS an application (usually by the AMHP) — the doctors recommend, the AMHP applies.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is Section 2, its duration and requirements?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• Admission for ASSESSMENT (± treatment)
  • up to 28 days, NOT renewable
  • AMHP (or nearest relative) applies on the recommendation of 2 doctors (one Section 12-approved).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is Section 3, its duration and requirements?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• Admission for TREATMENT
  • up to 6 months, renewable
  • AMHP (or nearest relative) + 2 doctors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: How do you distinguish Section 2 from Section 3?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• S2 = assessment, 28 days, not renewable (diagnosis/plan not yet established)
  • S3 = treatment, 6 months, renewable (disorder already known).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is Section 4?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• EMERGENCY admission when waiting for a second doctor would cause dangerous delay
  • 72 hours
  • 1 doctor + AMHP/NR
  • usually converted to S2 on arrival.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is Section 5(2) vs Section 5(4)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
Holding powers for a patient already admitted as a voluntary INPATIENT.
  • S5(2) = the doctor or approved clinician in charge of the patient's treatment, or their nominated deputy, for 72 hours, on any ward.
  • S5(4) = a registered mental health or learning disability nurse, for 6 hours, and only where the patient is receiving inpatient treatment for mental disorder.
Both only buy time for a full assessment and cannot treat against wishes.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: Do holding powers (S5(2)/S5(4)) apply in A&E?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: No — s5 applies only to a patient already admitted as an inpatient, so not in A&E and not to an outpatient. Other routes apply there: s136 (which now reaches hospital premises), or the MCA where the person lacks capacity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is Section 17A?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: A Community Treatment Order (CTO) — supervised community treatment, made only for a patient detained under s3, by the responsible clinician with AMHP agreement, lasting 6 months and renewable. Recall to hospital requires that the patient needs treatment in hospital for the mental disorder AND that there would be a risk of harm otherwise — non-compliance alone is not enough.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is Section 135 vs Section 136?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• S135 = a court warrant lets police enter a private dwelling to remove a person to a place of safety, accompanied by an AMHP and a doctor, for up to 24 hours.
  • S136 = police remove a person from any place other than a private dwelling (so a workplace, car park, or hospital premises including A&E), without a warrant, to a place of safety for up to 24 hours from arrival — extendable once by up to 12 hours — for MHA assessment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What are the key rights/safeguards for a detained patient?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• The right to appeal to a Mental Health Tribunal (and hospital managers)
  • a Second Opinion Appointed Doctor (SOAD) for certain treatments
  • and an Independent Mental Health Advocate (IMHA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: When is a SOAD (Second Opinion Appointed Doctor) required?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: Medication for mental disorder continued beyond 3 months requires a Second Opinion Appointed Doctor. ECT is stricter: it cannot be given to a detained patient who has capacity and refuses it, and a SOAD may certify it only where the patient lacks capacity. These safeguards are set aside for urgent treatment immediately necessary to save life, prevent serious deterioration, alleviate serious suffering or prevent danger.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is the key discriminator between the MHA and the MCA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back:
• The MHA can treat a mental disorder even in a patient WITH capacity (if detention criteria met)
  • the MCA only applies when capacity is LACKING and covers any decision in best interests.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.front: What is the 'overlap trap' between the MCA and MHA?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.back: You cannot use the MCA to give treatment that a valid advance decision refuses, nor to detain someone for a mental disorder where the MHA is the correct route. Conversely, an advance decision does not block treatment for mental disorder in a patient detained under the MHA — except ECT.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is a learning disability (LD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: A lifelong condition of significantly reduced intellectual ability AND reduced ability to cope independently (adaptive/social functioning), which started before adulthood and has a lasting effect on development.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What are the three defining elements of a learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back:
• (1) Impaired intelligence (IQ approximately below 70 — about two standard deviations below the mean, allowing for measurement error)
  • (2) impaired adaptive/social functioning
  • and (3) onset before adulthood
— all three are required.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Is a low IQ alone enough to diagnose a learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: No — IQ < 70 alone is NOT a learning disability without impaired adaptive functioning AND childhood onset; all three elements are required.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Does an adult who loses cognitive function later (dementia, brain injury) have a learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: No — LD must be present from the developmental period (before adulthood); acquired cognitive impairment in adult life is not a learning disability.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: How does 'learning disability' differ from 'learning difficulty'?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back:
• Learning disability = global intellectual impairment (UK term ≈ 'intellectual disability')
  • a learning difficulty (e.g. dyslexia) is a SPECIFIC difficulty without global intellectual impairment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What IQ range and functional level defines MILD learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: IQ ~50–69; often independent living with support, may have jobs/relationships — the majority of people with LD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What IQ ranges define moderate, severe and profound LD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back:
• Moderate 35-49 (need support with daily living)
  • severe 20-34 (significant support, limited communication)
  • profound below 20 (full support, often multiple physical disabilities)
— IQ bands are a guide only; severity is graded primarily on adaptive functioning and support needs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Which severity of LD is most common?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: Mild LD (IQ 50–69) — most people with LD have mild LD and can live relatively independently with support.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: List the genetic/chromosomal causes of LD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back:
• Down's syndrome (trisomy 21)
  • Fragile X (the commonest INHERITED cause)
  • Prader-Willi and Williams syndromes.
Down's syndrome carries specific risks — congenital heart disease, hypothyroidism, hearing and vision loss, atlantoaxial instability, leukaemia and early-onset Alzheimer's dementia; Fragile X is associated with autism, ADHD and anxiety. Klinefelter's and Turner's syndromes usually cause specific learning difficulties with IQ in the normal range, not a learning disability.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is the commonest inherited cause of learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: Fragile X syndrome.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Give antenatal and perinatal causes of LD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back:
• Antenatal — congenital (TORCH) infection, fetal alcohol syndrome, teratogens
  • perinatal — birth asphyxia (HIE), prematurity, kernicterus.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Give a metabolic and postnatal cause of LD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back:
• Metabolic — phenylketonuria (PKU) and other inborn errors (newborn blood spot)
  • postnatal — meningitis/encephalitis, head injury, non-accidental injury.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Which conditions commonly co-occur with learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back:
• Epilepsy (especially severe LD)
  • physical/sensory disability
  • cerebral palsy
  • mental illness (depression, anxiety, psychosis)
  • autism and ADHD
  • and behaviour that challenges.
The commonest causes of death are respiratory — especially aspiration pneumonia related to dysphagia — along with ischaemic heart disease, epilepsy and complications of constipation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is the key principle about 'behaviour that challenges' in LD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: It is often the expression of an underlying problem — pain, constipation, infection, dental problems, sensory overload or distress — so look for the cause, don't just sedate.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is diagnostic overshadowing?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: Wrongly attributing a person's symptoms to their learning disability rather than investigating a genuine physical/mental illness (e.g. assuming distress 'is just their LD' when they have appendicitis) — a major cause of avoidable harm/death.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What are 'reasonable adjustments', and what law underpins them?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: A legal duty (Equality Act 2010) to adapt care — longer appointments, easy-read information, a quiet environment, a hospital passport — so people with LD can access healthcare equitably.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is a hospital passport?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: A document the person brings that describes their needs, communication, likes/dislikes and how they show pain — supporting reasonable adjustments in hospital.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is the annual health check for people with LD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: People with a learning disability aged 14 and over who are on their GP practice's learning disability register are invited for an annual health check, producing a health action plan, to detect unmet or undiagnosed needs (they under-report symptoms).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What does STOMP / STAMP stand for?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: Stopping Over-Medication of People with a learning disability, autism or both (with psychotropics) / STAMP is the children's equivalent — reducing inappropriate psychotropic prescribing.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is LeDeR?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: Learning from lives and deaths — the national programme reviewing the deaths of people with a learning disability aged 4 and over and of autistic adults, to identify and reduce avoidable mortality. It has found a median age at death of around 63 against about 82 in the general population, with roughly twice the proportion of deaths judged avoidable.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: Statutory LD/autism training for health and social care staff, named after a young man who died from an antipsychotic given despite a known adverse reaction.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Which two concepts underpin safe healthcare for people with a learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: Diagnostic overshadowing (don't blame new symptoms on the LD — investigate) and reasonable adjustments (a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Does having a learning disability mean a person lacks capacity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: No — LD does NOT automatically mean lacking capacity; presume capacity, assess it decision-specifically, and provide support to decide (Mental Capacity Act). No relative can consent on an adult's behalf unless they hold a health and welfare lasting power of attorney or are a court-appointed deputy; otherwise a best-interests decision is made.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: How should communication be adapted for a person with LD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back:
Adapt to their level —
  • easy-read materials
  • pictures
  • short sentences
  • extra time
  • and involve carers who know them.
(Ask Listen Do is the separate national approach to making it easier for people and families to give feedback, raise concerns and complain.)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is the first-line, evidence-based approach to behaviour that challenges?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: Positive Behaviour Support (PBS) — after first looking for and treating any underlying cause (pain, constipation, infection, dental, distress, environment). If an antipsychotic is nevertheless used, it must be combined with psychological or other interventions, reviewed by the multidisciplinary team, and reduced or stopped if it is not clearly helping (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: What is the overarching management principle in learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: A multidisciplinary, person-centred support model — treat comorbidities, make reasonable adjustments, avoid over-medication (STOMP), and address the cause of behaviour that challenges; LD itself is not 'curable'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Who makes up the community learning disability team?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: LD nurses, psychiatry, psychology, SALT, OT, physiotherapy and social care — plus education/employment and family/carer support.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.front: Why is safeguarding especially important in learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.back: People with LD are at higher risk of abuse and neglect, so safeguarding awareness must be maintained in every contact.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What are eating disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Psychiatric illnesses with prominent physical consequences — disturbed eating behaviour with an over-valuation of weight/shape (anorexia, bulimia) or restricted intake (ARFID).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the 'core concept' of eating disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: They are serious medical as well as psychiatric conditions — anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (from medical complications + suicide) — so recognising physical risk sits alongside the psychological diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Describe the epidemiology of eating disorders.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Predominantly adolescents/young adults, commoner in females, with high comorbidity with depression, anxiety and OCD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: By what three features are the eating disorders distinguished?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Weight
  • the presence of binge/purge behaviour
  • and the driving belief

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Summarise anorexia nervosa (weight, behaviour, driving belief).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Low weight (restriction → underweight)
  • restriction ± excessive exercise (± purging)
  • driven by a fear of weight gain and a distorted body image

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Summarise bulimia nervosa (weight, behaviour, driving belief).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Usually normal or slightly high weight
  • a binge + compensatory purging cycle (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, exercise)
  • driven by a fear of weight gain and over-valuation of shape/weight (signs: Russell's sign, dental erosion)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Summarise ARFID (weight, behaviour, driving belief).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Low/normal weight from inadequate intake
  • avoidant/restrictive eating driven NOT by body image but by sensory aversion, fear of aversive consequences (e.g. choking), or low interest in food
  • there is no body-image disturbance

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: State the high-yield rule distinguishing the three eating disorders.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Anorexia = low weight + body-image disturbance
  • bulimia = normal weight + binge-purge cycle
  • ARFID = restricted intake WITHOUT body-image concern (its distinguishing feature)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Which psychiatric disorder has the highest mortality, and why?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Anorexia nervosa — from medical complications of starvation plus suicide.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What are the core clinical features of anorexia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• A markedly low body weight
  • an intense fear of weight gain
  • a distorted body image
  • and restriction ± excessive exercise/purging

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What are the cardiovascular/thermoregulatory physical signs of anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Bradycardia
  • hypotension
  • hypothermia and cold peripheries

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is lanugo hair, and why does it occur in anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Fine downy hair — a response to the loss of body fat (to conserve heat).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What other physical signs occur in anorexia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Enlarged (parotid) salivary glands where there is purging, and amenorrhoea.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the sit-up–squat–stand test, and what does it indicate in anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: A red-flag bedside test — an inability to rise without using the arms indicates severe proximal muscle wasting, a marker of severity/risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the memory hook for the biochemical picture of anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: 'Most things are low, but GH and the C's are raised.' Note that glucose is LOW, despite some revision sources listing it among the 'G's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Which values are LOW in anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Glucose (glycogen and gluconeogenic substrate are depleted — hypoglycaemia is a marker of medical risk)
  • potassium (especially with purging — often normal in pure restriction, so normal bloods do NOT exclude high physical risk)
  • FSH
  • LH
  • oestrogen
  • testosterone
  • and T3

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Which values are raised in anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Growth hormone (with a low IGF-1 — a state of GH resistance)
  • cortisol
  • cholesterol
  • and carotene
Note that glucose is LOW, not raised, despite some revision sources listing it among the 'G's'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Which values are raised in anorexia — the 'C's'?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Cortisol (stress response)
  • Cholesterol (cortisol mobilises fat)
  • and Carotenaemia (raised carotene)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Why does amenorrhoea occur in anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Hypothalamic suppression reduces FSH/LH and hence oestrogen, causing amenorrhoea.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Why do bradycardia, hypotension and hypothermia occur in anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: They are physiological adaptations to starvation — a reduced metabolic rate to conserve energy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the critical medical complication to anticipate when treating anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Refeeding syndrome.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is bulimia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: A disorder of recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory purging (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, diuretics or excessive exercise), driven by an over-valuation of weight/shape.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the key weight contrast between bulimia and anorexia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Bulimia is usually of NORMAL weight (or slightly high), whereas anorexia is markedly underweight — normal weight is the key distinguishing feature of bulimia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What defines the core behavioural cycle of bulimia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Recurrent binges (eating a large amount with a sense of loss of control) followed by compensatory behaviours to prevent weight gain — vomiting, laxatives, diuretics or excessive exercise.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What drives bulimia nervosa psychologically?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: An over-valuation of weight and shape — self-worth is excessively judged by body weight/shape, as in anorexia, but without the markedly low weight.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is Russell's sign?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Calluses or scarring over the knuckles/back of the hand, caused by repeated self-induced vomiting (teeth abrading the skin) — a high-yield sign of bulimia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What dental sign occurs in bulimia, and why?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Dental erosion and enamel loss — from repeated exposure of the teeth to gastric acid during self-induced vomiting.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Which glands enlarge in bulimia, and why?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: The (parotid) salivary glands — enlarge in response to repeated vomiting, giving a characteristic 'chipmunk' facial appearance.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the characteristic electrolyte/acid–base disturbance in bulimia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — H+ and Cl- are lost in the vomitus, and volume loss activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system so aldosterone wastes K+ in the urine (dangerous, as hypokalaemia risks arrhythmias).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: List the high-yield physical signs of purging in bulimia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Russell's sign (knuckle calluses)
  • dental erosion/enamel loss
  • enlarged parotid glands
  • and hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: State the high-yield rule distinguishing bulimia from anorexia.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Bulimia = normal weight + binge–purge cycle + signs of purging (Russell's sign, dental erosion, parotid enlargement)
  • anorexia = markedly low weight + body-image disturbance

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How is bulimia nervosa managed (NICE)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Guided self-help based on CBT first-line, then bulimia-specific CBT (CBT-ED)
  • an SSRI (fluoxetine, at a higher dose ~60 mg) may help
  • plus monitoring/correcting electrolytes and dental review

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Which antidepressant is specifically used in bulimia, and at what dose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Fluoxetine, at a higher dose than for depression (~60 mg daily) — the SSRI of choice in bulimia, but as an adjunct only: medication must not be the sole treatment (NICE). Check potassium and the ECG first, as purging patients are often hypokalaemic with a prolonged QTc.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is ARFID?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder — restriction or avoidance of food intake leading to nutritional/energy deficiency, WITHOUT any body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the defining feature of ARFID?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: The restriction is NOT driven by body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain — this is what separates it from anorexia nervosa.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What are the three drivers of restriction in ARFID?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Sensory sensitivity (texture/taste/smell aversion)
  • fear of an aversive consequence (e.g. choking or vomiting)
  • and low interest in eating/appetite

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What consequences define/justify a diagnosis of ARFID?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Significant weight loss or faltering growth
  • nutritional deficiency
  • dependence on supplements/enteral feeding
  • or marked psychosocial impairment

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: In whom is ARFID more common?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Children and people with neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g. autism spectrum disorder and ADHD).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Why is ARFID described as a diagnosis of exclusion?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: You must first rule out anorexia nervosa (no body-image disturbance in ARFID), organic GI causes and other medical illness before diagnosing it.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How does ARFID differ from normal 'fussy eating'?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: ARFID is distinguished by significant consequences — weight loss/faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, supplement dependence or psychosocial impairment — beyond ordinary picky eating.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How is ARFID distinguished from anorexia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Both may be underweight, but ARFID has NO body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain — the restriction is driven by sensory aversion, fear of an aversive event, or low interest in food.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How is ARFID managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: A multidisciplinary approach — dietetic support plus psychological therapy (often CBT-based, addressing the specific driver), with family involvement in children.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: State the high-yield one-line rule for ARFID.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: ARFID = restricted intake with nutritional consequences but WITHOUT body-image concern (its distinguishing feature), commonest in children and autism.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is refeeding syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: A dangerous metabolic shift when nutrition is reintroduced too quickly in a malnourished patient — carbohydrate drives an insulin surge that pushes potassium, magnesium and phosphate INTO cells, dropping their plasma levels.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the hallmark biochemical abnormality of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Hypophosphataemia (low phosphate) — the single most characteristic finding, alongside fluid shifts and thiamine depletion.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the high-yield biochemical triad of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: ↓Phosphate, ↓potassium and ↓magnesium (all driven intracellularly by the insulin surge).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the underlying mechanism of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Reintroduced carbohydrate → surge in insulin → insulin drives potassium, magnesium and phosphate into cells faster than depleted stores can tolerate → plasma levels fall; thiamine is also consumed as metabolism restarts.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What are the clinical features of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Oedema and fluid shifts
  • confusion and seizures
  • arrhythmias/tachycardia and cardiac failure
  • and hypokalaemic ECG changes (prominent U waves, flattened T waves)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What ECG changes occur with the hypokalaemia of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Prominent U waves and flattened T waves (hypokalaemia), with a risk of arrhythmias.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Why must thiamine be given in refeeding?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Restarting carbohydrate metabolism rapidly consumes thiamine (a cofactor); depletion risks Wernicke's encephalopathy — so thiamine (+ B vitamins) is given before/with feeding.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How is refeeding syndrome managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
Identify high-risk patients —
  • BMI under 16
  • unintentional weight loss over 15% in 3-6 months
  • negligible intake for more than 10 days
  • or a low K+/phosphate/magnesium before feeding
— and start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg/day in extreme risk), building to full requirements over 4-7 days with cardiac monitoring.
  • Replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium
  • give thiamine 200-300 mg daily plus B vitamins immediately before and throughout the first 10 days
  • monitor electrolytes closely
Correct electrolytes alongside feeding rather than withholding nutrition — sustained under-feeding is itself harmful.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the physiological link that explains refeeding syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: It is the fed-state insulin surge applied to a depleted body — insulin drives electrolytes intracellularly faster than depleted stores can cope with.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What electrolyte/acid–base picture results from recurrent vomiting (purging)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — seen with purging in either anorexia or bulimia. Note that laxative misuse causes the opposite picture: a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, also with hypokalaemia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Why does recurrent vomiting cause a metabolic alkalosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Vomiting loses H⁺ and Cl⁻ (gastric acid), so the loss of hydrogen ions produces a metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Why does recurrent vomiting cause hypokalaemia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Volume loss activates the RAAS → aldosterone retains Na⁺/water and excretes K⁺ in the urine → hypokalaemia; diuretic misuse compounds the potassium loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What ECG changes result from the hypokalaemia of purging?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Flattened T waves and U waves (as in any hypokalaemia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How does diuretic misuse affect the purging electrolyte picture?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: It compounds the potassium loss, worsening the hypokalaemia already caused by vomiting-induced RAAS activation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: How are eating disorders diagnosed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Clinically — from the history, eating behaviour and body-image beliefs, combined with a physical assessment; there is no single diagnostic test.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What must the physical risk assessment in an eating disorder cover?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Weight/BMI trend
  • observations (bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia)
  • muscle power (sit-up–squat–stand test)
  • bloods and an ECG

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: Which bloods are checked in an eating disorder assessment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• U&E
  • phosphate
  • magnesium
  • glucose
  • FBC
  • LFT and TFT

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is looked for on the ECG in an eating disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Bradycardia
  • a prolonged QTc (over 450 ms)
  • and features of hypokalaemia (flattened T waves, U waves)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What comorbidities/risks must be screened for in an eating disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Comorbid depression, anxiety and OCD, plus self-harm/suicide risk and substance misuse.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the SCOFF questionnaire?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: A brief 5-item screening tool for eating disorders (Sick, Control, One stone, Fat, Food); two or more 'yes' answers is a positive screen and prompts referral to a specialist eating disorder service.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the overarching management principle for eating disorders (NICE)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Psychological therapy is the mainstay
  • medical risk is treated in parallel
  • and drugs have only a limited role

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line psychological treatment for anorexia nervosa in ADULTS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
• Individual eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-ED)
  • MANTRA (Maudsley Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults)
  • or SSCM (Specialist Supportive Clinical Management)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line psychological treatment for anorexia nervosa in CHILDREN/young people?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-AN); CBT-ED is second-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the role of drugs in anorexia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: No drug is first-line for anorexia itself — psychological therapy is the mainstay, with medical risk managed in parallel (electrolytes, refeeding, monitoring) and admission if physical risk is high.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line management of bulimia nervosa in ADULTS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help; if unacceptable or ineffective after ~4 weeks, move to CBT-ED.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line management of bulimia nervosa in CHILDREN/young people?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Family therapy for bulimia (FT-BN); CBT-ED is second-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the drug adjunct in bulimia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: An SSRI (fluoxetine) can reduce binge/purge frequency — an adjunct, not the mainstay.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the first-line management of binge eating disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Guided self-help first-line, then CBT-ED if needed.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: What is the management of ARFID?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back: Multidisciplinary dietetic plus psychological management, tailored to the specific driver of restriction.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.front: When should a patient with anorexia be admitted?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.back:
When physical risk is high — for example
  • a heart rate below 40
  • systolic BP below 90 with a marked postural drop
  • temperature below 35.5C
  • inability to sit up or stand without using the arms
  • QTc over 450 ms
  • potassium below 3.0 mmol/L
  • hypoglycaemia
  • or a BMI below 13 in an adult
— to manage refeeding and medical risk safely.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What unites the depressive disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A shared core depressive syndrome — persistent low mood, anhedonia and reduced energy for ≥2 weeks, plus cognitive/biological symptoms — differing mainly in context, timing and trigger, not in the core symptoms.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the organising principle of the depressive disorders?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
The same underlying depression presenting in a different pattern:
  • major depression is the baseline
  • seasonal affective disorder is depression with a seasonal (usually winter) pattern
  • postnatal depression is depression with perinatal onset

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Summarise major depression within the group.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: The core depressive syndrome with no specific temporal pattern; managed with stepped/matched care — psychological options ± an SSRI, and ECT if severe/life-threatening.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Summarise seasonal affective disorder.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Depression with a recurrent seasonal onset (autumn/winter, spring remission), often with atypical features (hypersomnia, increased appetite/carbohydrate craving); treated as depression, with light therapy as an option.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Summarise postnatal depression.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Depression with onset within ~12 months of birth (peak in the early weeks), distinct from transient 'baby blues'; managed with psychological therapy matched to severity, adding an SSRI (sertraline if breastfeeding) for moderate-to-severe illness, and assessing the mother–infant bond.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What must never be missed in any depressive presentation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Screen for bipolarity (a past manic/hypomanic episode) and assess suicide risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What perinatal distinctions must be made in a depressed new mother?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Distinguish 'baby blues' (self-limiting, <2 weeks) and postpartum psychosis (a psychiatric emergency), and assess the risk to the infant.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Why must you screen for mania/hypomania before starting an antidepressant?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Because an unrecognised bipolar disorder given an antidepressant alone risks precipitating mania.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A mood disorder characterised by persistent low mood, anhedonia and reduced energy, with associated cognitive, biological and functional symptoms, lasting ≥2 weeks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: On what does the diagnosis of depression rest, and what is the key modern management principle?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Three core symptoms + other symptoms + duration (≥2 weeks); and, per NICE, a 'less severe vs more severe' matched-care model in which antidepressants are NOT routinely first-line for less severe depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What conditions must be excluded before diagnosing primary (unipolar) depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• Bipolar depression (any past mania/hypomania — changes management entirely)
  • organic/secondary causes (hypothyroidism, anaemia, B12 deficiency, Cushing's, drugs like steroids/β-blockers, substance misuse)
  • pseudodementia in older adults
  • grief/adjustment
  • and anxiety disorders

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the three core symptoms of depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• Low mood (often worst in the morning — diurnal variation)
  • anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure)
  • and reduced energy/fatigue

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: List the 'other' symptoms of depression.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• Reduced concentration
  • guilt and worthlessness
  • appetite/weight change
  • sleep disturbance (early morning waking)
  • suicidal ideation
  • psychomotor retardation/agitation
  • and reduced libido

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: State the ICD severity grades of depression.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Mild = 2 core + 2 other; moderate = 2 core + 3+ other; severe = 3 core + ≥4 other (± psychosis) — all for ≥2 weeks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the biological ('somatic') symptoms of depression, and their significance?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Early morning waking, diurnal mood variation (worse in the morning), appetite/weight loss, reduced libido and psychomotor changes — pointing to more significant depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the validated tool used to assess and monitor depression severity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: The PHQ-9 (the two Whooley questions are the case-finding screen).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the current NICE severity classification, mapped to PHQ-9?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Two categories: 'less severe' (subthreshold + mild, PHQ-9 <16) and 'more severe' (moderate + severe, PHQ-9 ≥16).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What investigations are used in depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• Clinical diagnosis (history + mental state exam + PHQ-9)
  • bloods to exclude mimics (TFTs, FBC, U&E, B12/folate, calcium, glucose, LFTs)
  • assess suicide/self-harm risk and screen for bipolarity

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the overarching management principle for depression (NICE)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Match treatment to severity + preference; antidepressants are NOT routinely first-line for less severe depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is LESS severe depression (PHQ-9 <16) managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Do NOT routinely offer an antidepressant first-line (only if it is the person's informed preference or has worked before); offer less intrusive psychological/behavioural options (guided self-help, group/individual CBT or behavioural activation, group exercise, mindfulness, IPT, counselling); an SSRI is on the menu but not preferred; active monitoring if treatment is declined.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is MORE severe depression (PHQ-9 ≥16) managed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Offer a combination matched to preference — antidepressant + individual CBT is typical first-line, or high-intensity psychological therapy, or an antidepressant alone; the first-line antidepressant is an SSRI.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: When should an antidepressant be reviewed after starting?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: At 2 weeks and in any case within 4 weeks — or at 1 week if the patient is under 25 or at increased risk of suicide (higher early suicidal-thought risk), and again 1 week after each dose increase.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: For how long should an antidepressant be continued after remission?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: At least 6 months after remission (longer if recurrent) to reduce relapse.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How should antidepressants be stopped?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: By reducing the dose in stages — each step a proportion of the previous dose, with smaller steps at lower doses, and the next step only once withdrawal symptoms have settled (NICE); fluoxetine's long half-life allows a shorter, simpler reduction but it is not stopped abruptly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the first-line antidepressant, in adults and in children/adolescents?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: An SSRI — sertraline in adults; fluoxetine in children/adolescents ('fluoxeTEEN'), started after specialist review and only alongside concurrent psychological therapy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the key side effects of SSRIs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: GI upset, early anxiety/agitation and sexual dysfunction; hyponatraemia/SIADH (older people, low body weight, on diuretics) — suspect it and check U&E in anyone who becomes drowsy, confused, unsteady or has a seizure; and GI bleeding. Citalopram and escitalopram prolong the QT: maximum citalopram 40 mg daily (20 mg if over 65 or in hepatic impairment) and escitalopram 20 mg (10 mg if over 65), avoided with known long QT or other QT-prolonging drugs (MHRA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the important SSRI drug interactions?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: SSRIs increase GI bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, aspirin, clopidogrel, DOACs or warfarin — do not normally offer an SSRI with an NSAID or with warfarin (consider mirtazapine instead), and add a PPI if an SSRI is unavoidable. Triptans and MAOIs risk serotonin syndrome.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is SSRI discontinuation syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: On abrupt stopping — GI upset, mood change, insomnia, restlessness, sweating, unsteadiness and paraesthesia ('electric shocks') — avoided by reducing the dose in stages (least likely with fluoxetine, because of its long half-life).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the pregnancy considerations with SSRIs?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A small increase in congenital cardiac malformations is reported mainly with paroxetine in the first trimester (absolute risk small — avoid paroxetine); 3rd trimester → persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn and neonatal adaptation symptoms. Do not stop an effective antidepressant abruptly on finding out about a pregnancy — decide with the perinatal mental health team.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the key caution with SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: They are associated with hypertension — check blood pressure before starting and at each titration.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe mirtazapine and its useful niche.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A tetracyclic that blocks α2 receptors → increased noradrenaline/serotonin; it has fewer interactions (good in the elderly/polypharmacy) and its side effects — sedation and increased appetite — make it useful where there is insomnia/poor appetite ('mirtaZapine — zzz + mmm').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe TCAs (amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Not first-line (side-effect burden and overdose danger); more used for neuropathic pain; they block histamine/muscarinic/adrenergic receptors → anticholinergic effects ('can't see, pee, spit, shit'), postural hypotension and QT prolongation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the features of TCA overdose?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Confusion, tachycardia, hypotension, mydriasis, a prolonged QRS + QTc, metabolic acidosis and seizures — TCAs are the most dangerous antidepressant class in overdose.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe MAOIs and their key dietary danger.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Phenelzine/tranylcypromine, used for atypical depression (rare); a tyramine ('cheese') reaction — aged cheese/cured meats with an MAOI → a hypertensive crisis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What causes serotonin syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Excess serotonergic activity — e.g. SSRI + MAOI, SSRI + a triptan/tramadol, or overdose.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the triad of serotonin syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• Neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity, tremor)
  • autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating)
  • altered mental state (agitation, confusion)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is serotonin syndrome managed, and how does it differ from NMS?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Stop all serotonergic drugs, arrange urgent hospital assessment, give IV fluids, benzodiazepines and active cooling — hyperthermia with rigidity is the life-threatening feature and needs critical care (antipyretics do not work) — with cyproheptadine in severe cases. Serotonin syndrome has hyperreflexia/clonus with rapid onset, whereas NMS has 'lead-pipe' rigidity + hyporeflexia with slower onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the indications for ECT, and its most important contraindication?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Severe, life-threatening or treatment-refractory depression — especially catatonia, refusal of food/fluids, strong suicidal intent, when a rapid response is needed, or where the person chooses ECT on the basis of their own past experience of it. There are no absolute contraindications; raised intracranial pressure is the most important relative one, and ECT is a risk-benefit decision made with the anaesthetist.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the side effects and delivery of ECT?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Headache, nausea, short-term memory impairment, retrograde amnesia (events around treatment) and cardiac arrhythmia; it is given under general anaesthesia + a muscle relaxant, as a course of treatments.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is seasonal affective disorder (SAD)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A form of recurrent depression with a seasonal pattern — episodes that reliably occur at a particular time of year (classically winter) and remit at another (spring/summer).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the 'core concept' of SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: It is not a separate disease but depression with a seasonal pattern specifier — diagnosis and management are those of depression, plus the seasonal timing and one SAD-specific option (light therapy).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the distinguishing feature of SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A regular, predictable relationship between mood episodes and the season, present for ≥2 consecutive years.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: State the high-yield rule for diagnosing SAD.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: SAD = depressive episodes with a consistent seasonal pattern (≥2 years); the winter pattern is classic (a rarer summer pattern exists), and a single winter of low mood is not enough.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the 'atypical' features of winter SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• Hypersomnia (sleeping more, not early-morning waking)
  • hyperphagia with carbohydrate craving → weight gain
  • and fatigue/leaden heaviness with low energy

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How do the symptoms of SAD contrast with typical depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: SAD (atypical) = hypersomnia, hyperphagia and weight gain; typical depression = insomnia (early-morning waking), reduced appetite and weight loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the epidemiology of SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Linked to reduced winter daylight; commoner at higher latitudes and in women.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the pathophysiology of SAD, and its therapeutic rationale?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Reduced winter daylight affects circadian rhythm and melatonin/serotonin regulation (less light → altered melatonin secretion and circadian phase) — the rationale for light therapy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is SAD assessed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Clinically — a history of recurrent depressive episodes with a seasonal pattern (seasonality over ≥2 years) and PHQ-9 for severity; exclude organic mimics (especially hypothyroidism, which also causes winter fatigue/low mood/weight gain), and screen for suicide risk and comorbidity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the overarching management principle for SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Treat it as depression (per NICE) — psychological therapy and/or an SSRI — with light therapy as a SAD-specific adjunct.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is SAD treated according to severity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• Less severe → psychological/behavioural interventions (e.g. CBT) first-line
  • more severe → an SSRI + psychological therapy (SSRI being the first-line drug)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is light therapy in SAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Exposure to a bright light box, particularly in the morning, which can help winter SAD; the evidence is modest/mixed so it is an adjunct/option, but it is the intervention uniquely associated with SAD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is SAD treated, and what is the prophylaxis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Treat as depression — psychological therapy and/or an SSRI matched to severity — with lifestyle measures (maximise natural daylight, exercise, regular routine). Light therapy is the SAD-specific option, though it is not recommended by NICE because the evidence is limited. Those with a reliable seasonal pattern may start treatment before the season begins.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the place of hypnotics in seasonal affective disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: They are not a treatment — hypnotics do not treat depression, and they add daytime sedation to an already hypersomnic, low-energy picture.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is postnatal (postpartum) depression (PND)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: A depressive episode arising in the postnatal period — meeting the criteria for depression, in the context of new motherhood — distinct from the transient 'baby blues'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the 'perinatal mood triad', and where does PND sit?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Baby blues (mild, transient) → postnatal depression (a true depressive illness) → postpartum psychosis (a psychiatric emergency); PND sits in the middle, and the triad is distinguished by timing and severity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe 'baby blues'.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Onset days 3–10; mild, transient tearfulness, mood lability, irritability and anxiety; resolves spontaneously within ~2 weeks; managed with reassurance and support only (very common, ~50–80%).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe postnatal depression (timing, features, course).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Onset over weeks–months (up to 1 year); a moderate–severe depressive illness with persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, guilt, poor bonding and sleep/appetite change; persistent without treatment (~10–15%).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Describe postpartum psychosis.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Acute onset (usually within the first ~2 weeks) of psychosis, mania, confusion or severe depression with psychotic features; a psychiatric EMERGENCY, rapidly evolving and dangerous (~1–2/1000), needing urgent admission (Mother & Baby Unit).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the key discriminator across the perinatal mood triad?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Baby blues resolves on its own within ~2 weeks — if low mood persists beyond 2 weeks or is severe, think PND; acute psychosis/mania in the first 2 weeks is postpartum psychosis (an emergency).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Why must perinatal mental illness be actively screened for?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: It is common (~10–20% of women) and a leading cause of maternal death (suicide) in the year after birth — so it must be actively sought and taken seriously.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What are the perinatal-specific clinical features of PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
Core depressive symptoms plus
  • concerns about/difficulty with maternal–infant bonding
  • guilt about not coping/not being a 'good mother'
  • and anxiety about the baby's health

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What two areas of risk must always be asked about directly in PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Thoughts of self-harm/suicide AND any thoughts of harming the infant — both must be asked about directly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: List risk factors for PND.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• A past history of depression/PND or other mental illness
  • family history
  • lack of social support
  • relationship difficulties
  • an unplanned/complicated pregnancy or birth
  • and socioeconomic stress
  • a history of postpartum psychosis or bipolar disorder is a major risk (especially for postpartum psychosis)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the validated screening tool for PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) — a 10-item tool (a score ~≥10–13 prompts further assessment; one item screens for self-harm); the Whooley questions are also used.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What must be excluded when assessing suspected PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Hypothyroidism (postpartum thyroiditis is common and mimics PND — check TFTs), anaemia and other organic causes; also distinguish baby blues (timing/severity) and postpartum psychosis (psychosis/mania — an emergency).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the overarching management principle for PND (NICE)?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: Treat it as depression matched to severity, with a low threshold for support; choose medication compatible with breastfeeding; and involve the perinatal/health-visiting team — with psychological treatment matched to severity (facilitated self-help for mild-to-moderate, CBT or IPT for moderate-to-severe) and an antidepressant added by severity and risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: How is PND managed by severity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back:
• Mild–moderate → psychological therapy first-line (CBT or IPT, guided self-help) with health-visitor/social support
  • moderate–severe → psychological therapy + an antidepressant
  • severe/at-risk → specialist perinatal mental health services and consider admission to a Mother & Baby Unit (keeping mother and baby together)

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: What is the antidepressant choice in a breastfeeding mother with PND?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: SSRIs are generally compatible — sertraline (and paroxetine) are favoured (low levels in breast milk); effective treatment should not be withheld for fear of breastfeeding, as untreated PND harms both mother and baby; and psychiatric medication should NOT be stopped abruptly in pregnancy/postpartum (relapse risk) — decide with specialist input.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.front: Summarise postpartum psychosis and its management.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.back: An acute (usually first 2 weeks) psychosis/mania/confusion or psychotic depression, strongly associated with bipolar disorder/previous postpartum psychosis; a psychiatric emergency needing urgent assessment and admission (Mother & Baby Unit), treated with antipsychotics/mood stabilisers ± ECT.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: An acquired, chronic, usually progressive decline in cognition (memory, language, executive function, personality) severe enough to impair daily function, occurring in clear consciousness.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the three-step framework for approaching dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: (1) Is it dementia at all, or a mimic (delirium, depression)? → (2) which subtype? → (3) manage cognition + BPSD + risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Why do the mimics of dementia matter most?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Because delirium and depression are reversible and must not be mislabelled as dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is BPSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back:
Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia —
  • agitation
  • psychosis
  • depression
  • and sleep disturbance.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Contrast the onset/course of dementia, delirium and depression (pseudodementia).
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back:
• Dementia = insidious (months–years), progressive, stable day-to-day
  • delirium = acute (hours–days), fluctuating (worse at night)
  • depression = subacute (weeks), relatively stable.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Contrast consciousness/attention and memory in dementia vs delirium vs depression.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back:
• Dementia = clear consciousness (attention preserved early), early memory loss with the patient often unconcerned
  • delirium = clouded/inattentive (the hallmark), poor registration
  • depression = clear consciousness, 'don't know' answers with the patient worried.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: State the three pattern rules for dementia vs its mimics.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back:
• Acute + fluctuating + inattentive + clouded → delirium (exclude first)
  • short history + biological symptoms + patient distressed about memory + 'don't know' answers + global loss → depression (pseudodementia)
  • insidious + progressive + clear consciousness + patient unconcerned → dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Give the one-line discriminators for the four main dementia subtypes.
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back:
• Alzheimer's = memory first, gradual
  • vascular = stepwise + vascular risk factors + focal neurology
  • DLB = fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism
  • FTD = personality/language change first with memory spared early (younger, <65).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the commonest dementia, and its underlying pathology?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Alzheimer's disease (~60%) — insidious, gradual, early memory loss; pathology is amyloid-β plaques + tau neurofibrillary tangles with a cholinergic (↓ACh) deficit.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the pathology of the non-Alzheimer's dementia subtypes?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back:
• Vascular = cerebrovascular disease (stepwise)
  • DLB = α-synuclein (Lewy bodies)
  • frontotemporal dementia = tau (Pick bodies)/TDP-43.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the clinical hallmark of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Early, prominent memory loss (recent memories lost first), gradually progressing to global cognitive decline; it is the commonest dementia (~60%).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What are the '4 A's' of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back:
• Amnesia (recent memories lost first)
  • Aphasia (word-finding difficulty, muddled/disjointed speech)
  • Agnosia (recognition problems — faces, objects)
  • and Apraxia (inability to carry out skilled tasks despite normal motor function).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is amnesia in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Loss of memory, with recent memories lost first.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is aphasia in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Word-finding difficulty with muddled/disjointed speech.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is agnosia in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Difficulty recognising things — faces and objects.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is apraxia in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: An inability to carry out skilled tasks despite normal motor function.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the pathology of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the neurotransmitter deficit in Alzheimer's, and its therapeutic rationale?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: A cholinergic deficit (reduced acetylcholine) — the rationale for acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: How does the onset/course of Alzheimer's distinguish it from the other subtypes?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Alzheimer's is insidious and gradual with memory affected first — versus vascular (stepwise + vascular risk), DLB (fluctuating + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism) and FTD (personality/language first, memory spared early).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine (boosting acetylcholine to counter the cholinergic deficit) — started on specialist advice from a memory service, after which prescribing may continue in primary care (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the role of memantine in Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: An NMDA-receptor antagonist: monotherapy for severe Alzheimer's, or for moderate disease where an AChE inhibitor is not tolerated or contraindicated; also added to an AChE inhibitor in moderate or severe disease (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: Which conditions/factors increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back:
• Increasing age
  • family history
  • Down syndrome (an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21)
  • the ApoE4 allele
  • and vascular risk factors.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Cognitive impairment caused by cerebrovascular disease — the second commonest dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.front: What is the characteristic progression of vascular dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.back: Classically a stepwise progression — each 'step' represents a further vascular insult — often with focal neurology.
