conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.explanation: Doctors recommend and the AMHP applies. Section 2 needs two medical recommendations, at least one from a Section 12-approved doctor, with the application made by an approved mental health professional (or, rarely, the nearest relative).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.question: A 15-year-old requests contraception without parental knowledge. Which framework assesses whether she can consent?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.explanation: For under-16s, Gillick competence assesses sufficient understanding to consent; the Fraser guidelines apply specifically to contraceptive advice.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.question: Which statement best captures the difference between the MCA and the MHA?
options: They are fully interchangeable and either may be used for any decision in any patient
The MHA can treat mental disorder despite capacity; the MCA applies only without capacity
The MCA provides the power to detain a patient in hospital to treat mental disorder
The MHA can only be used once a patient has been formally shown to lack capacity
Only the MCA involves doctors, as the MHA is applied entirely by social workers
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.answer: The MHA can treat mental disorder despite capacity; the MCA applies only without capacity
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.explanation: The MHA can detain/treat a mental disorder even in a patient with capacity; the MCA applies only when capacity is lacking and covers any decision in best interests.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.question: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for detention under the Mental Health Act?
options: A mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention
Necessary for the person's health or safety, or to protect others
The patient must lack capacity to refuse the admission
Appropriate treatment is available for the mental disorder
The person must be assessed by an approved mental health professional
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.answer: The patient must lack capacity to refuse the admission
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health La.explanation: Detention requires a mental disorder, risk, and (for the treatment sections) available appropriate treatment — but NOT incapacity. The MHA can be used on a patient who has capacity and refuses, which is the key contrast with the Mental Capacity Act.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: A 20-year-old man has an IQ of 62, has needed lifelong support with self-care and daily living, and these difficulties were present throughout childhood. Which diagnosis best fits?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: Impaired intelligence (IQ < 70) PLUS impaired adaptive functioning PLUS onset before adulthood together define a learning disability.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: A 45-year-old with an IQ measured at 65 has always coped fully independently with work and self-care, with no childhood difficulties. Why does this NOT meet the definition of a learning disability?
options: An IQ of 65 is far too high to fall within the range
Learning disability cannot be diagnosed after age 40
No genetic or chromosomal cause has been identified
Adaptive impairment and childhood onset are also required
Diagnosis additionally requires an abnormal brain scan
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: Adaptive impairment and childhood onset are also required
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: All three elements are required — a significantly low IQ, impaired adaptive/social functioning, and onset in childhood. A low IQ alone, in someone who has always coped independently, is not a learning disability.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: A patient with a moderate learning disability presents with new agitation and refusing food. Staff assume it is 'just his learning disability'. He is later found to have a dental abscess. Which error best describes this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: Attributing genuine new symptoms to the LD rather than investigating is diagnostic overshadowing — a major cause of avoidable harm.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: Which legislation places a duty to make 'reasonable adjustments' so people with LD can access healthcare equitably?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: The Equality Act 2010 places a legal duty to make reasonable adjustments (e.g. longer appointments, easy-read information, hospital passport).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: What is the commonest INHERITED cause of learning disability?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited cause of learning disability (Down's syndrome is common but usually sporadic trisomy 21).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: A young adult with a severe learning disability begins hitting his head and becomes withdrawn. What is the most appropriate FIRST step?
options: Start an antipsychotic to bring the behaviour under control
Sedate him with a benzodiazepine until he settles down
Look for and treat an underlying cause such as pain or infection
Admit him to a psychiatric unit for further observation
Increase the dose of his existing regular medication
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: Look for and treat an underlying cause such as pain or infection
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: Behaviour that challenges is usually communicating something. Look for and treat an underlying cause — pain, constipation, infection, dental problems, distress or the environment — before anything else, then Positive Behaviour Support. Antipsychotics are not first-line (STOMP).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: A GP is asked to see a 15-year-old with a learning disability who is entitled to a specific preventive review. What is this?
options: An annual health check (for people with LD aged 14+)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: An annual health check (for people with LD aged 14+)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: People with a learning disability aged 14 and over are entitled to an annual GP health check to detect unmet or undiagnosed needs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: Which initiative specifically aims to reduce inappropriate psychotropic prescribing in people with a learning disability or autism?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: STOMP (Stopping Over-Medication of People with a learning disability, autism or both) targets inappropriate psychotropic prescribing.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: What is the evidence-based, first-line approach to managing behaviour that challenges in learning disability?
options: Positive Behaviour Support after looking for and treating any underlying cause
Regular antipsychotics prescribed as a routine measure
Long-term benzodiazepines to keep the person settled
Physical restraint used whenever the behaviour occurs
Seclusion in a locked room as the first response
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: Positive Behaviour Support after looking for and treating any underlying cause
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: Positive Behaviour Support is the evidence-based first-line approach, used once any underlying physical, psychiatric, communication or environmental cause has been sought and treated. Antipsychotics are not a substitute and should be reviewed and reduced.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: A woman with a mild learning disability needs to consent to a minor procedure. What is the correct approach to capacity?
options: Assume she lacks capacity because of her LD
Presume capacity, assess it decision-specifically and provide support to decide
Ask her family to consent instead automatically
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: Presume capacity, assess it decision-specifically and provide support to decide
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: A learning disability does not automatically mean lacking capacity — presume capacity, assess decision-specifically and support the person to decide (Mental Capacity Act).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: Which programme reviews the deaths of people with a learning disability to reduce avoidable mortality?
options: LeDeR (Learning from Lives and Deaths Reviews)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: LeDeR (Learning from Lives and Deaths Reviews)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: LeDeR (Learning from Lives and Deaths Reviews) reviews the deaths of people with LD to identify and reduce avoidable mortality.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: Which statement about the severity of learning disability is correct?
options: Most people have mild LD (IQ 50–69) and can live relatively independently with support
Most people with LD have profound LD
Severity determines the person's legal rights
Only severe LD counts as a learning disability
Severity is based on age alone
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: Most people have mild LD (IQ 50–69) and can live relatively independently with support
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: Most people with LD have mild LD (IQ 50–69) and can live relatively independently with support; severity guides support needs, not the person's rights or worth.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: How does a 'learning disability' differ from a 'learning difficulty' such as dyslexia?
options: They are the same thing, and the two terms are wholly interchangeable in use
A learning difficulty is by definition the more severe of the two conditions
A learning disability is always acquired in adulthood following a head injury
A learning difficulty always lowers the measured IQ to below seventy points
A learning disability is a global intellectual impairment; a difficulty is specific
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: A learning disability is a global intellectual impairment; a difficulty is specific
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: A learning disability involves global intellectual impairment; a learning difficulty (e.g. dyslexia) is a specific difficulty without global intellectual impairment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.question: Compared with the general population, people with a learning disability are known to:
options: Live longer and have fewer physical health problems
Have health outcomes identical to the general population
Die younger, with more avoidable deaths from systemic failures
Have fewer comorbidities and lower rates of hospital use
Rarely develop epilepsy or other neurological conditions
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.answer: Die younger, with more avoidable deaths from systemic failures
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disabil.explanation: People with a learning disability die younger and have far more avoidable deaths, driven by systemic failures such as diagnostic overshadowing rather than by the learning disability itself. This is the rationale for reasonable adjustments and annual health checks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 17-year-old girl has a very low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted perception that she is 'fat' despite being underweight. Which eating disorder is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Anorexia nervosa
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Low weight with body-image disturbance and fear of weight gain is anorexia nervosa.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 22-year-old of normal weight has recurrent binges followed by self-induced vomiting and laxative use, driven by concern about her shape. Which eating disorder is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Bulimia nervosa
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: A normal weight with a binge–purge cycle and over-valuation of shape/weight is bulimia nervosa.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 10-year-old avoids most foods because of their texture and a fear of choking, with resulting poor weight gain, but has NO concern about body shape or weight. Which diagnosis fits?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: ARFID (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Restricted intake driven by sensory aversion/fear of choking (not body image), with nutritional consequences, is ARFID — the absence of body-image disturbance is its distinguishing feature.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which eating disorder carries the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Anorexia nervosa
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (medical complications of starvation plus suicide).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which combination of features distinguishes the eating disorders from one another?
options: Weight, the presence of binge/purge behaviour, and the driving belief
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Weight, the presence of binge/purge behaviour, and the driving belief
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: The eating disorders are distinguished by weight, binge/purge behaviour and the driving belief (body-image disturbance vs sensory aversion, etc.).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 16-year-old girl with a BMI of 14 has an intense fear of gaining weight and sees herself as overweight. Examination shows bradycardia, cold peripheries and fine downy hair over her body. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Anorexia nervosa
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Low weight with body-image disturbance/fear of weight gain, plus bradycardia and lanugo hair, is anorexia nervosa.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A patient with anorexia has fine, downy hair over the body. What is this called, and why does it develop?
options: Lanugo hair; a response to loss of body fat (to conserve heat)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Lanugo hair; a response to loss of body fat (to conserve heat)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Lanugo (fine downy hair) develops in response to loss of body fat, helping to conserve heat.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: During assessment of a patient with anorexia, they cannot stand up from squatting or sit up without pushing with their arms. What does this indicate?
options: A focal neurological lesion in the cord
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Severe proximal muscle wasting
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: This is the sit-up–squat–stand test: inability to rise without pushing with the arms indicates severe proximal muscle wasting and is a red flag for severity and medical risk in anorexia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which biochemical pattern is characteristic of anorexia nervosa?
options: Most values low; GH, cortisol and cholesterol raised
Every measured value is raised above the normal range
Every value is low, including cortisol and glucose
Raised potassium with a low serum cortisol level
Raised T3 with a raised fasting blood glucose
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Most values low; GH, cortisol and cholesterol raised
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: In anorexia most values are low (glucose, potassium, FSH/LH, oestrogen, T3), while growth hormone (with a low IGF-1), cortisol, cholesterol and carotene are raised. Glucose is LOW, despite some revision sources listing it among the raised 'G's — hypoglycaemia is a marker of medical risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A patient with anorexia has stopped menstruating. What is the hormonal basis?
options: Hypothalamic suppression → low FSH/LH → low oestrogen → amenorrhoea
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Hypothalamic suppression → low FSH/LH → low oestrogen → amenorrhoea
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Starvation suppresses the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis, lowering FSH/LH and oestrogen and causing amenorrhoea.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which cardiovascular finding is typical of severe anorexia nervosa?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Bradycardia and hypotension (with hypothermia)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Anorexia causes bradycardia, hypotension and hypothermia as physiological adaptations to starvation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which serum electrolyte abnormality is characteristically seen (and dangerous) in anorexia, especially with purging?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Hypokalaemia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Hypokalaemia is characteristic (worsened by purging) and can cause dangerous arrhythmias in anorexia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which feature best distinguishes anorexia nervosa from bulimia nervosa?
options: Both conditions are markedly underweight at diagnosis
Anorexia is markedly underweight; bulimia usually is not
Bulimia involves no concern about shape or weight
Only anorexia shows purging; bulimia never purges
The two disorders are clinically identical entities
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Anorexia is markedly underweight; bulimia usually is not
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Anorexia is defined by a markedly low weight with body-image disturbance, whereas bulimia typically occurs at a normal (or slightly high) weight with a binge–purge cycle. Both may purge and both over-value shape and weight.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 22-year-old woman of normal weight describes eating large amounts of food with a sense of loss of control, then making herself vomit, several times a week. She has calluses on her knuckles and eroded tooth enamel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Bulimia nervosa
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: A normal-weight patient with a binge–purge cycle, Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) and dental erosion has bulimia nervosa.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A patient with an eating disorder has calluses and scarring over the knuckles of one hand. What is this sign called, and what causes it?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Russell's sign; repeated self-induced vomiting
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Russell's sign is knuckle calluses/scarring caused by the teeth abrading the skin during repeated self-induced vomiting.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which single feature best distinguishes bulimia nervosa from anorexia nervosa?
options: The presence of purging behaviour after meals
Over-concern about body shape and weight
A marked female predominance in cases
A normal or slightly raised body weight
Typical onset during the adolescent years
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: A normal or slightly raised body weight
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Both disorders may involve purging and both over-value shape and weight, so the discriminating feature is weight: bulimia typically occurs at a normal or slightly high weight, whereas anorexia is markedly underweight.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A woman with bulimia who vomits several times daily is most likely to show which biochemical picture?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Loss of H+ and Cl- in the vomitus produces a metabolic alkalosis, while volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and aldosterone wastes potassium renally — hence hypokalaemia, which risks arrhythmias. Gastric fluid itself contains little potassium.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A patient with bulimia has bilateral swelling of the cheeks. Which structures are enlarged, and why?
options: The parotid (salivary) glands; a response to repeated vomiting
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: The parotid (salivary) glands; a response to repeated vomiting
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Repeated self-induced vomiting causes parotid (salivary) gland enlargement, giving a 'chipmunk' facial appearance.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: What is the first-line treatment for bulimia nervosa according to NICE?
options: Fluoxetine 60 mg daily as the sole treatment
Admission to hospital for supervised refeeding
Guided self-help based on CBT, then CBT-ED
A benzodiazepine to reduce the urge to binge
Light therapy in the winter months each year
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Guided self-help based on CBT, then CBT-ED
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help is first-line, moving to individual CBT-ED if it is unacceptable, contraindicated or ineffective after about 4 weeks. Medication is never the sole treatment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: If an antidepressant is used in bulimia nervosa, which drug and dose is preferred?
options: Fluoxetine at a higher dose (~60 mg daily)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Fluoxetine at a higher dose (~60 mg daily)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Fluoxetine at ~60 mg daily (a higher dose than for depression) is the SSRI of choice as an adjunct in bulimia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A young woman is found to have dental enamel erosion, enlarged parotid glands and hypokalaemia, but a normal BMI. Which behaviour best explains these findings?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Recurrent self-induced vomiting (purging)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Dental erosion, parotid enlargement and hypokalaemia at a normal weight point to recurrent self-induced vomiting, as seen in bulimia nervosa.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 9-year-old boy eats only a very narrow range of foods, refusing anything with certain textures, and has faltering growth. He has no concern at all about his body shape or weight and does not fear gaining weight. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: ARFID (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Restricted intake with faltering growth driven by sensory aversion and with NO body-image disturbance is ARFID.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: What is the single feature that distinguishes ARFID from anorexia nervosa?
options: The absence of body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: The absence of body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: ARFID lacks any body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain — the defining difference from anorexia nervosa.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised driver of food restriction in ARFID?
options: Sensory sensitivity to texture, taste or smell
Fear of an aversive consequence such as choking
Low interest in eating or appetite
Aversion following a past vomiting episode
A fear of weight gain / desire to be thin
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: A fear of weight gain / desire to be thin
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: A fear of weight gain / drive for thinness is characteristic of anorexia, NOT ARFID; ARFID is driven by sensory aversion, fear of aversive consequences, or low interest in food.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: In which patient group is ARFID most commonly seen?
options: Elderly men living in residential care
Women in the first year postpartum
Children and people with autism or ADHD
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Children and people with autism or ADHD
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: ARFID is most common in children and in people with neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism spectrum disorder and ADHD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A teenager with autism has significant weight loss and iron deficiency from eating only a few 'safe' foods, with no concern about body image. Before diagnosing ARFID, what must be done?
options: Admit for compulsory refeeding at once
Reassure that this is normal fussy eating
Exclude anorexia nervosa and organic disease
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Exclude anorexia nervosa and organic disease
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: ARFID is a diagnosis of exclusion — anorexia nervosa, organic gastrointestinal disease and other medical illness must be ruled out before the diagnosis is made.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: What is the appropriate management of ARFID?
options: Fluoxetine monotherapy at high dose, which is the licensed treatment for ARFID
Multidisciplinary care with dietetic support plus CBT-based psychological therapy
Admission to a Mother and Baby Unit for joint assessment of feeding behaviour
Bright light therapy each morning, as ARFID is a seasonal eating disturbance
No treatment, as ARFID always resolves spontaneously without any intervention
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Multidisciplinary care with dietetic support plus CBT-based psychological therapy
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: ARFID is managed with a multidisciplinary approach: dietetic support and psychological therapy targeting the driver, involving the family for children.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which finding would move a child's presentation from 'fussy eating' towards a diagnosis of ARFID?
options: A strong preference for sweet foods over savoury
Occasionally refusing to eat green vegetables
Faltering growth or dependence on supplements
Eating noticeably more slowly than other children
A dislike of one particular food group at meals
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Faltering growth or dependence on supplements
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: ARFID is separated from fussy eating by consequence: faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, dependence on nutritional supplements, or marked interference with psychosocial functioning — without any body-image concern.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 7-year-old avoids solid foods after a choking episode and now eats only pureed food, losing weight, but shows no body-image concern. Which driver of ARFID does this represent?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Fear of an aversive consequence (choking/vomiting)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Avoidance following a frightening choking episode reflects the 'fear of an aversive consequence' driver of ARFID.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A severely malnourished patient with anorexia (BMI 12) is admitted and started on full nutritional support. Two days later she becomes confused with peripheral oedema, and bloods show a markedly low phosphate. What complication has occurred?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Refeeding syndrome
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Reintroducing nutrition too quickly in a malnourished patient causes refeeding syndrome, whose hallmark is hypophosphataemia with fluid shifts and confusion.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which biochemical triad characterises refeeding syndrome?
options: High phosphate, high potassium, high magnesium
Low sodium, high potassium, low calcium
High glucose, low potassium, high magnesium
Low phosphate, low potassium, low magnesium
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Low phosphate, low potassium, low magnesium
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: The insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, producing the triad of ↓phosphate, ↓potassium and ↓magnesium.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: What is the underlying mechanism of refeeding syndrome?
options: An insulin surge shifting electrolytes into cells
Excess free water intake causing dilution
Acute kidney injury from renal hypoperfusion
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: An insulin surge shifting electrolytes into cells
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Reintroduced carbohydrate triggers an insulin surge that drives potassium, magnesium and phosphate intracellularly faster than depleted stores can tolerate — the basis of refeeding syndrome.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which single electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Hypophosphataemia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark biochemical abnormality of refeeding syndrome.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which vitamin must be given before or alongside feeding a high-risk malnourished patient, and why?
options: Vitamin D; to protect bone mineral density
Vitamin C; to prevent the onset of scurvy
Vitamin K; to prevent bleeding on refeeding
Folate; to prevent a macrocytic anaemia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Thiamine (B1); refeeding rapidly depletes it
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Thiamine is rapidly consumed when carbohydrate metabolism restarts, so stores are depleted and Wernicke's encephalopathy can be precipitated; it is therefore given before or alongside feeding.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: What is the correct approach to feeding a patient at high risk of refeeding syndrome?
options: Refeed slowly — start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day — replacing electrolytes and thiamine
Feed rapidly to restore body weight as quickly as possible
Withhold all nutrition for at least a week until stable
Give a large carbohydrate load on the first day of feeding
Restrict fluids and withhold electrolyte replacement entirely
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Refeed slowly — start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day — replacing electrolytes and thiamine
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: High-risk patients start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg/day in extreme risk), building to full requirements over 4-7 days, with phosphate, potassium and magnesium replaced and thiamine given before and during feeding. Correct electrolytes alongside feeding rather than withholding nutrition — sustained under-feeding is itself harmful.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A woman with bulimia who vomits several times daily has hypokalaemia. What is the acid–base disturbance, and its mechanism?
options: Metabolic alkalosis from loss of H⁺ and Cl⁻ in vomitus, with RAAS-driven K⁺ loss
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Metabolic alkalosis from loss of H⁺ and Cl⁻ in vomitus, with RAAS-driven K⁺ loss
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Vomiting loses H⁺ and Cl⁻ causing a metabolic alkalosis, while volume loss activates RAAS/aldosterone, excreting K⁺ and producing hypokalaemia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Why does recurrent vomiting lead to hypokalaemia even though little potassium is in gastric fluid?
options: Volume loss activates the RAAS, and aldosterone drives renal potassium excretion
Potassium is destroyed by gastric acid
Vomiting directly removes large amounts of potassium
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Volume loss activates the RAAS, and aldosterone drives renal potassium excretion
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Volume depletion from vomiting activates the RAAS; aldosterone retains sodium/water and excretes potassium, causing hypokalaemia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which ECG changes are characteristic of the hypokalaemia seen in both refeeding and purging?
options: Peaked T waves and widened QRS
Flattened T waves and prominent U waves
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Flattened T waves and prominent U waves
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Hypokalaemia (from either refeeding or vomiting) produces flattened T waves and prominent U waves on the ECG.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A patient who misuses both self-induced vomiting and diuretics is at particularly high risk of which abnormality?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Severe hypokalaemia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Diuretic misuse compounds the potassium loss caused by self-induced vomiting, producing severe and dangerous hypokalaemia alongside a metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A GP suspects an eating disorder in a young woman with weight loss and preoccupation with shape. Which brief screening tool is most appropriate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: The SCOFF questionnaire
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: The SCOFF questionnaire is the brief 5-item screening tool for eating disorders; a positive screen prompts specialist referral.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 19-year-old with anorexia nervosa (BMI 15) is assessed. According to NICE, what is the first-line treatment?
options: Admission for compulsory feeding in all cases
A psychological therapy — CBT-ED, MANTRA or SSCM
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: A psychological therapy — CBT-ED, MANTRA or SSCM
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: For adults with anorexia, NICE recommends first-line psychological therapy: individual CBT-ED, MANTRA or SSCM. No drug is first-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 14-year-old girl is diagnosed with anorexia nervosa. What is the recommended first-line psychological treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-AN)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: For children and young people with anorexia, anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-AN) is first-line; CBT-ED is second-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: What is the first-line management for an adult with bulimia nervosa according to NICE?
options: Fluoxetine 60 mg daily as sole treatment
Family therapy for eating disorders alone
Admission to a specialist inpatient unit
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Adults with bulimia nervosa are offered bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help first line (NICE); if this is unacceptable, contraindicated or ineffective after about 4 weeks, individual CBT-ED follows.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which statement about drug treatment in eating disorders is correct?
options: An SSRI is the first-line treatment for anorexia nervosa
An antipsychotic is the first-line treatment for bulimia
No drug is first-line; fluoxetine is an adjunct in bulimia
A benzodiazepine is the mainstay of treatment in both
Lithium is the first-line treatment for both disorders
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: No drug is first-line; fluoxetine is an adjunct in bulimia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: No drug is first-line in anorexia nervosa, where psychological therapy is the mainstay. In bulimia nervosa an SSRI (fluoxetine) is a useful adjunct that can reduce binge-purge frequency.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which set of investigations is most appropriate in the physical risk assessment of a patient with anorexia nervosa?
options: U&E, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, FBC, LFT, TFT and an ECG
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: U&E, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, FBC, LFT, TFT and an ECG
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: Physical risk assessment includes U&E, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, FBC, LFT, TFT and an ECG (for bradycardia, QTc and hypokalaemia).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: During assessment of anorexia, which bedside test specifically assesses proximal muscle power as a marker of severity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: The sit-up–squat–stand test
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: The sit-up–squat–stand test assesses proximal muscle power; inability to rise without the arms indicates severe wasting and high risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: A 13-year-old with bulimia nervosa is referred. What is the recommended first-line treatment?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Bulimia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-BN)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: For children and young people with bulimia, family therapy (FT-BN) is first-line; CBT-ED is second-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: What is the overarching principle of eating disorder management under NICE?
options: Medication is the mainstay, with psychological therapy having little role
Psychological therapy is the mainstay, with medical risk managed in parallel
Inpatient admission is required for everyone at the point of first diagnosis
Watchful waiting alone, since most eating disorders remit without any help
Dietary advice alone is sufficient, and no other treatment is ever required
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: Psychological therapy is the mainstay, with medical risk managed in parallel
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: NICE makes psychological therapy the mainstay, treats medical risk in parallel, and limits the role of drugs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.question: Which finding in a patient with anorexia would most strongly prompt inpatient admission?
options: A BMI of 19 with stable observations and normal bloods
A rapidly falling BMI with bradycardia and severe hypokalaemia
A single episode of binge eating followed by normal intake
A family history of anorexia in an otherwise well patient
Mild low mood with no suicidal ideation or self-harm
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.answer: A rapidly falling BMI with bradycardia and severe hypokalaemia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders.explanation: High physical risk drives admission: a very low or rapidly falling BMI with bradycardia, hypotension, ECG changes and electrolyte disturbance needs inpatient care to manage refeeding and medical risk safely.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: How do the different depressive disorders principally differ from one another?
options: In whether they respond to antidepressants
In their context, timing and trigger — the core depressive syndrome is shared
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: In their context, timing and trigger — the core depressive syndrome is shared
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: The depressive disorders share the same core syndrome (low mood, anhedonia, reduced energy ≥2 weeks) and differ mainly in pattern/context (seasonal, perinatal, etc.).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient becomes depressed each autumn/winter with hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving, remitting in spring. Which depressive disorder is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Seasonal affective disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: A recurrent seasonal (winter) pattern with atypical features (hypersomnia, increased appetite/carb craving) is seasonal affective disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A woman develops low mood, fatigue and poor bonding 6 weeks after childbirth. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what distinguishes it from 'baby blues'?
options: Postpartum psychosis; it has no psychosis
Postnatal depression; baby blues is self-limiting and resolves within ~2 weeks
Bipolar disorder; it needs lithium immediately
Adjustment disorder; it needs no treatment
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Postnatal depression; baby blues is self-limiting and resolves within ~2 weeks
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Postnatal depression develops within ~12 months of birth; 'baby blues' is transient and self-resolving within about 2 weeks, and postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Before starting an antidepressant in any depressed patient, what is the single most important screen?
options: A thyroid ultrasound scan before the first dose
A CT head to exclude a structural cause first
Asking about any past manic or hypomanic episode
A liver biopsy to check for hepatic impairment
A routine ECG in every patient before starting
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Asking about any past manic or hypomanic episode
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Always screen for past mania/hypomania — giving an antidepressant alone in unrecognised bipolar disorder can precipitate mania.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A new mother develops rapidly evolving confusion, delusions and thoughts of harming her baby days after delivery. What must this be treated as?
options: Postpartum psychosis — a psychiatric emergency (with risk to the infant)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Postpartum psychosis — a psychiatric emergency (with risk to the infant)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency; risk to the mother and infant must be assessed and urgent psychiatric input arranged.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A 45-year-old has 6 weeks of persistent low mood (worst in the mornings), loss of interest in everything, fatigue, early morning waking and weight loss, with feelings of worthlessness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: A depressive episode (major depression)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Low mood + anhedonia + reduced energy for ≥2 weeks with biological symptoms (early morning waking, diurnal variation, weight loss) and worthlessness is a depressive episode.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient has just been found to have had a past hypomanic episode. How does this change the plan to start an antidepressant?
options: It makes no difference to the choice or the plan
Never antidepressant monotherapy — refer for bipolar management
Double the antidepressant dose to prevent a relapse
Start the antidepressant but stop it again after two weeks
Switch from an SSRI to a tricyclic antidepressant instead
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Never antidepressant monotherapy — refer for bipolar management
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Any history of mania or hypomania changes management entirely. Antidepressant monotherapy risks precipitating mania, so treatment follows the bipolar pathway rather than the unipolar one.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A depressed patient has fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance. Which reversible cause should be excluded with a blood test?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Hypothyroidism (check TFTs)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Hypothyroidism is a classic organic mimic of depression; TFTs (with FBC, B12/folate, calcium, glucose) exclude reversible causes.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Under the current NICE classification, how is depression severity split, and by what score?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: 'Less severe' (PHQ-9 <16) vs 'more severe' (PHQ-9 ≥16)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: NICE uses 'less severe' (subthreshold + mild, PHQ-9 <16) and 'more severe' (moderate + severe, PHQ-9 ≥16).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient has 'less severe' depression (PHQ-9 of 12). According to NICE, what is the recommended first-line approach?
options: Offer a less intrusive option such as guided self-help or group CBT, not a routine SSRI
Routinely start an SSRI at full dose in everyone before considering any talking therapy
Start a tricyclic antidepressant first-line and review the response after three months
Refer immediately for electroconvulsive therapy as the most effective first treatment
Start a regular benzodiazepine for several months as the mainstay of depression treatment
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Offer a less intrusive option such as guided self-help or group CBT, not a routine SSRI
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: For less severe depression, NICE advises against routine first-line antidepressants; a menu of psychological/behavioural options is preferred (antidepressant only by informed preference).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient with more severe depression (PHQ-9 of 20) is treated. What is a typical first-line option?
options: Guided low-intensity self-help alone, with no antidepressant or other therapy
A regular benzodiazepine as monotherapy continued for at least twelve months
Bright light therapy alone, delivered each morning for several months at home
No treatment at all, with review in three months to see whether it settles
An antidepressant (SSRI) combined with individual cognitive behavioural therapy
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: An antidepressant (SSRI) combined with individual cognitive behavioural therapy
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: More severe depression is treated with a combination such as an SSRI + individual CBT (or high-intensity therapy, or an antidepressant alone), matched to preference.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which is the first-line antidepressant for an adult, and for a child/adolescent?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Sertraline (adult); fluoxetine (child/adolescent)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: SSRIs are first-line — sertraline in adults and fluoxetine in children/adolescents ('fluoxeTEEN').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A 22-year-old is started on an SSRI for depression. When should they be reviewed, and why?
options: At 6 weeks, as a routine first review
At 3 months, once the drug has worked
Only if the symptoms clearly worsen
No review is needed while on an SSRI
At 1 week, because they are under 25
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: At 1 week, because they are under 25
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Antidepressants are reviewed at 2 weeks and in any case within 4 weeks, but at 1 week if the patient is under 25 or at increased risk of suicide, because of the higher early risk of suicidal thinking. The 1-week review also applies after each dose increase.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient on an SSRI also takes regular ibuprofen. What should be co-prescribed, and why?
options: A proton pump inhibitor, because SSRIs + NSAIDs increase GI bleeding risk
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: A proton pump inhibitor, because SSRIs + NSAIDs increase GI bleeding risk
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: SSRIs increase GI bleeding risk, compounded by NSAIDs, so a PPI is co-prescribed. The preferred step is to avoid the combination altogether — mirtazapine is the usual alternative — with a PPI where an SSRI is unavoidable.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which SSRI is specifically associated with QT-interval prolongation?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Citalopram
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Citalopram (and escitalopram) can prolong the QT interval, a specific caution among the SSRIs.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: An SSRI is being stopped. How should this be done to avoid discontinuation syndrome?
options: Stop the SSRI abruptly at the full dose
Taper the dose gradually over several weeks
Double the dose for a week before stopping
Switch straight across to a tricyclic
Add a benzodiazepine and stop the SSRI
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Taper the dose gradually over several weeks
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Antidepressants are stopped by gradual dose reduction to avoid discontinuation symptoms such as GI upset, insomnia and 'electric shock' paraesthesiae. Fluoxetine's long half-life makes withdrawal less likely and allows a shorter reduction, but it is still reduced in stages.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient started on venlafaxine should have which parameter monitored?
options: Blood pressure (SNRIs are associated with hypertension)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Blood pressure (SNRIs are associated with hypertension)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) can raise blood pressure, so BP is checked before starting and at each titration.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A depressed elderly patient with insomnia and poor appetite would benefit from which antidepressant, and why?
options: Fluoxetine; its long half-life prevents insomnia
A tricyclic; free of anticholinergic effects
An MAOI; needs no tyramine dietary restriction
Citalopram; has no effect on the QT interval
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Mirtazapine; sedating and appetite-stimulating
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Mirtazapine is favoured here because its sedative and appetite-stimulating effects directly target the insomnia and poor appetite, and it has few drug interactions — useful in the elderly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which antidepressant class is the most dangerous in overdose, and what are the features?
options: SSRIs; profound bradycardia and heart block
TCAs; widened QRS, seizures and hypotension
MAOIs; entirely safe in acute overdose
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: TCAs; widened QRS, seizures and hypotension
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Tricyclics are the most dangerous in overdose, causing anticholinergic effects (confusion, tachycardia, mydriasis) and cardiotoxicity with a widened QRS and prolonged QTc, plus acidosis, hypotension and seizures — so they are avoided in those at suicide risk.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient on a MAOI eats aged cheese and cured meats and develops a severe headache and dangerously high blood pressure. What is this?
options: A tyramine ('cheese') reaction causing a hypertensive crisis
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: A tyramine ('cheese') reaction causing a hypertensive crisis
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: MAOIs plus tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats) cause a hypertensive crisis — the classic 'cheese reaction'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient on an SSRI is also given tramadol and rapidly develops agitation, sweating, tachycardia, clonus and hyperreflexia. What is the diagnosis and specific treatment?
options: Serotonin syndrome; stop the serotonergic drugs
A panic attack; reassurance and breathing advice
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Serotonin syndrome; stop the serotonergic drugs
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Excess serotonergic activity from an SSRI plus tramadol causing clonus, hyperreflexia, autonomic instability and altered mental state is serotonin syndrome. Treatment is stopping all serotonergic drugs with urgent hospital assessment, IV fluids, benzodiazepines and active cooling; hyperthermia with rigidity is what kills, and cyproheptadine is added in severe cases.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: How is serotonin syndrome distinguished from neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
options: They are identical syndromes given two different names by different specialties
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome characteristically produces sustained clonus
Serotonin syndrome characteristically produces hyporeflexia and a slow onset
Serotonin syndrome causes clonus and hyperreflexia; NMS causes lead-pipe rigidity
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is caused by SSRIs and triptans in combination
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Serotonin syndrome causes clonus and hyperreflexia; NMS causes lead-pipe rigidity
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Serotonin syndrome features clonus and hyperreflexia with rapid onset; NMS features lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia with slower onset.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient with severe depression is refusing all food and fluids with strong suicidal intent and has not responded to medication. Which treatment may be indicated?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: ECT is indicated for severe, life-threatening or treatment-refractory depression — including food/fluid refusal, catatonia and strong suicidal intent.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which is the most important contraindication to ECT?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Raised intracranial pressure
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Raised intracranial pressure is the most important contraindication to ECT, but none is absolute — it is a risk-benefit decision made with the anaesthetist. Common side effects are short-term memory impairment and retrograde amnesia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which antidepressant is considered safest following a recent myocardial infarction?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Sertraline
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Sertraline is regarded as the safest antidepressant after a myocardial infarction.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: For how long should an antidepressant be continued after a first episode of depression remits, to reduce relapse?
options: Stop as soon as mood improves
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: At least 6 months after remission
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Antidepressants are continued for at least 6 months after remission (longer if recurrent) to reduce relapse.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A depressed older adult has a short history of memory complaints, is very worried about their memory and answers 'I don't know'. What should be considered before diagnosing dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Depression (pseudodementia)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Pseudodementia (depression mimicking dementia) presents with a short history, biological symptoms and marked concern about memory — a reversible mimic to exclude.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A 34-year-old woman has become low in mood, oversleeping, craving carbohydrates and gaining weight every winter for the past three years, feeling well again each spring. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Major depression with no seasonal pattern
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Seasonal affective disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: A recurrent winter pattern of depression with atypical features (hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving, weight gain), remitting in spring, over ≥2 years is seasonal affective disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which symptom profile is characteristic of winter SAD, in contrast to typical depression?
options: Hypersomnia, hyperphagia (carbohydrate craving) and weight gain
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Hypersomnia, hyperphagia (carbohydrate craving) and weight gain
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Winter SAD features 'atypical' symptoms — hypersomnia, hyperphagia/weight gain and fatigue — whereas typical depression features insomnia and weight loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: What is required to diagnose seasonal affective disorder rather than a one-off winter low mood?
options: A single winter episode of low mood is sufficient
A positive family history of depression on its own
A raised PHQ-9 score recorded on one occasion
A seasonal pattern over at least 2 consecutive years
Onset confined to the summer months of the year
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: A seasonal pattern over at least 2 consecutive years
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: SAD requires a regular, predictable seasonal pattern of depressive episodes over at least 2 consecutive years.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient with winter low mood, fatigue and weight gain is being assessed for SAD. Which organic mimic should be excluded?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Hypothyroidism
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Hypothyroidism mimics seasonal affective disorder, causing winter fatigue, low mood and weight gain, so thyroid function should be checked in any depression work-up.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: What is the overarching management of SAD?
options: Sleeping tablets with simple reassurance alone
Lifelong lithium prophylaxis as a stabiliser
A regular benzodiazepine through the winter
Treat as depression, with light therapy as adjunct
No treatment, since it always remits alone
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Treat as depression, with light therapy as adjunct
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: SAD is managed as depression — psychological therapy and/or an SSRI — with light therapy as the SAD-specific adjunct.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which treatment is uniquely associated with (specific to) seasonal affective disorder?
options: Light therapy (a bright light box, particularly in the morning)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Light therapy (a bright light box, particularly in the morning)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Light therapy (bright light box, especially in the morning) is the SAD-specific option, alongside treating it as depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: What is the place of hypnotics in seasonal affective disorder?
options: They reliably precipitate a hypertensive crisis in SAD
They interact directly with light therapy and block it
They do not treat it and add to the daytime sedation
They are teratogenic and so avoided in this group
They are the recommended first-line treatment for SAD
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: They do not treat it and add to the daytime sedation
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Hypnotics do not treat depression, and SAD already features hypersomnia and low energy, which sedatives worsen.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A patient with a reliable winter pattern of SAD wants to reduce future episodes. What is a reasonable strategy?
options: Wait until the symptoms become severe
Start treatment before the season begins
Take a sedative hypnotic every night
Avoid all daylight during the winter
Stop all treatment during the winter
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Start treatment before the season begins
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Those with a reliable seasonal pattern can start treatment prophylactically — light therapy or an antidepressant — before the season begins, alongside maximising daylight exposure and exercise.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which statement best describes seasonal affective disorder?
options: A distinct disease unrelated to depression
A form of bipolar disorder with rapid cycling
An anxiety disorder triggered by cold weather
A subtype of dementia seen in older adults
Depression with a seasonal pattern specifier
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Depression with a seasonal pattern specifier
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: SAD is not a separate disease but depression with a seasonal pattern specifier, linked to reduced winter daylight affecting circadian rhythm and melatonin/serotonin regulation — the rationale for light therapy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A woman 8 weeks postpartum has 3 weeks of persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, guilt about not being a good mother, and difficulty bonding with her baby. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Postnatal depression
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: A persistent depressive episode weeks–months after birth, with poor bonding and guilt, is postnatal depression (baby blues would have resolved within ~2 weeks).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: How are the three conditions of the perinatal mood triad principally distinguished?
options: By the age of the mother at the time of delivery
By their timing after delivery and by their severity
By the sex of the baby and the mode of delivery
By whether or not the mother chooses to breastfeed
They cannot be reliably distinguished from each other
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: By their timing after delivery and by their severity
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: The perinatal mood triad is distinguished by timing and severity — baby blues (mild, days 3–10), PND (weeks–months) and postpartum psychosis (acute, emergency).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A mother is tearful and emotionally labile on day 4 postpartum, but is otherwise coping and the symptoms settle within 10 days. What is this, and how is it managed?
options: Baby blues; reassurance and support only
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Baby blues; reassurance and support only
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Transient tearfulness/lability in the first days that resolves within ~2 weeks is 'baby blues', needing only reassurance and support.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A woman develops acute confusion, grandiose delusions and hallucinations 10 days after delivery, with a history of bipolar disorder. What is this, and what is the appropriate action?
options: Baby blues, needing only reassurance and routine health visitor review
Mild postnatal depression, managed with guided self-help in primary care
Seasonal affective disorder, treated with bright light therapy at home
Postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency needing urgent admission
Normal postnatal adjustment, requiring no assessment or follow-up at all
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency needing urgent admission
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Acute psychosis or mania in the early postpartum period is postpartum psychosis — a psychiatric emergency strongly linked to bipolar disorder and previous episodes, requiring urgent assessment and admission, ideally to a Mother and Baby Unit.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: When assessing a woman with suspected postnatal depression, which risks must always be asked about directly?
options: Only her own thoughts of self-harm and suicide
Only her financial and housing circumstances
Both her suicidal thoughts and thoughts of harming the infant
Only the state of her relationship with her partner
Neither, as asking directly is intrusive and unhelpful
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Both her suicidal thoughts and thoughts of harming the infant
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: In PND, both maternal self-harm/suicide risk AND thoughts of harming the infant must be asked about directly.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: Which validated tool is used to screen for postnatal depression?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is the validated screening tool for PND (the Whooley questions are also used).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A woman with postnatal low mood, fatigue and weight change is being assessed. Which common organic mimic should be excluded?
options: Hypothyroidism (postpartum thyroiditis mimics PND — check TFTs)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Hypothyroidism (postpartum thyroiditis mimics PND — check TFTs)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Postpartum thyroiditis (hypothyroid phase) is common and mimics PND, so TFTs should be checked.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: What is the first-line treatment for mild-to-moderate postnatal depression?
options: An antidepressant prescribed for every woman
Immediate admission to a Mother and Baby Unit
Guided self-help or psychological therapy (CBT or IPT)
Bright light therapy every morning at home
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Guided self-help or psychological therapy (CBT or IPT)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Mild-to-moderate postnatal depression is treated first-line with guided self-help or psychological therapy such as CBT or IPT, alongside health visitor and social support. An antidepressant is added for moderate-to-severe illness.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A breastfeeding mother needs an antidepressant for moderate postnatal depression. Which is favoured, and what is the key principle?
options: Sertraline; low levels pass into breast milk
A tricyclic; it is the safest drug in overdose
Paroxetine; it must be avoided in all mothers
No antidepressant is safe while breastfeeding
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Sertraline; low levels pass into breast milk
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Sertraline (and paroxetine) are favoured in breastfeeding because of low levels in milk. The key principle is that effective treatment should not be withheld for fear of breastfeeding, as untreated postnatal depression harms both mother and baby.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: With which condition is postpartum psychosis most strongly associated?
options: Bipolar disorder / a previous episode of postpartum psychosis
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Bipolar disorder / a previous episode of postpartum psychosis
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Postpartum psychosis is strongly associated with bipolar disorder and a previous postpartum psychosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.question: A woman with severe postnatal depression poses a risk to herself and her baby. What is the appropriate service/setting?
options: Discharge home with a self-help leaflet and no arranged mental health follow-up
Admission to a general medical ward under the physicians for routine observation
Routine GP follow-up in six weeks with no specialist referral made in the interim
Specialist perinatal mental health services, considering Mother and Baby Unit admission
No intervention at all, since postnatal depression reliably remits within days
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.answer: Specialist perinatal mental health services, considering Mother and Baby Unit admission
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disor.explanation: Severe PND with risk warrants specialist perinatal mental health input and possible admission to a Mother & Baby Unit, which keeps mother and baby together.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: An 82-year-old becomes acutely confused over 2 days, is inattentive and drowsy, sees things that aren't there, and is much worse at night; he has new dysuria and frequency and is febrile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Vascular dementia after a silent stroke
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Delirium
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Acute onset with fluctuation, inattention and clouded consciousness is delirium — a reversible mimic that must be excluded before diagnosing dementia. Note that dementia is the biggest risk factor for delirium, so the two commonly coexist.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A 70-year-old presents with a few weeks of poor memory, low mood, poor sleep and appetite, answers 'I don't know' to questions, and is very distressed about his memory. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Depression (pseudodementia)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: A short history with biological symptoms, 'don't know' answers and marked concern about memory suggests depression (pseudodementia) — a reversible mimic.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which pattern best fits a diagnosis of dementia rather than its mimics?
options: Insidious, progressive decline in clear consciousness
Acute onset over hours with clouded consciousness
Fluctuating attention that is much worse at night
A few weeks of low mood with 'don't know' answers
Sudden inattention after starting a new drug
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Insidious, progressive decline in clear consciousness
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Dementia declines insidiously and progressively, with consciousness clear and attention preserved early, and the patient often unconcerned about the memory loss. This contrasts with delirium (acute, clouded, fluctuating) and depressive pseudodementia (subacute, distressed).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient has a stepwise decline in cognition with patchy deficits, focal neurological signs and a history of hypertension and stroke. Which dementia subtype is most likely?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Vascular dementia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: A stepwise course with patchy deficits, focal neurology and vascular risk factors is characteristic of vascular dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient has fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations and parkinsonism. Which dementia subtype is most likely?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism (± REM sleep behaviour disorder) indicates dementia with Lewy bodies (α-synuclein pathology).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: What does the term BPSD refer to in dementia?
options: The pathological plaques and tangles of dementia
A bedside cognitive screening tool for dementia
Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia
The vascular risk factors that drive dementia
The formal staging system for dementia severity
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: BPSD stands for the behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia — agitation, aggression, psychosis, depression, wandering and sleep disturbance — a major area of overlap with psychiatry.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A 74-year-old has 2 years of gradually worsening forgetfulness — losing recent memories first — with word-finding difficulty, getting lost, and trouble dressing, in clear consciousness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Alzheimer's disease
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: An insidious, gradual decline with early prominent memory loss and the 4 A's, in clear consciousness, is Alzheimer's disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient with Alzheimer's cannot carry out a skilled task (e.g. dressing) despite having normal power, coordination and sensation. Which of the '4 A's' is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Apraxia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Inability to perform skilled motor tasks despite intact motor function is apraxia, one of the 4 A's of Alzheimer's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: What is the characteristic neuropathology of Alzheimer's disease?
options: Amyloid-β plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Amyloid-β plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is characterised by extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: What is the rationale for using acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in Alzheimer's disease?
options: To reduce amyloid-beta production in the brain
To increase available acetylcholine in the brain
To block NMDA receptors and reduce excitotoxicity
To treat the associated parkinsonian symptoms
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: To increase available acetylcholine in the brain
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Alzheimer's disease involves a cholinergic deficit with reduced acetylcholine. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors raise the available acetylcholine and give modest symptomatic benefit.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which is the first-line drug treatment for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) are first-line for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease. Memantine is used for severe disease, for moderate disease where an AChE inhibitor is not tolerated or contraindicated, and as an add-on.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which drug, an NMDA-receptor antagonist, is used for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Memantine
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Memantine, an NMDA-receptor antagonist, is used in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's (alone, added to an AChE inhibitor, or if AChE inhibitors are unsuitable).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which condition is strongly associated with early-onset Alzheimer's disease due to an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Down syndrome carries an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21, strongly predisposing to (often early-onset) Alzheimer's disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: How does the memory pattern of Alzheimer's disease differ from that of frontotemporal dementia?
options: Alzheimer's affects memory early and prominently, whereas FTD spares it early
Both conditions spare memory early, presenting first with language problems
Frontotemporal dementia affects memory first, before any personality change
Neither condition affects memory at any stage of its clinical progression
Alzheimer's disease spares memory early, with behavioural change dominating
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Alzheimer's affects memory early and prominently, whereas FTD spares it early
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Alzheimer's presents with early, prominent memory loss; frontotemporal dementia presents with early personality/behaviour and language change, with memory relatively spared early.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A 76-year-old with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and two previous strokes has cognitive decline that has worsened in discrete 'steps', with focal weakness on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Vascular dementia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: A stepwise decline with focal neurology and vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, prior strokes) is characteristic of vascular dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: How does the course of vascular dementia typically differ from Alzheimer's disease?
options: Vascular is stepwise; Alzheimer's is gradual and insidious
Vascular is gradual and Alzheimer's is stepwise
Both follow a clear stepwise decline over years
Both decline gradually with no stepwise element
Vascular dementia follows no identifiable course
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Vascular is stepwise; Alzheimer's is gradual and insidious
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Vascular dementia classically declines in steps and is accompanied by focal neurological signs, whereas Alzheimer's declines gradually and insidiously with early prominent memory loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which set of risk factors is most associated with vascular dementia?
options: Hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation and smoking
A vegan diet and B12 deficiency
Young age and family history only
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation and smoking
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Vascular dementia is associated with cardiovascular risk factors — hypertension, diabetes, AF and smoking.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: What is the main management emphasis in vascular dementia?
options: Levodopa to slow the cognitive decline
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Controlling cardiovascular risk factors
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Management focuses on the modifiable part — cardiovascular risk factors such as blood pressure, diabetes, lipids and smoking — to reduce the risk of further vascular events and so further stepwise decline, alongside symptomatic treatment and advance care planning.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient has features of both stepwise vascular decline and gradual Alzheimer-type memory loss. What is this called?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Mixed dementia (vascular + Alzheimer's)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Coexisting vascular and Alzheimer's pathology is mixed dementia — a common combination.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Regarding cognitive-enhancing drugs in PURE vascular dementia, which statement is correct?
options: They are not routinely used in pure vascular dementia
They are first-line treatment in vascular dementia
They reverse the underlying cerebral infarcts
They are contraindicated in every form of dementia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: They are not routinely used in pure vascular dementia
