conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not routine in pure vascular dementia; they are considered only where a comorbid Alzheimer's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson's disease dementia is suspected.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which is a recognised subtype of vascular dementia?
options: Subcortical small-vessel dementia (also post-stroke and mixed)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Subcortical small-vessel dementia (also post-stroke and mixed)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Vascular dementia subtypes include post-stroke, subcortical small-vessel, and mixed (with Alzheimer's).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Why does vascular dementia often feature focal neurological signs, unlike pure Alzheimer's?
options: Because the underlying strokes/infarcts damage discrete brain regions
Because it spares the brain entirely
Because it has no structural basis
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Because the underlying strokes/infarcts damage discrete brain regions
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: The discrete infarcts of cerebrovascular disease damage focal brain regions, producing focal neurology — in contrast to the diffuse, gradual picture of Alzheimer's.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A 75-year-old has cognitive impairment that fluctuates markedly day to day, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations of people and animals, and mild bradykinesia and rigidity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations and spontaneous parkinsonism are three of the four core clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies (the fourth is REM sleep behaviour disorder); two core features support probable DLB.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which core feature commonly precedes dementia with Lewy bodies by years?
options: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams) is one of the four core features and often precedes DLB by years; autonomic dysfunction and falls are supportive features.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: What is the underlying pathology of dementia with Lewy bodies?
options: α-synuclein deposition (Lewy bodies) — the same protein as Parkinson's disease
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: α-synuclein deposition (Lewy bodies) — the same protein as Parkinson's disease
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: DLB is caused by α-synuclein (Lewy body) pathology, the same protein implicated in Parkinson's disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient develops dementia and, 8 months later, parkinsonism. Using the '1-year rule', which diagnosis fits?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism indicates DLB; parkinsonism preceding dementia by >1 year would be Parkinson's disease dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient has had parkinsonism for 5 years and now develops dementia. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Parkinson's disease dementia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Parkinsonism preceding dementia by more than a year indicates Parkinson's disease dementia (the '1-year rule').

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Why must antipsychotics be avoided if at all possible in dementia with Lewy bodies?
options: They have no effect on hallucinations of any kind
They can cause severe, sometimes fatal sensitivity reactions
They abolish the visual hallucinations immediately
They are equally contraindicated in all dementias
They accelerate cerebral amyloid plaque deposition
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: They can cause severe, sometimes fatal sensitivity reactions
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies carries a dangerous antipsychotic sensitivity, with markedly worsened parkinsonism, heavy sedation and NMS-like reactions that can be fatal. Antipsychotics are therefore avoided where possible, and if essential the lowest dose of an atypical is used with extreme caution.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient with fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations is given haloperidol for agitation and develops severe rigidity and marked deterioration. What has most likely occurred?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Antipsychotic sensitivity in undiagnosed DLB
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Severe rigidity/deterioration after an antipsychotic in someone with fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations suggests DLB with dangerous antipsychotic sensitivity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which feature best distinguishes DLB from Alzheimer's disease?
options: Early prominent memory loss as the first feature
A gradual, smooth decline without fluctuation
Stepwise decline with focal neurological signs
Early personality change with marked disinhibition
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: DLB is marked by fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations and parkinsonism, often with REM sleep behaviour disorder, whereas Alzheimer's presents with a gradual decline and early prominent memory loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A 58-year-old man develops progressive personality change over 2 years — becoming disinhibited, apathetic and losing empathy — with relatively preserved memory. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Frontotemporal dementia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Early personality/behaviour change (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy) with memory relatively spared, in a younger patient, is frontotemporal dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: What is the key clinical contrast between frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease?
options: In FTD, episodic memory loss is always the earliest and most prominent feature
In FTD, personality and language change come first with memory relatively spared
Both conditions spare memory entirely throughout the whole course of the illness
Both present with early prominent memory loss and no personality change at all
FTD occurs only in the very elderly, typically presenting after the age of eighty
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: In FTD, personality and language change come first with memory relatively spared
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: FTD presents with early personality/behaviour and language change with memory relatively spared; Alzheimer's presents with early prominent memory loss.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: What is the characteristic pathology of frontotemporal dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Pick bodies (tau) and/or TDP-43
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: FTD is characterised by Pick bodies (tau protein accumulation) and/or TDP-43 pathology.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Regarding drug treatment in frontotemporal dementia, which statement is correct?
options: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are avoided
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are the first-line drug
Memantine reverses the underlying frontal degeneration
Levodopa is the first-line treatment for all patients
Antipsychotics are absolutely contraindicated in every case
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are avoided
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not used in frontotemporal dementia: there is no cholinergic deficit to correct, they offer no benefit and may worsen behavioural symptoms. Management is largely non-pharmacological.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which age of onset is typical of frontotemporal dementia compared with Alzheimer's?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Younger onset, often before 65
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: FTD typically has a younger onset (often <65) than Alzheimer's disease.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient's frontotemporal dementia is dominated by a progressive difficulty with language rather than behaviour. What is this presentation called?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Primary progressive aphasia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: A language-led FTD presentation is primary progressive aphasia (progressive language impairment).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which cluster of features is most characteristic of the behavioural variant of FTD?
options: Disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and compulsive behaviours
Early memory loss and getting lost
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and compulsive behaviours
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: The behavioural variant of FTD is dominated by disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and compulsive behaviours.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A younger patient with early behaviour change and preserved memory is being distinguished from other dementias. Which finding would instead point to DLB?
options: Fluctuating cognition with visual hallucinations and parkinsonism
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Fluctuating cognition with visual hallucinations and parkinsonism
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism point to DLB; FTD is characterised by early behaviour/language change with spared memory, and vascular dementia by a stepwise course with focal neurology.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient with new cognitive decline is being investigated. Which set of blood tests is essential to exclude reversible causes?
options: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, calcium, glucose/HbA1c and B12/folate
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, calcium, glucose/HbA1c and B12/folate
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Reversible contributors (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, hypercalcaemia, etc.) must be excluded with TFTs, calcium, B12/folate, glucose and routine bloods.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Why is MRI brain performed in the dementia work-up?
options: To measure cerebral acetylcholine levels and thereby guide the drug choice
To diagnose depression and separate it reliably from a true dementia syndrome
To replace bedside cognitive testing, which is no longer recommended at all
To measure the cerebral amyloid burden directly in every patient assessed
To exclude structural causes and assess the pattern of atrophy and vascular load
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: To exclude structural causes and assess the pattern of atrophy and vascular load
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: MRI excludes reversible structural causes such as tumour, subdural haematoma and normal pressure hydrocephalus, and characterises the pattern of atrophy and vascular burden, supporting subtype diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which investigation specifically supports a diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies?
options: A DAT scan (reduced dopamine transporter uptake)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: A DAT scan (reduced dopamine transporter uptake)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: A DAT scan showing reduced dopamine transporter uptake supports DLB.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient with Alzheimer's disease taking donepezil progresses to severe disease. What does UK guidance advise?
options: Stop the donepezil and switch to memantine alone
Continue the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and add memantine
Stop all cognitive drugs, as they no longer help
Switch to an oral atypical antipsychotic instead
Start levodopa with a dopamine agonist alongside
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Continue the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and add memantine
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is not stopped because the disease has progressed to severe — memantine is added rather than substituted. Memantine is used as monotherapy for severe disease, for moderate disease where an AChE inhibitor is not tolerated or contraindicated, and as an add-on in moderate or severe disease (NICE).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient with vascular dementia (no suspected comorbid Alzheimer's) is reviewed. What is the appropriate drug approach?
options: Start donepezil in every patient with vascular dementia at the time of diagnosis
Control vascular risk factors; cognitive drugs only if comorbid AD, DLB or PDD
Start memantine routinely, as it is the licensed drug for vascular dementia
Start a regular antipsychotic to slow the progression of the vascular damage
No management of any kind is possible once vascular dementia is diagnosed
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Control vascular risk factors; cognitive drugs only if comorbid AD, DLB or PDD
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Pure vascular dementia is managed by controlling cardiovascular risk factors; cognitive drugs are reserved for suspected comorbid AD/DLB/PD dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Which dementia subtype should NOT be treated with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or memantine?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Frontotemporal dementia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: FTD does not benefit from (and may be worsened by) AChE inhibitors/memantine, so they are not used.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Before starting an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, which cardiac issue must be considered?
options: Hypertension, but no other cardiac concern
Severe aortic stenosis, but nothing else
A raised total cholesterol on screening
No cardiac problem is relevant before starting
Bradycardia, heart block and QT prolongation
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Bradycardia, heart block and QT prolongation
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are pro-cholinergic and can cause bradycardia, so caution or avoidance applies in bradycardia, QT prolongation and conduction disease; cognitive stimulation therapy is used instead if the QT is prolonged.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient with dementia becomes agitated. What is the first-line management of this BPSD?
options: Non-drug measures first, seeking triggers such as pain, infection or constipation
An immediate antipsychotic at the highest licensed dose before any assessment
A regular benzodiazepine started at once and continued indefinitely thereafter
Physical restraint applied routinely whenever any agitation appears on the ward
Sedation with a sedating antihistamine given regularly as the first-line measure
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Non-drug measures first, seeking triggers such as pain, infection or constipation
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: BPSD is managed non-pharmacologically first (identify/treat triggers, person-centred care); antipsychotics are reserved for severe distress/risk when non-drug measures fail.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: When are antipsychotics appropriate for BPSD, and what is the key risk?
options: Routinely for all agitation from diagnosis, as they carry no added risk in the elderly
First-line for any wandering or restlessness, then continued long-term at the maximum dose
Only for hallucinations in Lewy body dementia, where they are the safest drug class
Only for severe distress or risk after non-drug measures fail; they raise stroke and death risk
Long-term for every patient with dementia, with no need to review or attempt withdrawal
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Only for severe distress or risk after non-drug measures fail; they raise stroke and death risk
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Antipsychotics are reserved for severe distress/risk after non-drug measures fail (short-term, lowest dose) and carry increased stroke and mortality risk in elderly dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: In which dementia must antipsychotics be avoided wherever possible because of a dangerous drug sensitivity?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: DLB has a severe (sometimes fatal) antipsychotic sensitivity, so antipsychotics are avoided.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: During a dementia assessment, why should the medication list be reviewed?
options: Because a high anticholinergic burden worsens cognition
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Because a high anticholinergic burden worsens cognition
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Anticholinergic drugs worsen cognition, so the anticholinergic burden is reviewed and reduced where possible.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient presents with a short history of poor memory, low mood and 'don't know' answers. Which reversible condition must be screened for before diagnosing dementia?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Depression (pseudodementia)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Depression (pseudodementia) is a reversible mimic; a depression screen is part of excluding reversible causes before diagnosing dementia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: A patient with Alzheimer's has QT prolongation, making an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor unsuitable. What non-drug cognitive intervention can be offered?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Cognitive stimulation therapy
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Cognitive stimulation therapy is a non-drug cognitive intervention used, for example, where an AChE inhibitor is contraindicated (e.g. QT prolongation).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.question: Alongside cognitive and BPSD management, which measures are important across all dementias?
options: Drug treatment alone, since psychosocial measures have no role in dementia care
Nothing beyond medication until the person can no longer live independently
Antipsychotics for every patient from diagnosis to prevent behavioural symptoms
Lifelong hospital admission at diagnosis, as community care is never appropriate
Carer support and OT, advance care planning, capacity, DVLA notification, safeguarding
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.answer: Carer support and OT, advance care planning, capacity, DVLA notification, safeguarding
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psych.explanation: Supportive and planning measures — carer support, OT, advance care planning, LPA, capacity assessment, DVLA notification and safeguarding — apply across all dementias.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: An 80-year-old woman with cognitive decline insists that her husband has been replaced by an identical impostor who looks exactly like him. What is this delusion, and what must be considered?
options: Capgras delusion; consider an organic cause (e.g. dementia, especially Lewy body)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.answer: Capgras delusion; consider an organic cause (e.g. dementia, especially Lewy body)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: Believing a familiar person is replaced by an identical impostor is the Capgras delusion ('Capgras = Clone'); in an older patient with cognitive decline, an organic cause (dementia, esp. Lewy body) must be considered.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A patient believes that various strangers he meets are actually his brother in disguise. Which syndrome is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: Believing that strangers are a familiar person in disguise is Fregoli syndrome — the mirror image of Capgras.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A severely depressed patient with psychotic features believes that his internal organs have rotted away and that he is already dead. What is this syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: The nihilistic belief that one is dead/non-existent/rotting is Cotard syndrome, classically associated with severe (psychotic) depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A man has a fixed, unshakeable belief that his wife is having an affair, despite no evidence, and has begun following and threatening her. Which syndrome is this, and what is the key concern?
options: Erotomania; the risk is stalking of the perceived admirer
Capgras delusion; the key concern is an organic cause
Othello syndrome; high risk of violence towards the partner
Cotard syndrome; the key concern is a high suicide risk
Fregoli syndrome; the risk is persecutory misidentification
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.answer: Othello syndrome; high risk of violence towards the partner
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: A fixed, unshakeable belief in a partner's infidelity is Othello syndrome (pathological jealousy). It carries a significant risk of violence or harm to the partner, and to the alleged rival — a forensic-risk delusion that must be taken seriously.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A woman is convinced that a famous news presenter is secretly in love with her and sends her coded messages through the television, and she has started contacting him repeatedly. Which syndrome is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: The belief that a (usually higher-status) person is secretly in love with them, with 'secret messages', is erotomania (De Clérambault), which can lead to stalking/harassment.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A patient presents to dermatology convinced she is infested with tiny bugs, with scratch marks over her arms, and brings a matchbox of 'specimens' (which are skin flakes). What is this syndrome?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: A fixed belief of infestation with excoriations and the 'matchbox sign' is delusional parasitosis (Ekbom syndrome).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: An elderly man with macular degeneration describes seeing vivid images of children and animals in his room; he knows they are not real and is otherwise well. What is the diagnosis, and how is it managed?
options: Charles-Bonnet syndrome; reassurance and optimising vision (NOT antipsychotics)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.answer: Charles-Bonnet syndrome; reassurance and optimising vision (NOT antipsychotics)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: Complex visual hallucinations with eye disease, clear consciousness and retained insight are Charles-Bonnet syndrome (a release phenomenon of visual loss), managed with reassurance and optimising vision — not antipsychotics.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A patient believes their body or the world is dead or non-existent. What TYPE of delusion is this, and its classic association?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: A belief that oneself/the world is dead or non-existent is a nihilistic delusion, classically in psychotic depression (Cotard's).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A patient with mania believes he has special god-given powers to heal the sick. What type of delusion is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: A belief in special powers/status is a grandiose delusion, classically associated with mania.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: Which pair correctly contrasts Capgras and Fregoli?
options: Capgras = strangers in disguise; Fregoli = familiar person is an impostor
Capgras = a familiar person is an impostor/'clone'; Fregoli = strangers are a familiar person in disguise
Both mean a person is dead
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.answer: Capgras = a familiar person is an impostor/'clone'; Fregoli = strangers are a familiar person in disguise
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: Capgras = a familiar person replaced by an impostor; Fregoli = strangers seen as a familiar person in disguise — they are mirror images.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A patient with Cotard syndrome due to psychotic depression needs treatment. Which is most appropriate?
options: Antidepressant treatment (± an antipsychotic/ECT) for the psychotic depression
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.answer: Antidepressant treatment (± an antipsychotic/ECT) for the psychotic depression
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: Cotard's from psychotic depression is treated by treating the depression — antidepressants ± an antipsychotic, with ECT for severe/refractory cases.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A patient with Othello syndrome poses a risk to his partner. What is a key management priority?
options: Ignore the risk, as it is only a fixed belief
Prescribe the partner a depot antipsychotic
Treat only if he later becomes depressed
Reassure the partner that there is no real risk
Assess and manage the risk to the partner
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.answer: Assess and manage the risk to the partner
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: Pathological jealousy carries a high risk of violence towards the partner, so risk assessment and management — which may require separation or safeguarding — are priorities alongside treating the underlying disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: Which features would most strongly suggest a SECONDARY (organic) cause of a misidentification syndrome rather than a primary psychotic disorder?
options: Young age with chronic stable symptoms
Older age, cognitive impairment, acute onset, fluctuation or focal neurological signs
A clear family history of schizophrenia only
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.answer: Older age, cognitive impairment, acute onset, fluctuation or focal neurological signs
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: Older age, cognitive impairment, acute/fluctuating onset and focal signs point to a secondary/organic cause (e.g. dementia, delirium, lesion), prompting cognitive assessment and imaging.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: Which statement about the management of the delusional syndromes is correct?
options: Treat the underlying cause, plus antipsychotics except in Charles-Bonnet and Lewy body dementia
Antipsychotics are the established first-line treatment in Charles-Bonnet syndrome
All of these syndromes are treated with antidepressant monotherapy on its own
No treatment is ever effective for these, so only supportive care is offered
Electroconvulsive therapy is the first-line treatment for all of these syndromes
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.answer: Treat the underlying cause, plus antipsychotics except in Charles-Bonnet and Lewy body dementia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: Treat the underlying cause and use antipsychotics for the delusional content — but not in Charles-Bonnet syndrome, where insight is retained and the treatment is reassurance and optimising vision, and avoid them where possible in Lewy body dementia because of severe neuroleptic sensitivity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.question: A patient with somatic-type delusional disorder is convinced they have a serious medical illness despite thorough normal investigations. What TYPE of delusion is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Mis.explanation: A fixed belief in a physical/medical problem despite no evidence is a somatic delusion, characteristic of somatic delusional disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A 22-year-old is brought in after a week of barely sleeping, talking rapidly and jumping between grandiose plans, spending thousands he cannot afford, and now expressing the belief that he has special powers. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: A manic episode (bipolar I disorder)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Elevated mood ≥7 days with severe impairment, reduced sleep, grandiosity/reckless spending and psychotic (grandiose) beliefs is a manic episode, which defines bipolar I.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: What is the key difference between mania and hypomania?
options: Hypomania lasts considerably longer than mania and causes far more impairment
Hypomania always includes psychotic features, while mania never involves them
Mania lasts 7 days or more with severe impairment or psychosis; hypomania has neither
They are the same state, distinguished only by the degree of patient insight
Mania never impairs function and is fully compatible with normal daily work
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Mania lasts 7 days or more with severe impairment or psychosis; hypomania has neither
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Mania (≥7 days, severe impairment, ± psychosis) is distinguished from hypomania (at least 4 days with no upper limit, function preserved, no psychosis); psychotic features automatically make it mania.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A patient has had episodes of hypomania and depression but never a full manic episode. Which diagnosis fits?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Bipolar II disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Bipolar II is hypomania + depression with no full mania; a true manic episode would make it bipolar I.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: What single clinical question most reliably separates bipolar from unipolar depression?
options: 'Do you feel low or hopeless on most days?'
'Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?'
'Have you ever had a period of unusually high mood?'
'Do you have obsessions or compulsive rituals?'
'How much alcohol do you drink in a week?'
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: 'Have you ever had a period of unusually high mood?'
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Bipolar is defined by at least one manic/hypomanic episode, so asking about a past 'high' is the key discriminator from unipolar depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A manic patient's speech leaps rapidly between topics, but the links between them can still be followed. What is this called, and what does it indicate?
options: Flight of ideas; a manic thought disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Flight of ideas; a manic thought disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Flight of ideas (leaps with discernible links) is the manic thought disorder; knight's move thinking (leaps with no links) points to schizophrenia.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A patient not on treatment presents with acute mania. What is the first-line management?
options: Start an SSRI antidepressant at full dose
Lithium monotherapy started the same day
A benzodiazepine alone as sole treatment
An antipsychotic such as olanzapine or haloperidol
Reassurance with review in six weeks' time
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: An antipsychotic such as olanzapine or haloperidol
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Acute mania in a patient not already on treatment is managed first line with an antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone or haloperidol), started regardless of any antidepressant, which should then be considered for stopping as it may be driving the mania.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A manic patient is severely agitated and aggressive. What is the appropriate acute management?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: An IM antipsychotic ± a benzodiazepine
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: For agitated mania, an IM antipsychotic ± a benzodiazepine is used; without agitation, oral antipsychotic monotherapy is appropriate.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A patient with known bipolar disorder presents with a depressive episode. Which is the safest approach?
options: Start an SSRI alone and continue it as indefinite monotherapy once the mood lifts
Stop all existing treatment and observe, as bipolar depression is self-limiting
Start venlafaxine monotherapy, as it carries the lowest risk of switching to mania
Give only a benzodiazepine, since mood stabilisers worsen every depressive episode
Use quetiapine, olanzapine with fluoxetine or lamotrigine, not an antidepressant alone
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Use quetiapine, olanzapine with fluoxetine or lamotrigine, not an antidepressant alone
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Antidepressant monotherapy risks switching to mania in bipolar depression; quetiapine, olanzapine (± fluoxetine) or lamotrigine alone are used.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: Which antidepressant carries the highest risk of triggering a manic switch in bipolar disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Venlafaxine (also TCAs)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Venlafaxine (and TCAs) carry the highest switch risk, which is why antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar depression.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: What is the first-line long-term prophylactic mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder, with an added benefit?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Lithium; also reduces suicide risk
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Lithium is first-line prophylaxis (most effective) and additionally reduces suicide risk; valproate or an antipsychotic are alternatives, though valproate must not be started under 55 without two specialists documenting no alternative (MHRA).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: Which set of side effects is characteristic of lithium?
options: Alopecia, pancreatitis and acute liver failure
Fine tremor, hypothyroidism, polyuria and hypercalcaemia
A dry cough, angio-oedema and hyperkalaemia
Gum hypertrophy, hirsutism and coarse facial features
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Fine tremor, hypothyroidism, polyuria and hypercalcaemia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Lithium causes a fine tremor, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (polyuria), GI upset, weight gain, nephrotoxicity and hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcaemia (LITHIUM mnemonic).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A patient on lithium becomes toxic. Which of the following commonly precipitates lithium toxicity?
options: Drinking extra water during a spell of hot weather
Taking a daily vitamin C supplement with breakfast
Adding extra salt to food during a summer holiday
Taking regular moderate aerobic exercise each week
Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Dehydration, renal impairment and drugs that reduce lithium clearance — NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs and thiazide diuretics — raise lithium levels and precipitate toxicity.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A patient on lithium presents with a coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech and confusion, preceded by vomiting and diarrhoea. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Lithium toxicity; stop lithium and give IV fluids (± haemodialysis if severe)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Lithium toxicity; stop lithium and give IV fluids (± haemodialysis if severe)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: A coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria and confusion (often after GI symptoms) in a lithium-treated patient is lithium toxicity — stop lithium, rehydrate with IV fluids, and dialyse if severe.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: How should lithium levels and organ function be monitored?
options: Levels one hour post-dose monthly indefinitely, with no thyroid or renal tests
Levels 12 hours post-dose, weekly until stable, then 3-monthly for the first year
Levels checked only when the patient is symptomatic, with annual thyroid tests
No monitoring of any kind is required once a stable maintenance dose is reached
Annual levels only, with renal and thyroid function checked every five years
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Levels 12 hours post-dose, weekly until stable, then 3-monthly for the first year
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L). Levels are taken 12 hours post-dose, weekly until stable, then 3-monthly for the first year and 6-monthly thereafter, staying 3-monthly in higher-risk people. TFTs, renal function and calcium are checked every 6 months.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A 40-year-old man with bipolar disorder is being considered for valproate. What is the current prescribing restriction?
options: Valproate is first-line in bipolar disorder and may be started freely in any man
Valproate may be used safely throughout pregnancy at standard therapeutic doses
Do not start valproate under 55 unless two specialists agree there is no alternative
There is no prescribing restriction of any kind when the patient is a male adult
Valproate is banned entirely in the UK and may no longer be prescribed to anyone
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Do not start valproate under 55 unless two specialists agree there is no alternative
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Valproate must not be started in anyone (male or female) under 55 unless two specialists agree there is no alternative, and never in women of childbearing potential without a pregnancy prevention programme.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: Which set of adverse effects is characteristic of sodium valproate?
options: Vomiting, alopecia, liver toxicity, pancreatitis, weight gain, tremor — and it is teratogenic
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Vomiting, alopecia, liver toxicity, pancreatitis, weight gain, tremor — and it is teratogenic
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Valproate causes vomiting, alopecia, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis/pancytopenia, weight gain, tremor and enzyme inhibition, and is teratogenic (VALPROATE mnemonic).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: Before starting lithium, which baseline investigations are essential?
options: U&E/eGFR, thyroid function tests and calcium (± a pregnancy test)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: U&E/eGFR, thyroid function tests and calcium (± a pregnancy test)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Lithium affects the kidney, thyroid and parathyroid, so U&E/eGFR, TFTs and calcium are checked at baseline (with a pregnancy test given teratogenicity).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A patient has a chronic pattern of mild mood swings — short periods of feeling 'up' and periods of low mood — that never meet the full criteria for mania or a depressive episode. What is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Cyclothymia
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Cyclothymia is a chronic pattern of subthreshold highs and lows that does not meet the full criteria for bipolar disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A patient on long-term corticosteroids develops elevated mood, grandiosity and reduced sleep. What should be considered before diagnosing bipolar disorder?
options: Nothing — it is definitely bipolar I
Steroid-induced mania (and other secondary causes) should be excluded
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Steroid-induced mania (and other secondary causes) should be excluded
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Secondary causes such as steroid-induced mania, hyperthyroidism and stimulant use should be excluded before diagnosing primary bipolar disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A patient presents in a clearly manic state with risk to themselves. What is the appropriate referral urgency?
options: Urgent referral to the CMHT/secondary care
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Urgent referral to the CMHT/secondary care
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Mania (or severe depression) warrants urgent CMHT/secondary-care referral; hypomania can be referred routinely.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: Why is a collateral history particularly important in diagnosing bipolar disorder?
options: It is a legal requirement before diagnosis
It replaces the need for a mental state exam
Blood tests are diagnostic in place of history
Patients often lack insight into their 'highs'
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Patients often lack insight into their 'highs'
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Patients frequently lack insight into manic or hypomanic episodes and may not report them, so an informant (collateral) history is invaluable for establishing past episodes and the diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.question: A euthymic patient with bipolar I on lithium wants to stop it because they 'feel fine'. What is the best advice regarding prophylaxis?
options: Stop the lithium immediately as the patient is well
Halve the dose and stop routine lithium monitoring
Continue long-term lithium prophylaxis; do not stop abruptly
Stop lithium and switch to an antidepressant instead
Treat only during acute episodes, with no prophylaxis
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.answer: Continue long-term lithium prophylaxis; do not stop abruptly
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affectiv.explanation: Bipolar disorder is a relapsing illness, so prophylaxis is continued even when the patient is euthymic. Lithium reduces both relapse and suicide risk, and abrupt withdrawal carries a high risk of rebound mania.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient has persistent, uncontrollable worry across many areas of life most days, with restlessness and muscle tension, for the past 8 months. Which anxiety disorder does this best fit?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Generalised, free-floating, uncontrollable worry across multiple domains most days for ≥6 months is GAD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A person develops marked anxiety and dissociative symptoms hours after a serious car crash, which settle over a few days. What is this, and how does it differ from PTSD?
options: PTSD; the symptoms have lasted over a month
Panic disorder; the attacks are recurrent
Acute stress reaction; it resolves within days
GAD; the anxiety is free-floating and generalised
OCD; there are obsessions and compulsions
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Acute stress reaction; it resolves within days
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: An acute stress reaction begins within minutes to hours of an exceptional stressor and settles within days. PTSD is diagnosed only when symptoms persist beyond one month.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which therapy is the specific psychological treatment for OCD?
options: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: OCD is specifically treated with CBT incorporating exposure and response prevention (ERP), not generic CBT alone.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which features define panic disorder?
options: Constant low-grade worry about many everyday things
A single prolonged reaction to a severe trauma
Anxiety confined to social or performance settings
Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with anticipatory worry
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with anticipatory worry
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Panic disorder is defined by recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus persistent anticipatory worry about further attacks (the 'fear of fear') and associated avoidance between attacks.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Before diagnosing a primary anxiety disorder, what should always be excluded?
options: A personality disorder only, as no physical condition can ever mimic anxiety
Nothing at all, since the diagnosis is purely clinical and requires no work-up
A specific phobia, which must always be ruled out before any other diagnosis
Organic mimics such as hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia and caffeine or stimulant use
Dementia, which is the commonest organic cause of new anxiety at any adult age
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Organic mimics such as hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia and caffeine or stimulant use
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Organic/drug mimics (hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, caffeine/stimulants) must be excluded, and comorbid depression, substance use and suicide risk screened, before settling on a primary anxiety diagnosis.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A 40-year-old woman describes worrying uncontrollably about work, money, her family and health almost every day for the last 8 months, feeling on edge and tense with poor sleep, and cannot pin the worry to any one thing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Generalised anxiety disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Pervasive, uncontrollable, free-floating worry across many domains most days for ≥6 months with tension/sleep disturbance is GAD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient with anxiety symptoms also has a tremor, weight loss, tachycardia and heat intolerance. What must be excluded before diagnosing GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Hyperthyroidism (check thyroid function tests)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Hyperthyroidism mimics GAD; TFTs (along with excluding cardiac and drug/caffeine causes) should be checked before diagnosing primary GAD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which feature best distinguishes GAD from panic disorder?
options: GAD is constant pervasive worry, whereas panic disorder comes in sudden bursts
GAD occurs in short discrete attacks with entirely well periods in between
GAD is triggered by one specific feared object or clearly defined situation
GAD only ever develops in the weeks directly following a traumatic event
Panic disorder produces continuous symptoms for months without any break
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: GAD is constant pervasive worry, whereas panic disorder comes in sudden bursts
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: GAD is continuous, generalised worry; panic disorder consists of discrete attacks with relatively symptom-free intervals and anticipatory 'fear of fear'.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which validated questionnaire is used to screen for and grade the severity of GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: GAD-7
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: The GAD-7 is the validated screening/severity tool for generalised anxiety disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: For how long must generalised worry be present (more days than not) to diagnose GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: ≥6 months
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: GAD requires excessive worry present more days than not for at least 6 months.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What is the first-line drug treatment for GAD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: An SSRI (e.g. sertraline)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: An SSRI (sertraline is most cost-effective) is first-line drug treatment; benzodiazepines are avoided.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Why are benzodiazepines not used as regular treatment for GAD?
options: Because they are wholly ineffective for any anxiety
Because of dependence and tolerance with long-term use
Because they are not licensed for any indication
Because they worsen physiological tremor markedly
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Because of dependence and tolerance with long-term use
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Benzodiazepines cause dependence and tolerance and are associated with worse long-term outcomes, so they are avoided as regular treatment in GAD and reserved for short-term crisis use only.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient with GAD cannot tolerate SSRIs or SNRIs. Which third-line agent may be used, and what is a key caution?
options: Diazepam long-term; it carries no risk of dependence
Olanzapine; it is licensed first-line and needs no monitoring
Pregabalin; it is a controlled drug with dependence potential
Propranolol; it fully abolishes the psychological worry of GAD
Buspirone; it is first-line in GAD and free of any cautions
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Pregabalin; it is a controlled drug with dependence potential
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Pregabalin is a third-line option in GAD when SSRIs and SNRIs cannot be used. It is now a controlled drug with dependence and misuse potential, and requires caution in pregnancy.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What is the role of propranolol in GAD?
options: It is used to sedate the patient long-term
It relieves the autonomic symptoms (tremor, palpitations) only, not the worry itself
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: It relieves the autonomic symptoms (tremor, palpitations) only, not the worry itself
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Propranolol helps somatic/autonomic symptoms (tremor, palpitations) but does not treat the core worry, so it is only an adjunct.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient hyperventilating during a panic attack develops tingling around the mouth and in the fingers with carpopedal spasm. What is the mechanism?
options: Hyperkalaemia produced by catecholamine release during the acute stress response
Hypoglycaemia caused by the greatly increased work of breathing in the attack
A focal seizure arising in the parietal lobe and spreading to the motor cortex
Respiratory alkalosis raises calcium binding to albumin, lowering ionised calcium
A rise in ionised calcium driven by respiratory acidosis during overbreathing
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Respiratory alkalosis raises calcium binding to albumin, lowering ionised calcium
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂, causing respiratory alkalosis that increases calcium binding to albumin, lowering ionised calcium and producing peri-oral/peripheral tingling and carpopedal spasm.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Once an antidepressant is effective in GAD, for how long should it generally be continued?
options: Stop as soon as symptoms improve
At least 1 year (given the high relapse risk)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: At least 1 year (given the high relapse risk)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Effective drug treatment for GAD should be continued for at least a year because of the high relapse risk, with early review — if under 30, seen within 1 week and monitored weekly for the first month.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: According to NICE stepped care for GAD, what is the correct escalation from Step 1?
options: A benzodiazepine, then an antipsychotic drug
Drug treatment before any psychological input
Discharge if symptoms persist after Step 1
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Low-intensity psychological interventions
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: NICE stepped care for GAD runs: Step 1 identification, education and active monitoring → Step 2 low-intensity psychological interventions → Step 3 high-intensity CBT or drug treatment → Step 4 specialist referral. Escalation from Step 1 is therefore to low-intensity psychological work.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient develops anxiety symptoms shortly after starting a new inhaler and drinking large amounts of coffee. What should be considered?
options: Primary GAD requiring lifelong SSRI treatment
A specific phobia of medical procedures
An acute stress reaction to a recent trauma
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Drug- and substance-induced anxiety symptoms
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Beta-agonists such as salbutamol, plus caffeine, theophylline, steroids and stimulants, can all cause anxiety. These drug and substance causes should be reviewed and addressed before diagnosing primary GAD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient with GAD has not responded to an adequate trial of sertraline. Which is an appropriate next drug step?
options: Start an antipsychotic in primary care
Use propranolol as monotherapy for the worry
Switch to an alternative SSRI or an SNRI (e.g. venlafaxine/duloxetine)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Switch to an alternative SSRI or an SNRI (e.g. venlafaxine/duloxetine)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: If an SSRI is ineffective, an alternative SSRI or an SNRI (venlafaxine/duloxetine) is appropriate, mindful of withdrawal and overdose toxicity; pregabalin is third-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A 32-year-old has recurrent episodes of sudden intense fear that come 'out of the blue', with palpitations, chest tightness, breathlessness and a fear of dying, peaking within minutes. Between episodes he constantly worries about the next one and has attended A&E several times fearing a heart attack. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Panic disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks peaking within minutes plus persistent anticipatory worry ('fear of fear'), often misread as cardiac, is panic disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: How does a panic attack differ from panic disorder?
options: They are the same thing; a single attack is sufficient to diagnose panic disorder
A panic attack builds slowly over months and lasts for weeks without a break
A panic attack is a symptom of many conditions; panic disorder is recurrent and unexpected
Panic disorder is diagnosed after one episode triggered by a clearly identified cue
Panic attacks occur only within panic disorder and never in phobia, GAD or PTSD
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: A panic attack is a symptom of many conditions; panic disorder is recurrent and unexpected
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: A panic attack is a symptom (seen in GAD, phobias, PTSD, real threat); panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks with anticipatory worry.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which investigations are appropriate to exclude organic mimics of panic disorder?
options: ECG, thyroid function tests and blood glucose
MRI of the brain with a lumbar puncture
An EEG plus nerve conduction studies
No investigations are needed in any case
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: ECG, thyroid function tests and blood glucose
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Targeted tests — ECG for cardiac causes, thyroid function tests, glucose, plus a review of caffeine, stimulant and substance use — exclude organic mimics; over-investigation is then avoided so as not to reinforce health anxiety.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which cognitive mechanism maintains panic disorder and is the target of CBT?
options: Obsessional doubt driving repeated checking rituals
Intrusive flashbacks and re-experiencing of trauma
Compulsive washing to neutralise contamination fears
Free-floating worry across many everyday domains
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: The 'fear of fear' cycle — hypervigilance to and catastrophic misinterpretation of normal bodily sensations, which triggers further attacks — perpetuates panic disorder and is what CBT addresses.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient with panic disorder increasingly avoids buses, crowds and going far from home for fear of having an attack where escape is hard. What has developed?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Agoraphobia (often secondary to panic disorder)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Agoraphobia — fear/avoidance of situations where escape/help would be difficult during an attack — commonly develops secondary to panic disorder and can be disabling.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What is the first-line treatment for panic disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: CBT (best long-term evidence)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: CBT is first-line for panic disorder, targeting the catastrophic-misinterpretation cycle; an SSRI is the first-line drug option.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which is the appropriate first-line DRUG treatment for panic disorder?
options: An SSRI licensed for panic disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: An SSRI licensed for panic disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: An SSRI licensed for panic disorder (escitalopram, citalopram or paroxetine) is the first-line drug treatment; imipramine or clomipramine is second-line, and benzodiazepines are not recommended.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient with panic disorder has had no improvement after a 12-week course of an SSRI. Which is an appropriate next drug option?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Imipramine or clomipramine (a TCA)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: If an SSRI is unsuitable or ineffective after 12 weeks, a TCA (imipramine or clomipramine) is used; benzodiazepines/antipsychotics/sedating antihistamines are avoided.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which drugs does NICE advise AGAINST using for panic disorder?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Benzodiazepines, antipsychotics and sedating antihistamines
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Benzodiazepines (dependence/worse outcomes), antipsychotics and sedating antihistamines should not be used for panic disorder.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: When starting an SSRI for panic disorder, what should the patient be warned about?
options: That anxiety can transiently worsen on initiation, so it is started low and titrated slowly
That it must be stopped after one week
That it cures the disorder in 48 hours
That it causes dependence like a benzodiazepine
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: That anxiety can transiently worsen on initiation, so it is started low and titrated slowly
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: SSRIs can transiently worsen anxiety on initiation in panic disorder, so they are started low and titrated slowly, with the patient warned; treatment continues ≥6 months after response.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What is the typical time course of a single panic attack?
options: Builds over hours and lasts all day
A constant level of anxiety for weeks
A discrete surge of intense fear peaking within about 10 minutes and then settling
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: A discrete surge of intense fear peaking within about 10 minutes and then settling
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: A panic attack is a discrete episode peaking within ~10 minutes with ≥4 symptoms, then self-limiting — though terrifying at the time.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient with clear recurrent unexpected panic attacks has had a normal ECG and TFTs. He keeps requesting further cardiac tests. What is the best approach?
options: Explain the diagnosis, avoid over-investigation, and offer CBT
Arrange repeated invasive cardiac investigations to reassure him
Prescribe a long-term benzodiazepine to settle the attacks
Refer urgently back to cardiology for a further opinion
Tell him nothing is wrong and discharge without any treatment
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Explain the diagnosis, avoid over-investigation, and offer CBT
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Once the pattern is clear and organic mimics have been excluded, further testing reinforces health anxiety. Explain the diagnosis, stop investigating, and offer CBT, with an SSRI if he prefers a drug or CBT is insufficient.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A 19-year-old is tormented by intrusive thoughts that his hands are contaminated; he recognises the thoughts as irrational and his own but feels compelled to wash his hands for hours, which briefly relieves the anxiety. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Ego-dystonic intrusive obsessions (contamination) driving compulsions (washing) that only temporarily relieve anxiety, with insight retained, is OCD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What is the key distinction between OCD and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD)?
options: OCD is a lifelong personality trait present continuously since early adulthood
OCPD is defined by true obsessions and compulsions performed to relieve anxiety
They are the same disorder simply described under two different diagnostic labels
OCD is characterised by complete absence of insight into the intrusive thoughts
OCD is ego-dystonic and resisted, whereas OCPD is ego-syntonic rigid perfectionism
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: OCD is ego-dystonic and resisted, whereas OCPD is ego-syntonic rigid perfectionism
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: OCD is an ego-dystonic anxiety disorder (distressing, resisted); OCPD is an ego-syntonic personality trait (perfectionism the person sees as correct).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which cycle maintains OCD and is targeted by treatment?
options: Obsession → anxiety → compulsion → temporary relief → reinforcement
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Obsession → anxiety → compulsion → temporary relief → reinforcement
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: OCD is maintained by the obsession→anxiety→compulsion→temporary relief→reinforcement cycle; ERP breaks it by exposure with response prevention.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What is the specialised first-line psychological therapy for OCD?
options: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: ERP (exposure to the trigger with prevention of the compulsion, leading to habituation and extinction) is the specific psychological treatment for OCD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What is the first-line DRUG treatment for OCD, and how does its use differ from depression?
options: A benzodiazepine, at the same dose as used in anxiety
An SSRI, at higher doses than in depression and for longer
An antipsychotic, given as a short course at a low dose
Clomipramine as the first choice ahead of any other drug
A sedating antihistamine taken regularly at night-time
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: An SSRI, at higher doses than in depression and for longer
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: First-line is an SSRI (fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline or citalopram), typically at higher doses than in depression, with response taking up to about 12 weeks and treatment continued for at least 12 months if effective.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: If an SSRI is effective in OCD, for how long should it be continued?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: At least 12 months
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Effective SSRI treatment for OCD is continued for at least 12 months (longer than the ~6 months used in depression).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: An SSRI has been ineffective and poorly tolerated in a patient with OCD. Which second-line drug is appropriate?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Clomipramine (a serotonergic TCA)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Clomipramine, a TCA with strong serotonergic action, is second-line for OCD when an SSRI is ineffective or not tolerated (or with a prior good response).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient with severe OCD has failed an SSRI, combined SSRI + ERP, and clomipramine. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Stop all treatment and simply monitor for a year
Refer to a specialist OCD multidisciplinary team
Reassure the patient and discharge to the GP
Switch to a sedating antihistamine long term
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Refer to a specialist OCD multidisciplinary team
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Treatment-resistant OCD is referred to a specialist OCD multidisciplinary team, where options include augmentation with an antipsychotic alongside further intensive CBT with exposure and response prevention.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which feature distinguishes OCD obsessions from psychotic delusions?
options: In OCD, the obsessions are held as absolutely true with no insight whatsoever
In OCD, insight is retained and the thoughts are recognised as the person's own
Delusions are always about contamination and the fear of spreading infection
OCD involves no distressing thoughts at all, only repetitive observable acts
They are indistinguishable and both respond only to high-dose antipsychotics
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: In OCD, insight is retained and the thoughts are recognised as the person's own
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: OCD obsessions are ego-dystonic with retained insight; psychotic delusions are held as true beliefs with no insight.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient is preoccupied with a perceived defect in their appearance and repeatedly checks mirrors. Which condition is this, and how is it managed?
options: Body dysmorphic disorder; treated on the same NICE pathway as OCD
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Body dysmorphic disorder; treated on the same NICE pathway as OCD
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Body dysmorphic disorder (preoccupation with a perceived defect + related compulsions like mirror-checking) is treated on the same NICE pathway as OCD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A child develops abrupt-onset OCD and tics shortly after a streptococcal throat infection. Which association is this?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: PANDAS (paediatric OCD/tics after streptococcal infection)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: PANDAS refers to paediatric OCD/tics arising after streptococcal infection — a recognised association/risk factor for OCD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: According to NICE, how is MODERATE OCD managed?
options: Combined SSRI + CBT + specialist referral for all
Either an SSRI OR more intensive CBT (including ERP), by patient choice
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Either an SSRI OR more intensive CBT (including ERP), by patient choice
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Moderate OCD is managed with either an SSRI or more intensive CBT (including ERP) according to patient choice; mild is low-intensity CBT/ERP, and severe is combined SSRI + CBT/ERP with referral.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What is the difference between an obsession and a compulsion in OCD?
options: Obsessions are intrusive thoughts; compulsions are acts done to relieve anxiety
Obsessions are the behaviours, while compulsions are the intrusive thoughts
They are one phenomenon described using two entirely interchangeable terms
Compulsions are involuntary motor tics that arise without any mental urge
Obsessions always concern symmetry and are never about harm or contamination
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Obsessions are intrusive thoughts; compulsions are acts done to relieve anxiety
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Obsessions are intrusive unwanted thoughts/images/urges; compulsions are the repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed in response to reduce the anxiety.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A man is assaulted and, over the next few days, has flashbacks, feels 'in a daze' and unreal, is hypervigilant and cannot sleep. Two weeks later the symptoms are settling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Acute stress reaction/disorder
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: A transient trauma response within the first 4 weeks (with prominent dissociation) that is settling is an acute stress reaction; PTSD is diagnosed only if symptoms persist beyond a month.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A trauma survivor still has intrusive flashbacks, avoidance and hyperarousal 6 weeks after the event. How does the diagnosis change?
options: It becomes post-traumatic stress disorder (symptoms persisting >1 month)
It remains an acute stress reaction
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: It becomes post-traumatic stress disorder (symptoms persisting >1 month)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: A trauma response persisting beyond a month is, by definition, PTSD — the diagnosis changes with the timing.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient develops low mood and difficulty coping within a month of a divorce, which gradually resolves over a few months as they adapt. What is this?
options: Adjustment disorder (preoccupation plus failure to adapt)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Adjustment disorder (preoccupation plus failure to adapt)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Adjustment disorder is preoccupation with an identifiable stressor plus failure to adapt, arising within ~1 month and resolving within ~6 months as the person adapts. It does not meet the threshold for a depressive episode, and there is no re-experiencing or persistent sense of current threat.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Which symptom cluster is often especially prominent in an acute stress reaction compared with PTSD?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Dissociation (daze, unreality/derealisation, time distortion)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Dissociative symptoms (feeling in a daze, derealisation/depersonalisation, time-slowing) are often especially prominent early in an acute stress reaction.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient has mild stress-reaction symptoms 1 week after a traumatic event. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start a benzodiazepine to prevent PTSD
Active monitoring with follow-up contact within about a month
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Active monitoring with follow-up contact within about a month
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Most acute stress reactions resolve; subthreshold symptoms are managed with active monitoring and follow-up. Single-session psychological debriefing is not offered — it does not prevent PTSD and may worsen outcomes.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: A patient has severe, distressing acute stress symptoms in the first month after a trauma. What is the first-line intervention?
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Trauma-focused CBT (TF-CBT)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: If intervention is needed for severe symptoms within the first month, trauma-focused CBT is first-line.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: What does current NICE advise regarding drug treatment after acute trauma?
options: Do NOT offer drug treatment (including benzodiazepines) to prevent PTSD
Give a benzodiazepine to all to prevent PTSD
Start an SSRI immediately in everyone
Sedate the patient for a week
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Do NOT offer drug treatment (including benzodiazepines) to prevent PTSD
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: NICE advises against drug treatment (including benzodiazepines) to prevent PTSD; benzodiazepines are not recommended (dependence, possible worse outcomes).

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Why is follow-up important after an acute stress reaction?
options: To repeatedly debrief the patient in detail
To detect those progressing to PTSD later
To titrate the benzodiazepine dose upwards
To confirm that the trauma really occurred
To arrange compensation and legal reports
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: To detect those progressing to PTSD later
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: A proportion of people progress to PTSD, so follow-up at around a month identifies those whose symptoms persist beyond 1 month and who need reassessment and management as PTSD.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: The clinical features of an acute stress reaction largely mirror which disorder?
options: A specific isolated phobia of an object
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Acute stress reaction mirrors the PTSD symptom clusters (intrusion, avoidance, arousal, negative mood), but occurs acutely and often with especially prominent dissociation.

conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.question: Why is a benzodiazepine inappropriate for a patient with an acute stress reaction and insomnia after trauma?
options: They are far too expensive to be prescribed for insomnia anywhere in the NHS
They would resolve the acute stress reaction too quickly to allow adjustment
They cause dependence and sedation that impedes trauma-focused therapy
They are absolutely contraindicated alongside every class of antidepressant drug
They invariably precipitate a psychotic episode when given after any trauma
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.answer: They cause dependence and sedation that impedes trauma-focused therapy
conditions__PSYCHIATRY__Anxiety & Stress.explanation: Benzodiazepines are avoided after trauma: UK guidance says not to offer drug treatment to prevent PTSD, and they risk dependence and sedation that impedes trauma-focused therapy. Management is active monitoring, with trauma-focused CBT if symptoms are clinically important.
